Masataka Watanabe, a theoretical physicist, points out an unexpected identity between two-dimensional quantum gravity and the statistics of a growing interface. Jackiw-Teitelboim gravity is the workhorse toy model of quantum gravity, and the Kardar-Parisi-Zhang equation describes how rough surfaces grow. Watanabe connects them through two better-known systems: the double-scaled SYK model, whose Schwarzian limit captures the gravity side, and the weakly asymmetric exclusion process, whose fluctuations obey the growth equation.

The claim is precise. The path-integral measure that defines the Euclidean evolution between two end-of-the-world branes in the gravity theory is exactly the stationary measure of the KPZ equation on an interval with Neumann boundary conditions. Correlation functions match as well. Correspondences of this kind matter because each side's hard questions can sometimes be answered with the other side's tools.
arxiv-2511-02829:
Alex Takeda proves a structural property of a certain dioperad, an algebraic object that encodes operations with several inputs and outputs. The dioperad in question encodes bialgebras with a product, a coproduct of a shifted degree, and a rank three cyclic tensor, all obeying a deformed form of the balanced infinitesimal bialgebra rule. His 2025 paper shows this dioperad is Koszul, a strong duality property.

The proof studies special subcomplexes of the assocoipahedra built by Poirier and Tradler. Those parts match a class of special differentials on the complex projective line, which Takeda calls cloven Strebel differentials. The geometric picture controls the shape of these parts. That control forces key cohomology groups to vanish, which is what the Koszul property requires.
arxiv-2511-03029:
Kajol Kulkarni and seven colleagues report how a European exascale project learned to measure the energy its simulations burn. Supercomputing faces rising power bills as machines grow. Their 2025 paper shares the CEEC project's experience across major European systems, reviewing ways to measure energy and the metrics worth reporting, then testing real fluid flow codes.

Four programs ran on machines including LUMI, MareNostrum5, MeluXina, and JUWELS Booster, on both standard and graphics hardware. The team compared the energy a job used against the time it took. Graphics hardware and mixed precision math cut energy use while keeping results accurate. The authors urge centers to make energy data easy to gather, so users can act on it rather than guess.
arxiv-2511-03229:
Yong Huang and co-authors present U-Print, a method that can identify smartphone users just by watching encrypted Wi-Fi traffic. Earlier attacks could tell which app was open, but they could not tell who held the phone. U-Print works passively, reading frames in the air without joining the network at all.

People favor different apps and tap through them in different ways, and those habits leave distinct traffic patterns. U-Print reads those patterns with tailored neural networks, then groups behavior traces to name the user. In tests across three real settings, it reached high accuracy for user guesses and also named most apps and actions correctly. The result shows how much private habit can leak from traffic that looks locked.
arxiv-2511-03929:
NVIDIA, credited as the collaboration name in the arXiv record, introduces Nemotron Nano V2 VL, a vision-language model aimed at document understanding, long video comprehension, and reasoning. It succeeds an earlier eight-billion-parameter Nemotron vision-language release and claims gains across vision and text domains.

The model builds on a hybrid Mamba-Transformer language model and adds token reduction methods that raise throughput on long documents and video. Architecture, datasets, and training recipes all changed from the prior version. Checkpoints are released in three numeric formats, and large parts of the datasets, recipes, and training code are shared, making the release unusually open for a corporate model report.
arxiv-2511-04329:
Jonas Berx, writing alone, studies optimal lossy compression of a fluctuating stochastic signal into a few discrete readout states. The signal drives transition rates of a two-state system. The encoder must trade retained mutual information about the system's state against a fixed encoding cost, tracing a Pareto frontier between the two.

Genetic algorithms map those optimal trade-offs numerically. Fronts are concave in places and show convex intrusions split by first-order transitions in the best protocol elsewhere. A high-rate expansion finds a universal cube-root law for optimal threshold density, mixing the prior with Fisher information. Non-Gaussian signals can beat Gaussian stand-ins outright, needing fewer states for the same information.
arxiv-2511-04429:
Pablo Gómez and three colleagues built Cutana, a tool for cutting small images from huge sky surveys. The Euclid mission's first quick release holds thirty million sources over about sixty-three square degrees. Later releases will reach petabyte scale, and older tools cut one source at a time.

Cutana pulls batches of cutouts at once using fast array operations. It schedules work to fit the memory at hand and runs locally or in the cloud. Output can be saved as FITS or Zarr files, with several common ways to scale brightness. In tests on the Euclid data, it beat the standard Astropy tool in every case.
arxiv-2511-04529:
Kalyan Banerjee and two colleagues construct imaginary biquadratic fields with large class groups. Class groups measure how far a number field sits from unique factorization. Finding whole families where that failure is large is a delicate task.

The team builds two distinct families, each with infinitely many members. Elliptic curves and their quadratic twists produce the first family. The second mixes elliptic and hyperelliptic curves in its construction. Key inputs come from results by Soleng and by Banerjee and Hoque. Infinite families like these give number theorists firm ground for testing claims about class group growth.
arxiv-2511-04629:
Saswata Mandal and his co-author propose pair mixing as the source of time-reversal breaking in a layered superconductor. Experiments on 4Hb-TaS2 and related hybrids show spontaneous breaking, hinting at chiral superconductivity. Yet its transition temperature matches plain forms that show no such signal.

Their state mixes a dominant conventional s-wave pairing channel with a weaker chiral p-wave one. A finite Cooper-pair momentum couples the two channels together. Symmetry analysis, statistical mechanics, and quasiclassical theory support the picture. Pair mixing could explain exotic signals appearing without any change in the basic transition temperature.
arxiv-2511-04729:
Rucha Deshpande leads nine authors hunting shape artifacts in synthetic medical images. Synthetic data can ease data scarcity for training clinical models. Unexamined fakes, though, may carry distortions that hurt performance and real-world use.

Their knowledge-based detector works in two stages. A new feature extractor studies angle gradients along anatomical boundaries in each image. An isolation forest then flags images whose shape features look abnormal. Tests on two synthetic image sets show the method catches network-made shape flaws. Screening synthetic data this way could stop quiet artifacts from reaching clinical model training.
arxiv-2511-05029:
Sakiko Obuchi and co-authors report ID830, a radio-loud quasar at redshift 3.4 that shines bright in X-rays. It is the most X-ray bright radio-loud quasar found in the eROSITA final survey field of the equator.

Data from radio, infrared, and optical bands show a dust-red quasar with a steep X-ray slope. From a magnesium line width, the team weighs its black hole at a few hundred million solar masses. Its glow hints at an Eddington rate above the norm, which may mark a short shift phase in how such black holes feed.
arxiv-2511-05829:
Somnath Dutta leads a large team using the ALMA observatory to rank three very young protostars by age. Jets from protostars reveal how far star formation has run in each core. The team picked the three sources with the shortest jet timescales, marking them among the youngest known.

They mapped several molecules and dust emission at two resolutions, tracing where molecules freeze out or boil off the dust. One source shows a warm envelope and signs of a more advanced stage. Another has no dense central structures, suggesting it is younger. The third, with a cool envelope and compact emission, looks youngest of all. Comparing the three orders the earliest steps of star birth.
arxiv-2511-05929:
Jiaxuan Li and co-authors speed up masked autoencoders, a self-teaching method where an image model hides part of an image and learns to rebuild it. Random hiding works well but takes many training rounds, and the vision transformer inside uses its parameters poorly because every layer keeps one fixed resolution.

Their system, CoMA, hides image parts in a complementary pattern so every pixel gets sampled evenly across rounds. A new hierarchical transformer varies its attention windows dynamically, cutting parameters and compute while learning finer detail. Pretrained on a standard image set, their model matched the usual approach using only a small share of the training rounds. Each round also ran faster, which the authors cite as proof of better learning per step.
arxiv-2511-06329:
Fei Li and Junjie Cao compare three supersymmetric models to see which can naturally host light dark matter. The candidates are the minimal model, its Z3-symmetric next-to-minimal extension, and the general next-to-minimal model. All must satisfy limits from dark matter abundance, the LUX-ZEPLIN 2024 experiment, Higgs data, and collider searches.

Only the general model naturally fits dark matter lighter than one hundred giga-electronvolts, with a mainly singlino-like candidate. Its advantage is separating the interactions that set the relic abundance from those governing direct detection. Two mass orderings are studied; one allows a light higgsino scale with little tuning, while the other needs a much heavier scale and more fine-tuning.
arxiv-2511-06529:
Hongnan Ma and co-authors generate counterfactual explanations for decisions made on multivariate time series. A counterfactual shows what minimal change would flip a model's verdict, but time series explanations built by swapping in chunks from other examples often look unrealistic. Generative alternatives fix realism yet hug the decision boundary, so a small model change can void the explanation.

TriShGAN works inside a generative adversarial framework with triplet loss added for distance learning. Explanations stay close to the original series, resemble the desired outcome class, and keep a safer margin from the boundary. A shapelet extractor picks the most telling segments of the series, keeping the suggested changes sparse and readable.
arxiv-2511-06629:
Changfeng Gui and co-authors prove that fully localized solitary waves of the three-dimensional capillary-gravity water wave problem are conditionally stable. These waves sit in finite depth under strong surface tension and were built by a non-variational reduction method, so they are not energy minimizers. Standard stability machinery, which leans on minimization, cannot be applied directly.

The proof adapts the Grillakis-Shatah-Strauss framework through Mielke's approach to bridge the gap between the well-posedness space and the energy space. Spectral analysis of the linearized dynamics does the core work, supported by careful handling of the Hamiltonian structure set by the energy and momentum functionals. Orbital stability follows under the stated conditions.
arxiv-2511-06829:
Zhun-Yong Ong studies how sound-like vibrations, called phonons, travel through a chain of atoms whose masses vary randomly because of isotopic defects. In such a disordered chain, repeated scattering normally makes transmission fall off exponentially with distance. Ong asks whether the placement of the defects, rather than their number, can change that fate.

Using the static structure factor as a guide, he gives a systematic recipe for arranging defects to suppress or enhance scattering inside a chosen frequency window. Numerical tests show transmission rising toward transparency or dropping toward opacity in that window, confirmed by changes in how localized the vibrations are. The idea may extend to layered substances built to pass or block heat-carrying vibrations.
arxiv-2511-07129:
Seungeon Lee, Soumi Das, Manish Gupta, and Krishna P Gummadi make collections of LoRA adapters usable on inputs whose domain is unknown in advance. LoRA fine-tunes large language models cheaply, but each adapter is trained for one task, while real traffic spans many domains. Current ways to combine adapters at inference time need labeled data or extra task-certain training, which is expensive at scale.

Their system, LoGo, is training-free: it selects and merges adapters per input instance. It uses signals from a single forward pass through the adapters to judge relevance and set each adapter's contribution on the fly. Across five NLP benchmarks, twenty-seven data sets, and three model classes, LoGo beat training-based baselines on some tasks by up to 3.6 points and stayed competitive elsewhere, without sacrificing inference throughput.
arxiv-2511-07329:
Yash Mittal, Dmitry Ignatov, and Radu Timofte generate neural network designs from fractal templates instead of searching for them expensively. Neural design search is powerful but computationally heavy. Their FractalNet system defines a structured space of convolutional networks through recursive fractal patterns, systematically varying fractal depth, column width. Layer configurations, with a generator producing candidates, a template module enforcing the recursive multi-path structure, and a runner handling training and logging.

Over twelve hundred distinct designs were generated and tested automatically on the CIFAR-10 image benchmark, trained in PyTorch with mixed precision and gradient checkpointing. Fractal designs trained stably and performed competitively, averaging sixty to seventy percent validation accuracy with a peak above eighty percent after only five epochs. The authors pitch recursive structure as an interpretable, resource-efficient route to design exploration.
arxiv-2511-07529:
Subhash Bose and colleagues report a rare supernova with no visible home galaxy. Supernova 2021hem is a Type Ia event, the kind used as cosmic distance markers. Its peak brightness and missing second infrared hump match the overluminous 2003fg-like subclass, which breaks standard patterns.

Slow light curves and early carbon absorption lines support that label. A fireball fit dates first light about sixteen days before peak, yet a detection came even earlier than the fireball rise. That early glow does not fit companion or surrounding gas interaction. Shallow or hidden hosts remain possible. Odd cases like this test explosion models.
arxiv-2511-07729:
Neil Sehgal, Hita Kambhamettu, and Sai Preethi Matam design mental-health chatbots with Indian teenagers, not just for them. Stigma and scarce professional help shape how adolescents seek support. A survey of three hundred sixty two teens plus fourteen interviews map their habits and wishes.

Teens report low shame about themselves but high social stigma around them. They prefer typing to voice, carry smartphones widely, yet rarely use mental health apps. Privacy, emotional warmth, and local content matter, while current bots lack personalization. A design-tensions framework names the trade-offs builders must balance, offering guidance grounded in lived teen experience.
arxiv-2511-07829:
Manu Sebastian, Sreenath Balakrishnan, and Safvan Palathingal engineer culture dishes whose stiffness cells can feel changing live. Cells respond strongly to substrate mechanics, but standard tunable dishes cannot change traits mid-experiment. Compliant parts offer a switch instead.

A compliant switch flips the substrate between positive and negative Poisson response, with size of effect that can be set. Stiffness between two points can switch from near zero toward set limits. Living cultures could then experience varied mechanics in one run. Dynamic substrates open experiments on how cells react when their world changes under them.
arxiv-2511-07929:
Yihang Wu and Ahmad Chaddad federate a vision-language model across hospitals without pooling patient scans. Medical image models need diverse data, but privacy law and ethics bar central collection. Federated learning trains locally and shares updates, though hospital data differ and vision-language models are heavy.

FedMedCLIP adapts CLIP for federated medical classification with a masked feature adaptation module that trims communication and compute. Heterogeneous scanners and populations are the explicit target. Resource-efficient federation matters because many hospitals run modest hardware. A shared model that respects both privacy and budgets could bring advanced image classification to smaller clinics.
arxiv-2511-08029:
Aarush Sinha, Pavan Kumar S, Roshan Balaji, and Nirav Bhatt improve biomedical search by mining hard negative examples from citations. Retrieval models learn best when near miss documents are clearly marked as wrong answers. In medicine those near misses are hard to spot by similarity alone, since related papers look alike.

Cited papers share context with a source paper without being duplicates, so they make natural hard negatives. Using citation links from twenty thousand PubMed articles, the team fine tunes small GTE retrievers. The models gain on in domain and out of domain tests, including long tailed topics, with little extra training.
arxiv-2511-08129:
Giovanni Romano and Raffaele Barretta offer a critical review of basic ideas in continuum mechanics, the theory of soft materials. Landmark mid century volumes by Truesdell and his partners set the field language, and their depth earned wide respect. The authors argue that this respect shielded several delicate basic notions from the careful checking they needed.

Followers, they contend, spread unsatisfactory formulations through the later literature. A missing engineering viewpoint made the problem worse. Using a geometric approach in four dimensional Euclidean spacetime, Romano and Barretta aim for clarity in notions, methods, and results that the usual approach cannot reach, and they catalogue errors they find.
arxiv-2511-08329:
D-M Mei and co-authors design a germanium based detector that could sense low mass dark matter through tiny phonon signals. Their phonon to charge transducer joins a slow phonon crystal region with radio frequency quantum point contact readout, cooled to four kelvin. A calibrated collection model folds together guiding, survival, and detection of primary phonons to give corrected energy thresholds in a very low range.

Background estimates use nanosecond timing gates and frequency band power windows. A one hundred gram module, under standard halo assumptions, projects sensitivity to dark matter scattering on electrons and nuclei below cross sections reached before. Heavy and light mediator cases are both covered, with systematic uncertainties and a staged path to larger exposures.
arxiv-2511-08529: Andrew Li and Hua Wang count colored compositions in which only some parts may receive colors, with the allowed colors depending on where a part sits in the composition. A composition is an ordered way of splitting a number into parts, and coloring adds a further layer of counting choices. The authors obtain the counting sequences through generating functions. They also discuss connections to many other combinatorial objects, supplying combinatorial arguments for those observations and generalizing them beyond the cases first noticed.
arxiv-2511-08629:
Jian Guo and four co-authors study online learning for systems that report only binary outcomes, where an attacker may tamper with the data stream. Offline methods cannot keep up with live control loops, so the team builds recursive estimators that update with each new observation.

A first-order gradient method handles the basic case, and a second-order quasi-Newton method converges faster without needing persistent excitation, a condition feedback systems rarely meet. Versions cover both known and unknown tampering strategies, and the estimates are proven to converge almost surely. The second-order method extends to adaptive control with a stated tracking error bound. Simulations and a vehicle emission control test confirm the methods resist tampering and sharpen detection of excess-emission events.
arxiv-2511-08929:
Q. Qian and five co-authors write simulation code for next-generation laser-plasma work. Their particle-in-cell algorithm tracks the spin of particles and the polarization of light inside strong-field quantum electrodynamics. The newest laser facilities accelerate particles to near light speed within microns and push fields toward the quantum critical limit.

The extension, built into the OSIRIS framework, resolves QED emission processes by spin and polarization. It does not average over them. That matters because the coming experiments aim to measure exactly those traits. The authors lay out the theory, then describe how the code was built and checked. Only ab-initio modeling this complete can capture the coupled electromagnetic, relativistic, and quantum processes at once.
arxiv-2511-09029:
Leonie Böhlke and two co-authors map how listeners perceive concert room acoustics without asking them for words. Instead of rating scales, music is convolved with measured binaural room impulse responses, and listeners judge similarities between the results, letting multidimensional scaling reveal the hidden axes of perception.

Five perceptual dimensions emerge from the scaling. Each one lines up with a measurable acoustic quantity: echo density, fractal correlation dimension, roughness, loudness, and early decay time. The method sidesteps two older habits, matching measures to experts' memories of halls and hunting correlates for bipolar rating scales. Because the dimensions come from the listeners' own similarity judgments, the authors present the approach as a cleaner route to what audiences actually hear in a room.
arxiv-2511-09129:
Jordan Moncrieff and four co-authors ask whether the gas discs around feeding black holes in galactic centers can marry two black holes of wildly unequal mass. The gravitational wave event GW190814 paired a twenty-three solar mass black hole with a companion under three solar masses, a ratio isolated binary evolution struggles to produce.

Suites of N-body simulations, coupling a self-consistent disc torque model with a regularized code carrying post-Newtonian terms, map the outcomes of encounters inside active galactic nucleus discs: captures, mergers, and resonant dances. Analytic models then tie capture and merger rates to local disc properties across all mass ratios. Capture probability follows a log-Gaussian law in a single governing parameter, the ratio of libration time to resonance crossing time. A low-luminosity galactic nucleus turns out to be a plausible birthplace for GW190814 itself.
arxiv-2511-09229:
Valery V. Ryzhikov studies weighted averages along flows in ergodic theory, the mathematics of systems that mix over time. He considers homothetic averages and more general weighted ones for dynamical flows. The work sharpens a result of Kozlov and Treshchev on nonuniform averages for ergodic flows.

Ryzhikov allows absolutely continuous convolutions of singular weights, widening the averaging schemes covered. From these convergence results he defines a notion called almost mixing, stated through homothetic weighted averages. He gives an example of a flow that is almost mixing without actually mixing. He also proves that rigid flows, which periodically return near their start, are never almost mixing.
arxiv-2511-09329:
Andreas Konstantin Kruff and four co-authors release Sim4IA-Bench, a benchmark suite for judging how well user simulators imitate real searchers. Simulation promises cheaper evaluation of search systems, but the field lacked shared measures and data. The suite grows out of a shared task at the Sim4IA workshop held with SIGIR 2025.

The dataset holds 160 real search sessions from the CORE search engine. For 70 sessions, up to 62 simulator runs predict the user's next query or utterance, split across two tasks. The suite also introduces a new measure for scoring next-query predictions. Beyond benchmarking, it supports studies of query reformulation, intent drift, and interaction-aware retrieval evaluation.
arxiv-2511-09729:
Qian-Ze Zhu, Paul Raccuglia, and Michael P. Brenner teach one neural model to emulate many partial differential equations, including equations it never saw in training. Numeric PDE solving is costly, and learned surrogates usually specialize in one equation with fixed settings. Their approach instead conditions the model on a vector encoding the equation's terms and coefficients.

Four modeling methods are compared as baselines, trained on a family of 1D equations from the APEBench suite. The approach performs strongly on held-out parameter values. It stays stable beyond the training time window and extends to an entirely unseen equation, they report. Data and code are public, supporting a broader push toward automated scientific software.
arxiv-2511-10029:
Jiangshu Du, Wenpeng Yin, and Philip Yu propose ScaleFormer, a plug-and-play way to give pre-trained encoder-decoder transformers a long memory. Standard self-attention grows quadratically with length, which blocks long documents, and efficient variants usually demand new architectures plus costly retraining. ScaleFormer instead cuts a long input into overlapping chunks and builds a compressed, context-aware representation for the decoder.

Its fusion trick is parameter-free: each chunk's boundary representations are enriched with cumulative context vectors gathered from every chunk before and after it. That gives the model a sense of the document's overall flow while keeping complexity linear. On long-document summarization the method proved highly competitive with, and often better than, state-of-the-art systems, without architectural changes or external retrieval.
arxiv-2511-10329:
Sunil Chandra, Pankaj Kushwaha, Pranjupriya Goswami, and Michael Zacharias dissect more than a decade of multi-wavelength data on the blazar CGRaBS J0211+1051. They hunt the origin of its high-energy emission. Two major gamma-ray flares, in 2011 and 2019, came with brightness in other bands, yet some optical outbursts had no gamma-ray counterpart. The source's X-ray spectrum is unusually soft for its class, and its ultraviolet and optical spectrum does not extrapolate cleanly into X-rays.

Modeling four broadband spectral energy distributions in quiet and flaring states, purely leptonic scenarios struggled against the steep optical-ultraviolet shape. Lepto-hadronic models fit better. The hadronic reading makes the blazar a candidate neutrino emitter and potentially bright above ten TeV, a test bed for multi-messenger jet physics.
arxiv-2511-10429:
Wouter Jongeneel writes on attractors in dynamical systems, the sets toward which a system's motion settles over time. When attractors are compact, several rival definitions agree and the theory is fairly complete. Without compactness the picture blurs, and basic structural questions about closed attractors have stayed open.

Jongeneel characterizes when a closed, asymptotically stable attractor is a strong deformation retract of its domain of attraction. In plain terms, the whole basin can be continuously shrunk onto the attractor without tearing. The result works on locally compact metric spaces and needs no compactness of the attractor itself. It is meant to support a deeper structural study of feedback stabilization problems, where such attractors arise naturally.
arxiv-2511-10529:
H. Thankful Cromartie and seven co-authors report fifteen years of radio timing of the millisecond pulsar PSR J1231-1411, gathered with the Nançay and Green Bank telescopes. The pulsar is a prime target for the NICER X-ray telescope, and weighing it precisely would help reveal what neutron star interiors are made of.

The team targeted specific orbital phases to catch the Shapiro delay, a relativistic slowdown of pulses passing near the companion star. Both frequentist and Bayesian analyses give relatively weak mass constraints, around 1.9 solar masses for the pulsar with wide uncertainty, though the orbital inclination is pinned down much more tightly. Capping the allowed pulsar mass lowers the estimate somewhat, and the authors draw lessons for future high-precision mass campaigns.
arxiv-2511-10829:
Mikhail Masliaev, Dmitry Gusarov, Ilya Markov, and Alexander Hvatov test whether neural operators, models that learn to solve whole families of partial differential equations, can be pretrained once and transferred widely. Training these models is expensive, and transformer-based versions had previously been applied only to specific problems.

The team studies a general transfer learning setting: pretrain on simpler or mixed problems, then fine-tune elsewhere. Their experiments cover extrapolation to unseen physical parameters, absorbing new variables into a problem, and transfer from datasets containing several equations at once. The results show advanced neural operator designs can indeed carry knowledge across different PDE problems effectively, a step toward all-purpose operators that do not start from scratch for every new physics task.
arxiv-2511-11029:
Özgür Akgün, Mun See Chang, and their colleagues tackle wasted search in solvers that work with abstract structures such as nested sets. Modelers write problems in high-level languages, but solvers need those structures recast in simpler forms first. Many problems also contain symmetries, and breaking them early can speed the search by a vast amount.

Standard symmetry breaking adds order rules that pick one member from each symmetric set. For abstract types, that route creates a huge number of complex rules that run poorly. The authors show a new partial method that breaks such symmetries in a better way. Their aim is faster solving without losing the gains symmetry breaking brings.
arxiv-2511-11529:
Luisa Mao and three co-authors introduce SPACER, a method that builds terrain costmaps telling off-road robots which ground is cheap or costly to cross. Good costmaps must handle new terrain types and also let operators re-rank surfaces quickly when a mission changes, two strengths earlier methods rarely combined.

SPACER trains on synthetic data to generalize to unseen ground, then adapts at test time through a scaled preference context that a user supplies. Tests on large aerial maps show it can reweight terrain costs on demand without retraining. For field robots in farming, rescue, or exploration, that mix of flexibility and reach could matter a great deal.
arxiv-2511-11929:
Ghani Imadouchene builds a symmetric bimetric cosmology, a universe described by two metrics at once, one leaning anti-de Sitter and one de Sitter, coupled through a scalar field. Bimetric gravity doubles geometry to enrich cosmic dynamics while hoping to keep the standard model's successes.

Starting from Einstein-Hilbert terms for both metrics plus an inter-metric potential, modified Friedmann and Klein-Gordon equations govern the pair. In the symmetric effective-fluid limit, the model reproduces the standard cosmology's main behavior with one small dynamical correction that fades with redshift, and Vainshtein screening keeps local gravity tests satisfied. The construction is offered as a minimal extension worth calibrating against data.
arxiv-2511-12029:
Nicholas Tetteh Ofoe, Weilun Wang, and Lei Wu determine how short a forecast horizon a battery operator can get away with. Model predictive control of energy storage re-plans constantly under volatile prices, and the plan is only as good as the price forecast, yet longer horizons cost computation and compound forecast error.

A trajectory-alignment definition sharpens the question: the minimum horizon is where every rolling decision matches the full-horizon global optimum. Their algorithm finds it exactly, where earlier methods gave only sufficient conditions and could ignore inconsistencies between successive control actions. Tests use real price data from a bidding zone. Storage assets earn money on timing, and knowing the shortest sufficient lookahead is money.
arxiv-2511-12329:
Arman Pourghorban and Dipankar Maity study a target defense game where intruders arrive one after another and a single defender must stop as many as possible. Both sides move with Dubins dynamics, meaning they turn like a vehicle with a minimum turning radius. Each intruder tries to breach the target perimeter, and the next appears at a random point on a circle once the last is caught or breaks through.

The defender's ending spot in one round becomes its start in the next, linking the rounds. The authors split each round into partial and full information phases. They use Dubins paths and guarding arcs to judge capturability. They then estimate capture rates for finite and endless sequences. Random trials check those rates.
arxiv-2511-12529:
Sanchaita Hazra, Doeun Lee, Bodhisattwa Prasad Majumder and Sachin Kumar run a randomized trial. It tests the value of AI help in scientific writing. That task demands precision, synthesis across modes and domain skill. The test focuses on writing abstracts. Experts are split into author and reviewer pools in a mock conference setup, with incentives that push authors to edit drafts to publishable quality.

The design varies two factors: whether the draft abstract was written by a human or a model, and whether that source is disclosed. Authors edit human drafts most, compared with undisclosed model drafts, guided in part by the higher perceived readability of model text. Once the source is revealed, editing effort converges across conditions.
arxiv-2511-12629:
Shiyun Lin studies learning in housing markets, the classic matching model where each agent starts owning a house and holds private preferences over all houses. The goal is an allocation in the core, where no group can all do better by trading among themselves. The model is widely studied, but usually preferences are assumed known.

Lin places the market in a multi-player bandit framework, where agents learn their preferences from random rewards over repeated rounds. A new measure, core regret, captures the market objective for each player. Both centralized and decentralized learning approaches are analyzed, with logarithmic regret bounds proved for each, and a matching lower bound for the decentralized case showing the rate cannot be improved in general.
arxiv-2511-12729:
Amirhossein Hassanzadeh and four co-authors build an uncertainty workflow for land surface temperature maps from the Landsat satellites. Current Landsat temperature products use a single-channel method, and their stated uncertainty is often too large because it leans on a cloud mask that flags clear pixels as cloudy. From Collection 3, a split-window method will produce the temperatures instead. That change needs its own uncertainty estimates, and this paper supplies them for Landsat 8 and 9.

Their workflow ties uncertainty to total precipitable water, the moisture in the air column. Since Landsat cannot measure that quantity directly, they train an XGBoost model to infer it from Landsat's thermal bands, using a MODIS product as reference, and reach high accuracy. Standard error propagation then turns the moisture estimate into per-product uncertainty. The result is a dedicated uncertainty chain matched to the new split-window temperatures.
arxiv-2511-12829:
Michael Chen and five co-authors run a controlled comparison of how particle physics foundation models should learn. Rival training objectives compete in the field, but they are usually tested inside rival systems, so wins are hard to attribute. Here one transformer encoder for particle clouds, one preprocessing pipeline, and one jet classification dataset are held fixed. Contrastive objectives, both supervised and self-supervised, masked particle modeling, and generative reconstruction are then trained under the same regimen and judged by one evaluation protocol.

The study separates what the objective contributes from what the surrounding machinery contributes, and it reports each method's strengths and limits. Targeted supervised changes to the architecture reached state-of-the-art benchmark scores. The authors offer the setup as a reference point with reproducible baselines, so future base-model work in particle physics can show cleaner progress.
arxiv-2511-12929:
Z.-H. Peng and twenty-eight co-authors present observations of supernova 2016iog, one of the fastest-declining Type II-L supernovae known. Their photometry and spectroscopy track the explosion from near peak, about fourteen days after it blew, through late phases. The supernova faded unusually steeply after a bright peak, and its early spectrum was a nearly featureless continuum, a sign that the blast was already crashing into material around the star. Broad hydrogen lines persisted throughout.

A late spectrum showed a double-peaked hydrogen feature, pointing either to dust forming in a cool dense shell or to unevenly distributed circumstellar material. The team argues the whole picture fits a red supergiant star wearing a low-mass hydrogen envelope, wrapped in thin surrounding gas that the supernova kept hitting. The study adds a well-documented extreme case to the small family of fast-declining hydrogen-rich supernovae.
arxiv-2511-13029:
Declan Jackson and three co-authors grade frontier language models on knowing, and on knowing that they do not know. AA-Omniscience asks six thousand questions drawn from authoritative academic and industry sources across forty-two economically relevant topics in six domains. Its Omniscience Index runs from minus one hundred to one hundred, jointly penalizing hallucination and rewarding abstention when uncertain, so a model that guesses wildly scores worse than one that stays silent. Zero means a model is right as often as it is wrong.

The results are humbling. Claude 4.1 Opus topped the ranking at four point eight, and only three models scored above zero at all. Leadership also changed by domain, with three different labs' models leading the six areas. For knowledge-critical work, choose models by domain performance and calibration, not reputation. .
arxiv-2511-13129:
Julien Marché and Seokbeom Yoon connect two invariants that knot theory and quantum topology each compute in their own language. Their objects are two-bridge knots, a tractable family labeled by two integers, and the adjoint Reidemeister torsion of such a knot, evaluated at parabolic representations. The authors establish an explicit formula relating that torsion to the Frobenius algebra. That algebra governs the signatures of the vector spaces produced by SU(2) topological quantum field theory at a root of unity.

Two applications follow. First, the sum of the inverse torsions is constant for every two-bridge knot. Second, along sequences of roots of unity of a certain form, the TQFT signatures behave asymptotically exactly as the Verlinde formula predicts. Such bridges let results proved on one side be spent on the other.
arxiv-2511-20229:
Ruffing, Petrov, Zillien, and Wendzel fingerprint malware hiding inside DNS traffic. Their 2025 paper applies locality sensitive hashing to covert channels. Malware abuses DNS lookups to chat with control servers. The hidden data rides inside subdomain names. Spotting traffic is easier than naming the culprit.

Subdomain sequences are hashed into similarity features. Similar inputs land in similar buckets by design. A random forest classifier reads those features. It separates malware families from benign traffic. It also infers what the malware is doing. Uploading, downloading, and idling leave distinct patterns. Accuracy beat prior approaches across several datasets. False positive rates dropped markedly at the same time. Modified and unseen malware samples were still caught. That robustness matters as malware mutates constantly. Idle traffic with low variance stays hard, they admit. Extra timing or meaning features may close that gap. Forensic attribution gains a practical new tool.
arxiv-2511-20329:
Haqq-Misra, Kopparapu, and Profitiliotis plan how to spot alien industry using Earth's own futures. Their 2025 paper maps technosignature searches onto ten Earth scenarios. The scenarios project our tech future a thousand years ahead. Each is self-consistent, spanning different development paths. Future telescopes need concrete targets to design against.

The Habitable Worlds Observatory opens the stepwise strategy. It could catch a carbon dioxide plus nitrogen dioxide pair. That pair signals burning and heavy industry. Up to eight of ten scenarios show it detectably. Radio follow-up could find directed narrow-band beacons. Two scenarios include such transmissions. The LIFE interferometer would probe mid-infrared fingerprints. CFC features appear in four scenarios there. One adds a fluorinated gas triple marker. Farm gases form a detectable triple in two scenarios. A solar gravitational lens mission could image surfaces. Flying a probe out remains the conclusive option.
arxiv-2511-20729:
Sean Bin Yang and five colleagues present in 2025 a tutorial survey of trajectory foundation models, a young field adapting the foundation-model idea to movement data. A trajectory is a timed sequence of positions, the digital trail left by a person, vehicle, or animal. Researchers now want the same train-once flexibility for trajectory tasks like travel-time estimation and path ranking.

The tutorial runs as a 90-minute lecture in four parts, from basic definitions through data types and learning methods to open problems. It sorts methods by data type: raw GPS points, map-matched road segments, grid-based paths, and mixes adding text or images. Learning approaches range from contrastive methods, which teach models by comparing similar and dissimilar paths, to augmentation schemes that manufacture extra training views. The authors close with challenges around building models that are robust, responsible, and transferable, the systematic map the field lacked.
arxiv-2511-20929:
Anton Baychkov, Markus Brill, and Jannik Peters ask in 2025 how much total welfare a famously fair budget rule must sacrifice. In participatory budgeting, citizens vote on projects and the Method of Equal Shares splits the budget evenly among voters, letting groups pool their shares to buy projects they approve. Fairness can cost efficiency: the chosen bundle may please fewer people overall than a greedy pick. The authors derive minimum welfare guarantees for the rule.

The guarantees cover DNS satisfaction functions, including the two standard utility measures: total cost of approved projects funded, and their count. Bounds depend on the cheapest and priciest projects, and collapse to the known multiwinner guarantee when all costs are equal. The bounds are asymptotically tight among rules meeting a strong proportionality axiom, so no fairer-style rule can promise more welfare. With wildly varying costs, they also show, no meaningful guarantee exists for any rule.
arxiv-2511-21029:
Kaixing Yang and colleagues present in 2025 FlowerDance, a music-to-dance generator built for speed as much as beauty. Diffusion-style dance models need many sampling steps, leaving no compute headroom for high-fidelity 3D rendering in live applications. FlowerDance uses MeanFlow, learning the average velocity of the motion trajectory so a dance can be sampled in only a few steps. Physical consistency constraints pull each step back toward plausible human motion, with reconstruction, velocity, and joint-position losses.

The backbone is BiMamba, a sequence model whose cost grows linearly with length rather than quadratically like attention, fused with music through channel-level cross-modal mixing. Generation is non-autoregressive, and users can edit motion interactively. On the AIST++ and FineDance benchmarks, FlowerDance topped prior methods on motion quality and on efficiency alike, including inference speed and memory use. The target is real-time virtual performers and choreography tools.
arxiv-2511-21329:
Chien-Hua Chen extends a classical counting tool into higher rank in a 2025 paper on Drinfeld modules, the function-field cousins of elliptic curves. Modular polynomials encode when two such objects are linked by an isogeny, a structure-preserving map, and for rank two they are well understood. For rank three and above, even writing down the right bivariate polynomial was unclear, a gap earlier work by Breuer and Rück framed but did not close computationally.

Chen gives an explicit procedure to construct the self-isogenous modular polynomial for Drinfeld modules of rank at least three with complex multiplication. For the prime ideal generated by T, he provides a computing algorithm. For the ideal generated by T squared plus T plus 1, he proves an explicit degree bound. He also formulates a generalized volcano structure for the isogeny graph, layered like a crater, and proves it appears for these modules.
arxiv-2511-21529:
Jasper De Witte and twelve coauthors stamp quantum light sources onto a photonic chip with factory-grade reliability, in 2025. Scalable quantum photonics needs single-photon emitters inside low-loss circuits. The best emitters, indium gallium arsenide quantum dots, live in gallium arsenide, not in the silicon nitride platform favored for circuits. Their solution is micro-transfer printing, a pick-and-place tool that prints emitter waveguides onto the nitride chip.

De Witte and his coauthors report a processing yield of about 95 percent using a commercial printer, the reliability large circuits demand. Each emitter sits in a p-i-n diode, which quiets charge noise for near blinking-free output. The diode also tunes the emitter's wavelength with ordinary CMOS-level voltages, letting many dots be brought into mutual resonance despite fabrication scatter. The result is a credible route to chips carrying many quantum building blocks at once.
arxiv-2511-21629:
Anna Marklová, Ondřej Vinš, Martina Vokáčová, and Jiří Milička ask whether readers can tell machine-written Czech poetry from human work, in 2025. Most such studies use English, which dominates AI training data. Czech is a morphologically complex, low-resource Slavic language, a harder test of generative fluency. Native speakers judged poems and guessed each one's origin.

They guessed at chance: 45.8 percent correct on average, no better than coin flips, and neither poetry familiarity nor literary training helped. The twist is bias. Readers who believed a poem was AI-generated rated it worse, even though AI poems actually scored equal or better than human ones when judged blind. The more a reader liked a poem, the less accurately they assigned its authorship. Beliefs about who wrote a poem, the study shows, steer aesthetic judgment itself.
arxiv-2511-21729:
Single author Jithin Krishnan reports that in retrieval-augmented generation, how components combine matters more than how strong each one is, in 2025. RAG systems fetch documents before answering, and builders keep adding hybrid search, multi-model checking, and adaptive confidence thresholds. Krishnan tested each upgrade alone and together in a multi-agent setup.

The ablation study ran 50 queries: 15 answerable, 10 edge cases, and 25 adversarial. Deployed alone, adaptive thresholding, ensemble verification, and hybrid retrieval each gave zero improvement. Integrated properly, they cut abstention from 40 percent to 2 percent, a 95 percent reduction. The paper also unmasks a measurement trap: inconsistent verdict labels made safe behavior look like a 40 percent hallucination rate. Ensemble confidence ran very high at 0.988, so query-adaptive thresholds were needed to stop over-answering. Retrieval alone engaged in 40 percent of queries yet helped only when paired with stronger verification.
arxiv-2511-22229:
Wang, Cheng, Wu, and colleagues dub silent videos with a speech language model. Video dubbing must synthesize speech that matches the script, clones a reference speaker's voice. Lands syllables on the actor's lip movements; earlier systems stitched together lightweight specialist modules and sounded mediocre, while modern speech large language models sound excellent but ignore the video's timing. Their VSpeechLM bridges the two by teaching a speech LLM to take orders from the picture.

A text-video aligner first learns fine-grained correspondence between phonemes and lip movements, then emits an expanded phoneme sequence carrying explicit lip-synchronization cues, which the speech decoders consume as their prompt. In experiments VSpeechLM significantly outperforms previous visual text-to-speech methods on overall quality, speaker similarity, and synchronization metrics. The authors flag harder conditions, partially invisible lips and low-quality video, as the next frontier for the approach.
arxiv-2511-22329:
Beauville, a leading algebraic geometer in Nice, surveys when a family of geometric shapes varies as richly as it possibly can. A linear system is a family of hypersurfaces cut out by sections of one line bundle. It has maximal variation when a general member has the maximum possible number of moduli, meaning almost no two members are isomorphic. So the family genuinely explores the whole moduli space rather than tracing a thin slice of it. A simple differential criterion exists, but checking it in practice proves surprisingly hard.

Four expected settings get detailed treatment: hypersurfaces, double coverings of projective space, K3 surfaces, and abelian varieties. Beauville proves maximal variation outright for abelian varieties; the first three yield only partial results, and closing sections collect counterexamples marking the phenomenon's boundary. The survey maps what is known versus merely expected.
arxiv-2511-22729:
Labate and colleagues solve a practical blocker for AI agents using tools: answers too big to read. When a tool returns a huge output, it can overflow the model's context window and kill the task, while truncation or summarisation lose information scientific workflows genuinely need in full. Their method changes what the model handles: instead of raw data flowing through the context, tool results are stored in memory and the model manipulates pointers to them.

Tools are redefined to accept and return these memory references, so bulky payloads never enter the context and responses of any length stay usable without information loss. The method is validated on a real materials science application conventional workflows cannot execute. In a comparative experiment where both approaches succeed, the pointer workflow used roughly seven times fewer tokens than the traditional one, with faster execution.
arxiv-2511-22829:
Tian and Lin build a lane-changing planner treating safety as a guarantee rather than a hope. Their pipeline starts with dynamic risk fields, maps scoring collision risk from surrounding vehicles, capturing static obstacles and velocity-dependent danger. It then generates time-varying convex feasible spaces, regions certified to satisfy kinematic limits and stay collision-free as traffic moves.

Inside them, a constrained iterative Linear Quadratic Regulator optimises smoothness, control effort, and risk exposure over a finite horizon while keeping strict feasibility. In simulations it beat traditional approaches on safety and efficiency together: collision-free lane changes over 28.59 metres in 2.84 seconds, cutting distance and time by 32.4 and 61.0 percent against artificial-potential-field and model-predictive-control baselines in the reported comparison. In dense roundabouts it kept larger margins, a minimum distance of 4.23 metres, lower jerk, smoother curvature, a 99.2 percent success rate, and 12.3 millisecond computation.
arxiv-2511-22929:
Padó and Thomas test how far vision-language models get at reading paintings as art historians do: emotionally. Emotion is central to art but is realised abstractly, changes historically, and leans on symbols whose reading takes expertise. They presented 38 artworks to three models, a LLaVA-Llama system and two Qwen models, with four question sets: content, emotional content, how emotions are expressed, and emotion symbols.

The models recognised content well and identified which emotions a work depicts and how they are expressed, independent of period and style. The Qwen models showed more detailed art historical knowledge than LLaVA-Llama. Performance was best on concrete images and failed on abstract or symbolic ones: recognising emotion symbols remained fundamentally difficult, demanding long inference chains, and the models gave inconsistent answers to related questions. The authors see cataloguing and accessibility description as uses, with experts still reviewing the output.
arxiv-2511-23029:
Inui and colleagues build a text-guided generator that paints realistic textures onto digital terrain, the surface coloring used in games and film previsualization. The hard part is fidelity: the painted ridges, valleys, and land cover must follow a supplied elevation map, called a DEM, rather than inventing their own hills. And hand-painting such maps is slow, labor-intensive work.

Their pipeline, Geodiffussr, uses flow matching, a generative method related to diffusion, and injects elevation features into its network at several resolutions, a step they call multi-scale content aggregation. Against a version without that step, image quality scores improved sharply, with FID falling by 49.16 percent and LPIPS by 32.33 percent in their tests, while the height-appearance mismatch dropped close to zero. They also release a worldwide training set pairing elevation maps with Sentinel-2 satellite images and written captions of the visible land cover.
arxiv-2511-23129:
Mamonova and colleagues built a model of flares on young M dwarfs, the magnetically violent stars that host many Earth-sized planets. Flare ultraviolet light can erode a planet's atmosphere or help start prebiotic chemistry. Their Young M Dwarfs Flare model combines radiative-hydrodynamic simulations of the stellar atmosphere with beams of high- and low-energy electrons, the energy-deposition picture.

The model reproduces the brightening of the continuum in the TESS telescope's band and in the far-ultraviolet A range across flares of many sizes. It misses the blue continuum rise in the far-ultraviolet B segment, a gap for future work. It also matches the energy released in optical and ultraviolet light. The team finds that flare frequency distributions for young M dwarfs follow a statistical law, a two-coefficient broken power law. The module uses it to generate synthetic flare populations.
arxiv-2511-23329:
Palma-Amestoy and Provenzi recast color enhancement algorithms, the filters that fix contrast and color casts in photographs. As an optimization problem guided by how human vision actually works. Rather than hand-designing another algorithm, they write down basic requirements that any perceptually inspired energy functional should satisfy. Exhibit an explicit class of functionals meeting all of them, and single out three members of basic interest for detailed study.

Minimizing such a functional turns out to balance two opponent mechanisms. A local nonlinear contrast boost and a control keeping pixel values dispersed sensibly around middle gray and around the original image. The family also reunites famous models, since one member reproduces the ACE algorithm and another amounts to a symmetrized Retinex. And the authors cut the computation from quadratic in the pixel count to nearly linear, proving stability and existence of minima along the way.
arxiv-2511-23429:
Tang and colleagues introduce Hunyuan-GameCraft-2, a generative world model that lets players steer a generated video game world with free-form natural language instructions instead of only fixed keyboard actions. Built on a 14 billion parameter image-to-video mixture-of-experts foundation model, it also accepts keyboard and mouse signals. And a text-driven injection mechanism gives fine-grained control over camera motion. Character behavior, and environment dynamics in real time.

To train it, the team defines the concept of interactive video data and builds an automated pipeline converting large-scale unstructured text-video pairs into causally aligned training sets. Then evaluates on a new benchmark called InterBench. Instructions like open the door, draw a torch, or trigger an explosion produce temporally coherent, causally grounded video responses. And the model outperforms prior state-of-the-art systems across interaction fidelity, visual quality, and temporal coherence in their reported experiments.
arxiv-2512-00029:
Connected devices now run urgent tasks across small edge units, local hubs, and distant cloud servers. Andreas Kouloumpris and three co-authors present an optimization framework, in a 2025 study, for deciding where each task should run. The setting differs from standard edge computing because it often uses one sensing edge device paired with one hub.

The framework aims to assign work across these layers in a clean, streamlined way so demanding applications run well. Such applications need fast responses and careful use of limited local hardware. For system designers, the study offers a structured way to split tasks among edge, hub, and cloud rather than sending everything to one place.
arxiv-2512-00129:
Deep learning systems can flag breast cancer in mammograms, but they often fail on images unlike their training data. Jayan Adhikari, Prativa Joshi, and Susish Baral tackle that reliability problem in a 2025 study. Scans from other modalities or different equipment can lead to wrong detections and misdiagnosis.

Their approach filters out-of-distribution inputs with a ResNet50-based stage, then detects cancer with YOLO models. Explainability methods and domain adaptation are part of the design. The goal is a screening tool that stays dependable when hospital equipment and imaging conditions change, instead of performing well only in the lab. Reliability under changed conditions is the theme that runs through the whole design.
arxiv-2512-00229:
Neural networks often fail silently when given inputs unlike anything in their training data. Suhail, Afroz, and Sethi present TIE in 2025, a framework for detecting such out-of-distribution inputs. The name stands for training, inversion, and exclusion, its three main stages.

Dependable systems need to estimate uncertainty and flag unfamiliar samples in a unified way, because overconfident predictions can be dangerous. TIE is designed to stay visually interpretable while it decides. The work matters for medical, driving, and security systems, where recognizing the unknown is as important as classifying the known. Interpretability is built into the framework's name and design, not added afterward. Uncertainty estimates give downstream systems a principled way to abstain.
arxiv-2512-00829:
Md Mehrab Hossain Opi, Sumaiya Khan, and Moshammad Farzana Rahman study faster training for Bangla language models in a 2025 paper. Training such models takes heavy computing power and long hours. In Bangla natural language processing, access to high-end hardware is often limited, so costs bite harder.

The team tests automatic mixed precision training. That method does much of the math in a lighter numeric format, while keeping key steps precise. Done right, it speeds training and saves memory without hurting model quality. Their work checks whether those savings hold for Bangla tasks, which would help local researchers do more with modest machines.
arxiv-2512-01029:
Vladimir Dragović and David Kalaj construct minimal surfaces over special quadrilaterals in a 2025 math paper. A Pitot quadrilateral has two pairs of opposite sides with the same total length, a property first tied to tangent circles. Minimal surfaces are shapes that locally minimize area, like soap films.

The authors build Scherk-type minimal graphs over any Pitot quadrilateral, with a fully explicit framework. First they produce a harmonic map from the unit disk onto the quadrilateral. Its stretching is the square of a Möbius map fixed directly by the quadrilateral's vertices. Explicit formulas make these surfaces computable, not just provable.
arxiv-2512-01629:
Yumeng He and co-authors rebuild articulated objects from a single photo for simulation. Objects with moving parts fill homes and workplaces. Robots need sim-ready models of them, with part trees and joints. Hand modeling those assets is slow expert work.

Their frame, SPARK, uses vision-language knowledge to infer parts. It outputs physically consistent, kinematic part models. Each part gets a place in a hierarchy with motion limits. One-photo assets could stock training worlds for robots far faster than hand modeling allows. Vision-language priors supply part names and joint guesses, which cuts the need for motion capture rigs in building each new asset.
arxiv-2512-02329:
Software engineering may be heading toward teams where autonomous AI agents do the core building, guided by human-set norms. Hoa Khanh Dam and four co-authors sketch in 2025 a new class of software engineering agents powered by large language models and equipped with beliefs, desires, intentions, and memory.

Such agents would reason about their work in a human-like way rather than merely completing tickets. The paper envisions autonomous normative multi-agent systems, teams of agents that also follow shared rules of conduct. It is a position paper, mapping how human-AI development teams could be reorganized around agents as primary drivers.
arxiv-2512-02429:
Algebraic geometers simplify complicated shapes by running the minimal model program, a sequence of surgeries toward a canonical form. Donghyeon Kim and Dae-Won Lee study in 2025 how that program behaves on the generic fiber of a fibration whose fibers are mostly of log Calabi-Yau type.

The setting assumes that over a dense set of the base, each fiber is a mildly singular log Calabi-Yau space. What the program does on the typical fiber governs the geometry of the whole family. Results here feed the classification of higher-dimensional varieties, where fibrations are the main tool for taking shapes apart.
arxiv-2512-02629:
C. Ramos Almeida and a large team study dust around feeding black holes using the James Webb telescope. Type-2 quasars hide their central black hole and inner gas behind thick dust and gas. Mid infrared spectra can still probe the dusty torus, the donut shaped cloud doing the hiding.

Webb's MIRI instrument recorded spectra from the centers of five nearby quasars of this type. Silicate emission in those spectra constrains the torus shape and how radiation pushes back on it. Better torus models sharpen our picture of how black holes grow inside their dusty cocoons. Dust that glows in this way tells on the shape of the cloud that hides the hole at its heart.
arxiv-2512-03229:
A combined galaxy catalog can tighten cosmic growth measures. H. Zou presents such a measure in this 2025 work, using the maximum likelihood fields method. The work joins three DESI first-release sources into one analysis.

The combined catalog holds hundreds of thousands of galaxy redshifts. It also holds tens of thousands of peculiar velocity measures from two distance methods. Blending both kinds of data gives a fuller picture of how matter moves. The resulting growth rate constraint helps test models of gravity and dark energy. Blending catalogs also cross-checks distance methods against each other in one frame.
arxiv-2512-03729:
In May 2025, a small free-flying robot aboard the International Space Station was steered by a reinforcement learning policy. Samantha Chapin and colleagues from the US Naval Research Laboratory describe that experiment, named APIARY, in a 2025 robotics preprint. Their goal is autonomous assembly work in orbit, where robots must act without a human hand on the controls.

The team trained a control policy for the NASA Astrobee robot inside a physics simulator, using an actor-critic method called Proximal Policy Optimization. Training randomised target poses and mass distributions so the policy would cope with surprises. The paper walks through simulation tests, ground tests, and the flight run itself. The authors argue the flight run shows learned control can work in orbit. That is a step toward robots handling exploration and logistics tasks with less human guidance.
arxiv-2512-03829:
High-power proton cyclotrons feed applications such as accelerator driven systems, but tuning their beams by hand is slow and rarely optimal. M. Haj Tahar and a large team at the Paul Scherrer Institute report a first in a 2025 accelerator physics preprint. They deployed a reinforcement learning system to tune the Injector 2 cyclotron, a testbed for high-power operation.

Their framework pairs a tailored learning algorithm with live diagnostics and control. One physics-inspired trick, an overshoot strategy, cut magnetic field settling times nearly sixfold. Across a twelve-day campaign, the agent learned stable tuning policies within hours for each operating point, then ran overnight evaluations with low beam losses. Policies trained at low current still worked at far higher currents. The authors call it the first such demonstration on a high-power cyclotron, with lessons for future driver machines.
arxiv-2512-03929:
Quantum measurement is usually told as a story of an apparatus that must itself be treated quantum mechanically, spawning an endless chain of couplings. Dagomir Kaszlikowski and Pawel Kurzynski cut that chain in a 2025 quantum physics preprint. In their framework, a single qubit couples directly to a classical measurement bit, with no quantum apparatus in between.

The trick lies in how states and interactions are written. The qubit becomes a positive probability distribution spread over a pair of classical bits. The apparatus is one more classical bit. The interaction between them is a map that may use negative transition probabilities, even though every state stays positive. When this process acts, it produces a collapsed state and an outcome with exactly the probabilities quantum mechanics predicts. The nonclassical character of measurement, the authors argue, lives in the interaction itself.
arxiv-2512-04129:
Multi-agent systems let language models hand work to each other. Whatever an upstream agent says, downstream agents tend to trust and execute. Ruichao Liang and colleagues show how an attacker can ride that trust in a 2025 security preprint. Their topology-guided attack plants contamination at exposed edge agents. The system's own wiring carries it, hop by hop, to high-privilege agents.

The scheme combines reconnaissance of the agent topology, a model of how contamination propagates, and payloads wrapped in layers so they survive reinterpretation along the way. Success rates across three frameworks and five layouts ranged widely, and two real-world applications fell in most tested scenarios. The authors propose a defence, a topology-trust mitigation that blocked nearly ninety-five percent of these attacks in their tests. Their broader warning is that multi-agent security cannot be assessed one agent at a time.
arxiv-2512-04229:
Dark matter may have been made in the reheating era after inflation, cooked through a heavy mediator particle called a Z-prime. Stephen E. Henrich, Yann Mambrini, and Keith A. Olive map that production in a 2025 particle physics preprint. Three regimes, freeze-out, freeze-in, and ultra-relativistic freeze-out, shade smoothly into one another, and no study had covered all three for this portal.

The authors find much of the available parameter space sits in the ultra-relativistic regime. That holds for dark matter masses from keV to TeV, when the mediator weighs between about a TeV and a PeV. When the mediator outweighs both the dark matter and the reheating temperature, the mechanism robustly yields cold dark matter. Particles born hot cool down if freeze-out happens during reheating. Compared with standard freeze-in, the regime also tolerates stronger couplings and lighter mediators.
arxiv-2512-04529:
Xin Liang, Zhilin Zhang, Xiang Zhang, and co-authors present SlideGen, a team of AI agents that turns a research paper into a clean slide deck. Making slides is not just cutting text down. A presenter must pick a story, choose which figures and formulas to show, and lay pages out without crowding. Prior tools mostly picked text, leaving decks unbalanced and hard to follow. Their 2025 arXiv paper splits the job among specialist agents.

One agent plans the narrative outline. Others ground each claim in the paper's figures, tables, and formulas. A layout agent then composes pages with visual balance in mind. The agents pass drafts back and forth, much like a human team. The result aims for decks with a clear arc and tidy pages. Such a tool could save researchers hours before talks, while keeping the slides faithful to the source.
arxiv-2512-05029:
Amin Mosallanezhad and six co-authors show that lumpiness may be the missing ingredient in winds blown off accretion discs. Around white dwarfs and the black holes in galactic centers, gas spiraling inward can be pushed back out by starlight pressing on its spectral lines. In simulations, though, the light over-strips the gas of electrons, the push fades, and the wind dies — at odds with what telescopes see.

Using a standard shortcut, the team's new simulations treat the gas as clumped into small dense knots. They find that even modest clumping lowers the stripping, strengthens the push, and raises the outflow sharply. The clumpy winds produce the ultraviolet fingerprints missing from smooth models and can reprocess a large share of the disc's light. Since real winds are expected to be patchy anyway, clumping gives a physical way to square the theory with observation for both kinds of system.
arxiv-2512-05329:
Anqi Feng and eight co-authors present CATNUS, a tool for carving the thalamus into its component nuclei on brain scans. The thalamus is a relay hub whose individual nuclei serve distinct functions and are hit differently by neurological and psychiatric disease. Yet drawing their borders is hard. Many nuclei are tiny, contrast inside the thalamus is faint, and anatomy varies between people. CATNUS attacks the problem with a three-dimensional neural network given a sense of position.

Coordinate-aware layers help the network localize large and small nuclei across thirteen nuclei or groups. Pretrained versions accept the clinical scan types as well as quantitative maps, widening where the tool can run. Benchmarked against methods, CATNUS segments accurately, repeats reliably on rescans, and holds up on travelling-subject data gathered across scanners, field strengths, and vendors. The authors aim it at large-scale brain studies and clinical assessment alike.
arxiv-2512-06129:
Alexandros Efstratiou, Kayla Duskin, Kate Starbird, and Emma Spiro dissect a famous claim about Twitter's algorithm in the window after the ownership change but before the rebrand to X. Earlier work reported right leaning gains in the algorithmic feed. The boost replicates. The harder question is what traveled with it. The advantage, they find, was not necessarily politics itself. Those accounts posted more agitating content, and drew the owner's attention.

Legacy verified accounts actually lost exposure. The algorithm may run a behavior market, where outrage converts to reach. Reform should target incentives, not viewpoints. Platforms shape discourse by reward schedule.
arxiv-2512-06229:
Lucas Colucci and Marco D'Emidio prove a bound in Ramsey theory, the branch of math that looks for order hidden in large networks. Take a huge set of points joined by every possible link, and paint each link with a label from a prime sized cycle of numbers. Their question asks how big the set must be before some fixed tree like shape is forced to appear with labels that add to zero.

The authors show that, for any forest shape meeting a few plain conditions, the needed size grows in a straight line with the shape, not faster. Their bound links the count of points, the prime, and the edge count in one clean formula. Results like this sharpen what math knows about when neat patterns must show up inside large, wildly labeled structures.
arxiv-2512-06429:
Jaeyong Hwang, Ana Maria Rey, and their co authors turn the shaking of two atoms into a hybrid quantum device. The atoms sit in a laser trap, an optical tweezer, and interact with each other. Their motion can play the part of an oscillator, a quantum swing, while an internal state plays a qubit. By pulsing the trap in a steady rhythm and tuning how uneven its pull is, the team enacts a full set of operations on the swing, plus versions steered by the qubit.

That control can sense the faint magnetic pull between the atoms, reaching very small frequency shifts in seconds and finer ones in minutes across a grid of traps. The scheme gives labs a flexible handle on the motion of atom pairs. It suits studies where spins meet oscillators, and precise probes of the forces and traps around the atoms.
arxiv-2512-06529:
Md Abdullah Al Kafi, Walayat Hussain, and Raka Moni study why computing students often shrug off the non computing courses their degree requires. Required courses in other fields can fill seats without being seen as real computing knowledge. The authors call that gap a curricular legitimacy gap, and model two responses apart: devaluation, judging such courses needless, and integrative intention, the will to reuse what they teach later.

They surveyed computing undergraduates in Bangladesh and fitted their model with careful statistical checks, including thousands of resampled fits. Feeling burdened by the extra courses fed devaluation, and devaluation in turn cut the will to reuse the learning. Feeling the courses were useful worked the other way, both directly and by lowering devaluation. The model captured a large share of the spread in both responses. Degrees, they suggest, win students by cutting burden and showing clear use.
arxiv-2512-06729:
Priyankush Ghosh and five co authors release XODIAC, a fast model of the chemistry of exoplanet atmospheres, built for the Webb telescope era. Rich new spectra keep arriving, and reading them means simulating how starlight drives chemistry in a planet's air. Slow models bottleneck that work. XODIAC runs on graphics processors, solves one dimensional photochemistry, and carries a built in equilibrium solver plus an updated database of reaction data.

Three chemical networks ship with it, including a new house network linking hundreds of species through thousands of reactions. The team benchmarked the model on the well studied hot Jupiter HD 189733 b against two established codes. Agreement was excellent, and when the same network and starting state were used, the solving scheme itself barely mattered. The authors then revisited that planet's chemistry across all three networks, showing how the choice of network colors what telescopes should see.
arxiv-2512-06929:
MinCheol Jeon designs a forecasting model for time series that refuse to sit still. Real data drift, shift their averages, and carry patterns at several time scales at once, all of which break ordinary models. His architecture, AdaMamba, opens by cleaning each series: an adaptive block pulls out trends at multiple scales and rescales each channel, steadying what remains.

The cleaned sequence then passes through an encoder that chops it into patches and reads it with a Mamba-enhanced transformer. A mixture-of-experts layer lets different parts of the network specialize, catching both long-range links and quick local moves. A light head issues forecasts for several horizons ahead, and the removed trends are folded back in at the end. Tests against transformer baselines show steadier, more accurate predictions across varied data sets. The modular design also leaves room for versions that report uncertainty, not just single best guesses.
arxiv-2512-07029:
Yuan-Zhe Dai and co-authors assemble the largest catalog yet of planets in star clusters, places where stars are born together and share a known age. Cluster planets are precious because their ages are pinned down, letting astronomers watch planetary systems grow up. The team separates true open clusters from looser moving groups using a size criterion, then asks whether their planets differ.

Cross-matching the newest cluster lists with transit surveys yields a catalog of confirmed planets plus a larger set of candidates inside both kinds of group. The authors refit each group's structure and hunt for substructures with two clustering algorithms. Moving groups consistently host a higher share of planets than open clusters, especially giant hot Jupiters.
arxiv-2512-07429:
Nina Effenberger, Maxim Samarin, Maybritt Schillinger, and Reto Knutti wrote this 2025 climate science paper. It deals with Central Europe and the planning of wind and solar power. Planners need fine local climate detail, yet full regional models are costly and slow to run.

The team trains a machine learning emulator on older global and regional simulations. The emulator learns how coarse global fields map onto fine regional ones. Tested on newer global runs it had never seen, it still gives realistic local detail. With it, they study days when weak wind and dim sun strike together. Such energy drought days, their results suggest, are likely to grow less common in the future. The method offers a fast partner to full regional climate modeling efforts.
arxiv-2512-07529: Patrick Cabau wrote this 2025 mathematics paper, published in Italian, on a new geometric structure. He introduces the notion of a partial Jacobi manifold. The work sits inside the convenient smooth framework built by Frölicher, Kriegl, and Michor. Cabau gives explicit examples in both finite and infinite dimensions. He also analyses the characteristic distribution that comes with the structure. The paper closes by pointing to research directions that deserve further study.
arxiv-2512-07729:
Aidas Aglinskas and Stefano Anzellotti wrote this 2025 paper on how machines and people recognize actions. A video of an action carries two kinds of clues. The body's pose and motion form one stream; the background scene forms the other.

Networks trained on a large action dataset lean strangely on the second stream. Remove the body, and their accuracy barely drops at all. Remove the background instead, and they fall to chance level. Human viewers behave in the opposite, more balanced way. People read actions well from body alone and scene alone alike. Their body-only scores beat their scene-only scores by a clear margin. The brain, after all, keeps separate regions for bodies and for scenes. The authors copy that layout into a new network design.
