The text also serves as a tribute to Chatawate (Flame) Ruethaimetapat, a young scholar in the field who died in August 2024. The primer keeps the tools basic so new readers can follow the proof ideas.
arxiv-2601-18029:
Kengo Deguchi, Haider Munawar, and Runjie Song derive simple tests for when a swirling flow stays calm. Their 2026 preprint studies inviscid shear instability in axisymmetric flows. The base flows run in annuli and pipes. The authors seek plain criteria that say whether such a flow is stable or will break into disturbance. They treat both symmetric and non-symmetric disturbance types.

Their sufficient condition for stability sharpens a classical result. It builds on the second Kelvin-Arnold stability theorem. Simple, sound tests save heavy computation in design work. Flows in pipes and rings sit inside engines, reactors, and lab rigs, so the tests have wide reach.
arxiv-2601-18129:
Kunat Pipatanakul and Pittawat Taveekitworachai present Typhoon-S, an open effort to give smaller language communities their own large models. Their 2026 preprint notes a skew in the field. Top models are trained and tested mostly in high-resource languages like English and Chinese. They are also built by a few groups with huge compute and data. Sovereign models aim to break that dependence for other nations and tongues.

The authors describe a minimal, open post-training recipe. Minimal means the steps are kept few and clear, so others can copy them. Open means the results can be checked and reused. The work serves countries that want AI in their own language, on their own terms.
arxiv-2601-18429:
Corentin Barloy and three colleagues study how small logic rules can keep track of sets of words as they change. The frame is a live one: a word list is kept up to date while bits flip one by one. A rule set counts as fit if it can state, after each flip, which words still pass a fixed test. Past work showed the full set of plain word tests can be kept in this way.

The team sort the word tests into finer ranks. For each rank they ask what kind of maths the rules must hold to stay in step. Their ranks use forms from algebra, the study of sets with rules for join and swap. The work ties two fields that seem far apart: the shape of words and the shape of change. That tie may help in checks on live data streams.
arxiv-2601-19029:
An unnamed author argues that piano playing should be judged from sound, not just from note data. Scores in MIDI form list which notes were hit and when, but they miss the tone and touch that make playing expressive. The author instead uses audio foundation models, large models trained on sound itself.

Two such models, MuQ and MERT, feed a system that scores many sides of performance quality. The target list spans a wide set of traits that listeners hear. If sound based scores beat note based ones, teachers and exam tools gain a judge that hears what an audience hears.
arxiv-2601-19129:
Puzhen Wu and eight co-authors fix badly exposed photos with help from a vision language model. Poor exposure wipes out detail, shifts colors, and flattens contrast. Fixes face two snags. They ignore what each object in the scene is, which causes odd color shifts. And real photos rarely come with a corrected twin to learn from.

Their method is unsupervised and aware of scene meaning, guided by CLIP. Object aware fixes can treat sky, skin, and shadow in ways that suit each one. Work that needs no hand made ground truth can scale to the messy photos people truly take.
arxiv-2601-19229:
Benling Li and Wei Zhao report analytic facts on Finsler manifolds that break Riemannian habits. Finsler geometry lets distance depend on direction, a looser frame than the Riemannian one. In the Riemannian world, every flat Cartan-Hadamard manifold is just Euclidean space in disguise.

That sameness underlies the sharpness of key inequalities, like Hardy's and the uncertainty principle. On Finsler manifolds, the pair find phenomena with no Riemannian twin. Such surprises warn analysts about tools built for the classic setting. Those tools may fail, or change meaning, when direction starts to matter. The pair mark the exact spots where the old intuition gives way.
arxiv-2601-19729:
Aldo Gardini and Lorenzo Mori work on a measurement problem in public health. Health surveys sample few people in each small area, so direct estimates for those areas are noisy. Small area estimation borrows strength across areas to sharpen the numbers. The authors apply these methods to mapping smoking behaviour.

Their outcome data come from self-reports, which suffer from coarsening. People round answers and favour certain digits, blurring the true values. Ignoring that blur can bias the maps. The authors build a Bayesian two-part model that handles coarsened data directly. Better local estimates help target anti-smoking programs where they are needed most. The method suits other self-reported health measures too.
arxiv-2601-19829:
M. Khodas, Libor Šmejkal, and I. I. Mazin explore superconductivity in a newly recognised kind of magnet. P-wave magnets have no net magnetisation, yet their electron bands split by spin in a non-relativistic way. That combination resembles altermagnets, another recent class of magnetic materials. The spin polarisation in these systems points in a fixed direction across momentum space.

The authors discuss whether such magnets can host superconductivity, and of what kind. They call the possibility nonrelativistic-Ising superconductivity. Pairing in a spin-split band structure should differ sharply from ordinary superconductors. If realised, it could yield devices that marry magnetism with zero-resistance current. The paper maps the theoretical ground for experimentalists to test.
arxiv-2601-20029:
Enhyeok Jang and six colleagues cut the training cost of a quantum optimization algorithm. QAOA tackles combinatorial problems by alternating quantum operations tuned by classical parameters. Its multi-angle variant gives every Hamiltonian term its own parameter. That freedom improves answers with fewer layers, but the parameter count inflates classical training cost.

Their cyclic layerwise training scheme organises the optimization to tame that cost. Training proceeds layer by layer in a repeating cycle. The scheme aims to keep multi-angle quality while restoring practicality. Optimization problems from logistics to finance motivate the algorithm. Cheaper training decides whether such quantum methods ever leave the lab. The cost is paid in plain cash and time.
arxiv-2601-20329:
A. Rahmatinejad, T. M. Shneidman, and N. Jovancevic calculate level densities for two plutonium isotopes, split by parity. Level density counts how many quantum states a nucleus has at a given energy. The authors track the ratio between positive and negative parity across a broad range of shapes, from spherical to strongly deformed.

Their range covers both the ground-state shape and the second minimum, the fission isomer. They compare the energy at which the two parities reach equilibrium between these shapes. Such densities feed into models of fission and neutron capture, where the nucleus passes through its deformed states.
arxiv-2601-20429:
Junseo Lee and four colleagues present GRTX, an efficient ray tracing method for rendering scenes built from 3D Gaussians. Gaussian splatting renders scenes fast and with high quality, but most systems use rasterization, which projects shapes onto the screen. Rasterization has fundamental limits, such as trouble with reflections and complex light paths.

Ray tracing can handle those effects but is costly on Gaussian scenes. GRTX aims to make it practical. Efficient ray tracing would let Gaussian scenes gain realistic lighting and shadows while keeping their speed edge, a gain for games, simulation, and virtual production.
arxiv-2601-20529:
Julia Richter and a large team set out a practical framework of key performance indicators for multi-robot field tests on the Moon and other planets. Robots will prospect for resources such as ilmenite, rare earth elements, and water ice. Analog field trials pursue these goals, but their results are hard to compare because platforms and setups differ so much.

The authors propose shared indicators so trials can be measured on common ground. Common measures would let space agencies and teams learn from each other's tests instead of starting over. That speeds the path to robots that can scout the Moon reliably.
arxiv-2601-20829:
Minwu Kim, Safal Shrestha, and Keith Ross tackle a stall in training reasoning models. Their 2026 paper studies reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. That method has greatly improved the reasoning of large language models. But training stalls once problems become saturated. Saturated problems are ones the model now almost always solves. They stop teaching it anything new.

The authors name the core issue: informative failures are hard to reach. The learning signal lives in failed attempts, yet standard rollouts rarely produce them. Their fix is failure-prefix conditioning. Training starts the model from the front part of a failed attempt. From there, useful failures become common again. The method aims to keep hard training sets useful for longer.
arxiv-2601-20929:
Wendy Sun, Rohan Naidu, and a large team argue that the centers of Little Red Dots are a new kind of object. Their 2026 paper studies these compact red sources, seen by JWST in the early universe. Their central engines may be black hole stars. Such a star is an early stage of black hole growth wrapped in dense gas. The best evidence comes from a few sources.

In those sources, the host galaxy is fully outshone. Their spectra show steep Balmer breaks, a mark of dense gas. The title's sums state the claim: take away the host, and a black hole star remains. The authors propose one at the center of each Little Red Dot. If right, this rewrites how the first black holes grew.
arxiv-2601-21029:
Samuel Stanek and four co-authors study a flaw that dims a fast laser scanner. Their 2026 paper concerns electro-optical deflectors made from KTN crystals. These deflectors steer laser beams with unmatched speed. They serve laser-scanning microscopy and other applications. Their weakness is a limited deflection range. KTN devices offer some of the highest counts of resolvable spots. They work by fields from trapped electrons inside the crystal.

The paper examines photoionization in these deflectors. The light used lies in the near-infrared imaging window. Ionization by that light can disturb the trapped charge that steers the beam. Understanding the effect is key to wider, steadier scans. The study joins materials physics with instrument design. It helps builders of fast microscopes push their range.
arxiv-2601-21529:
Robert van der Klis, Ricardo Chávez Torres, Max van Spengler, Yuhui Ding, Thomas Hofmann, and Pascal Mettes build fast neural networks that live in hyperbolic space. That curved space suits data with tree-like structure, such as categories and family trees. A sound math base for networks in this space has been slow to arrive.

The authors give a formulation that is both efficient and faithful to the geometry. Their networks use the Lorentz model, prized for numerical stability. Fast, correct hyperbolic layers could lift tasks from language hierarchies to recommendation, where tree shapes are everywhere but flat models flatten them away.
arxiv-2601-21629:
Daniel Mills, Ifan Williams, Jacob Swain, Gabriel Matos, Enrico Rinaldi, and Alexander Koziell-Pipe teach a learner to order quantum circuit optimizations. Quantum toolkits ship many optimization passes, each well tested on its own. The order in which passes run, though, is left to the user or to a generic default.

The authors use reinforcement learning to compose pass sequences for each circuit. A good order for one circuit can be poor for another, so adapting per circuit beats one fixed recipe. Better ordering means smaller, faster circuits. That helps today's small quantum machines, where every saved operation counts.
arxiv-2601-21729:
A.Ya. Maltsev studies whether extremely complex conductivity diagrams can arise in metals with cubic symmetry. The analysis uses the nearly free electron approximation, a standard first model of electrons in a crystal. Conductivity diagrams map how current responds as conditions vary.

Estimates show that ultra-complex diagrams need the Fermi level to land in very narrow energy windows inside the conduction band. Such windows are rare, which explains why the wildest diagrams are seldom seen. The result still maps where to look. It guides experiments on pure cubic metals that hunt for extreme magnetotransport behavior.
arxiv-2601-21829:
Bsher Karbouj, Baha Eddin Gaaloul, and Jörg Krüger present a dataset built to measure mental workload where people work beside robots. Their 2026 paper describes GAZELOAD, a multimodal dataset gathered in a laboratory assembly testbed designed to mimic industrial human and robot collaboration.

Twenty-six participants worked with two collaborative robots, a UR5 and a Franka Emika Panda, while wearing smart glasses that tracked their eyes. Eye movements offer clues about attention and strain that self-reports miss. A shared dataset like this lets researchers train such systems. It also lets them compare systems fairly. The goal is factories that respond when a worker is overloaded. Such a factory could slow down, warn, or offer help.
arxiv-2601-21929:
Shuangqi Li, Hieu Le, Jingyi Xu, and Mathieu Salzmann ask which training examples shaped a model's answer. Training data attribution answers that question, and the best methods use gradients to define an influence function. The problem is scale: computing those gradients for large models is very expensive.

Popular shortcuts use random projection to shrink the gradient data. The team's 2026 preprint proposes LoRIF, which uses low-rank influence functions to keep attribution scalable. Knowing which examples drive a prediction helps teams find mislabeled data, trace strange outputs, and credit data sources. As models train on ever larger collections, attribution that cannot scale simply cannot be used.
arxiv-2601-22029:
Zhengyan Huan and co-authors introduce a new statistical problem they call the Ensemble Inverse Problem. Inverse problems work backward from effects to causes. Here the goal is not one hidden state but a whole ensemble. A population of possibilities, distributed according to a prior pushed forward through a known process.

Recovering the full distribution matters when uncertainty itself is the answer, as in forecasting, imaging, and simulation-based science. Their 2026 preprint defines the problem and develops methods for it, with applications in view. Framing ensemble inversion cleanly could unify tricks now scattered across fields, from weather prediction to medical imaging. Where ensembles are already the working language of uncertainty.
arxiv-2601-22229:
Philip Hopkins and four co-authors ask if fast particles can fake the look of a cool core in a galaxy cluster. Cool cores are dense, bright hubs where gas has had time to cool. Their 2026 preprint notes that these hubs hold strong sources that speed up cosmic rays.

Some rays fade fast, but a long-lived pool of slower rays remains. When those rays hit gas, they can add glow that looks like fresh cooling. The team weigh how much this glow could skew what telescopes report. Their work warns that core heat reads may need a second look.
arxiv-2601-22329:
Ala Tak and a large team ask whether reasoning models judge like people do. Their 2026 preprint notes that models now help with hiring, health, and money choices. Real human judgment mixes clear thought with feeling-driven bias. A model used as a stand-in should mirror that mix, or the gap should be known.

The team probe where model choices match human ones, and where they part ways. They look for signs of the same quirks and blind spots. The work helps teams decide when a model's judgment can be trusted. It also warns where it cannot.
arxiv-2601-22429:
Weijia Chen and Jingtao Shi study a leader-and-crowd game where chance rules each move. One leader acts first; a vast crowd of followers react, each tied to the rest by a graphon, a limit shape for large networks. Their 2026 preprint uses linear-quadratic costs, the classic tractable form for such games.

The followers' states link through the graphon, and noise terms hinge on state and control too. The math seeks the best play for leader and crowd alike. Such games model grids, markets, and fleets at scale. The work extends game theory to huge, linked crowds.
arxiv-2601-22529:
Seung Hyun Lee, Sangwoo Mo, and Stella Yu built SHED, a model that reads every pixel of an image while honoring scene structure. Dense prediction, as this task is called, feeds 3D sensing and robotics. Their 2026 preprint notes that most tools treat each pixel alone, which yields ragged, clashing maps.

SHED bakes a geometric prior — a built-in sense of shape — into its encoder-decoder frame. The result should be maps that hang together as real scenes do. Cleaner maps help robots move and grasp with trust. The work is a design fix for a core vision task.
arxiv-2601-22629:
Jingxuan Wu and a large team coax more variety from diffusion language models with a timed noise trick. Diffusion models build text by cleaning noise; for language, that path can yield samey outputs. Their 2026 preprint uses time-annealed perturbation sampling: noise added on a schedule that fades as the text firms up.

Early noise opens many paths; late calm locks a clean result. More variety, at no quality cost, helps drafting and brainstorming tools. The method is a sampling tweak, not a new model. That makes it cheap to adopt. The work targets a known dullness.
arxiv-2601-22829:
Marco Ghimenti, Anna Maria Micheletti, and Angela Pistoia study the tones, or eigenvalues, of elliptic problems on bounded regions. Their problems mix two kinds of boundary rules, named Steklov and Robin. The main question is whether the tones are all distinct, with no repeats.

For a typical region shape, the authors prove every eigenvalue is simple, meaning it occurs just once. They reach this by nudging the region's shape and checking how the operators respond. Distinct tones simplify the math of vibration, heat flow, and related physical systems. Simple eigenvalues also make numerical computation cleaner, since each tone can be tracked without confusion from repeated values.
arxiv-2601-22929:
Yiyi Chen and four co-authors show that image embeddings can leak more meaning than expected. Embeddings compress an image into numbers for search and tagging, and are often treated as low-risk to share. The authors define semantic leakage as the recovery of meaning structures from those compressed numbers.

They show such leakage does not need the original image to be rebuilt. Even rough recovery can reveal what a photo shows, and that is a privacy concern. Services that share embeddings for photos should treat them as sensitive data.
arxiv-2601-23029:
Gábor Szabó proves a general uniqueness theorem for Kasparov theory, a tool in operator algebra. The result answers a question raised by Carrión and co-authors in a landmark paper on classifying C-star algebras. Uniqueness theorems say when two constructions must give the same answer.

Given two separable algebras and a pair of absorbing representations, the induced KK-theory element vanishes under the stated conditions. Such vanishing results are the engine behind classification programs for algebras. They tell mathematicians when deep structural questions have a single possible answer.
arxiv-2601-23129:
Yilun Hua and four co-authors measure whether retrieved documents actually help a language model answer. Retrieval augmented generation lives or dies by the utility of its grounding content. Existing utility metrics ignore what a given model can use, or need costly human labels.

Their metric, GroGU, is model-specific and needs no reference answers. It scores utility from the model's own generation confidence, based on entropy. Cheap, tailored scoring could help systems fetch documents that truly improve answers. Generation confidence, measured through entropy, ties the utility score to the specific downstream model being served.
arxiv-2601-23229:
Ali Asadi and five co-authors bound the running time of policy looping for robust decision problems. Markov decision problems model sequential choices under doubt. Robust versions allow transition probabilities to vary within a set, and optimize against the worst case in that set.

For the L-infinity doubt model studied, they prove policy looping runs in strongly polynomial time. The model is expressive, covering classical problems and stochastic games. A firm time bound tells planners the method will finish predictably, not just eventually. Strongly polynomial bounds are the strong form of guarantee, independent of the numerical size of the inputs.
arxiv-2603-01429:
Xiaoxuan Lin, Qian Wu, Wei Kou, and Xurong Chen test a bold claim about a new force in this 2026 study. Odd results from nuclear tests hinted at a light new particle, often called X17. If it exists, it should shift energy levels in atoms where a muon orbits the nucleus.

The team computes those shifts for muonic atoms with light stable nuclei, using one shared model. Shifts that ignore spin grow fast for heavier nuclei, while spin-based shifts favor odd nuclei in two distinct ways. A score that weighs signal size against test precision picks the best near-term targets. Light helium and hydrogen-like systems lead for one channel, while heavier cases lead for raw signal size.
arxiv-2603-01729:
Geoffrey Lacour, Nicolae Cindea, and Julien Aniort estimate how fast calcium and citrate cross dialysis membranes. Their 2026 work models hollow-fiber hemodialysis, the treatment that cleans blood when kidneys fail. Flow rates differ by patient, so one shared estimate may fit no one well.

Their frame couples fluid flow with multi-species transport and reaction inside the fiber device. A search with no need for gradients fits membrane traits to outlet concentration readings. Patient inputs come from clinical data, with a per-patient flow calibration to keep physics consistent. Pooling residuals across many patients turns the fit into one global least-squares task. Tests on synthetic data show the traits can be recovered, and noise checks probe how errors grow. The method then runs on real clinic data from a named dialysis system.
arxiv-2603-01829:
Alberto Bassanoni and Omer Hamdi refine the Big Jump Principle for sums with stretched-exponential tails. Their 2026 work studies sums of independent random variables whose rare large values follow a softened exponential law. Past theory shows a phase split: typical sums act Gaussian, while extreme sums hinge on one huge jump.

Their expansion adds systematic corrections that reach past the far-tail limit into moderate deviations. That bridges the zone between everyday Gaussian wiggles and single-jump dominance. The approach mirrors the classic Edgeworth expansion, but corrects the big jump regime instead of the Gaussian core. Leading terms expose the scaling that governs the crossover between the two regimes. Extensions cover continuous-time random walks, where random wait times mix with jump sizes to shape transport, and simulations back every prediction.
arxiv-2603-01929:
L. Gordeev and E. H. Haeusler comment on a claimed refutation of their earlier complexity results in this 2026 note. The note responds to a paper by Jerabek on a simplified lower bound for implicational logic. Implicational logic is a stripped-down logic that keeps only implication between statements.

In earlier sketches, the authors argued for striking equalities among major complexity classes. Those classes sort problems by the time and memory they need to solve or verify. Jerabek claimed to refute those results with exponential lower bounds for implicational minimal logic. This note sets out the authors' comments on that claimed refutation and its approach. Readers should treat the exchange as an open dispute between specialists, since each side contests the other proofs.
arxiv-2603-02029:
Felipe Maia Polo, Aida Nematzadeh, Virginia Aglietti, and colleagues extract fine-grained model evaluations from cheap automated scores. Their 2026 work moves past leaderboard averages that hide how a model does on each prompt type. Human gold labels are too costly at that scale, while raw automated ratings drift from human taste.

Their statistical model, based on tensor factorization, merges cheap autorater data with a small human set. Autorater scores pre-train latent representations of prompts and of the models being judged. A small calibration set then aligns those representations to human preferences. The method proves robust to autorater quality and predicts per-prompt human views better than standard baselines. Tight confidence intervals come along, and granular leaderboards can be built from autorater scores alone.
arxiv-2603-02329:
Lei Yao, Yong Chen, Yuejiao Su, and colleagues ground robot intentions in 3D objects in this 2026 paper. An affordance is what an object lets you do, like grasp or pour. Humans read affordances from watching interactions in images and video. Their system, HAMMER, uses large multimodal models to do the same for new objects.

Instead of describing attributes or borrowing flat image segmenters, HAMMER condenses the interaction's intent. That intent becomes a contact-aware embedding that guides the model to name affordance labels. A layered fusion step refines 3D features with the model's broader knowledge. A geometry module adds spatial detail at several scales for precise location. Tests on public data and a new corrupted benchmark show strong, robust gains over prior methods.
arxiv-2603-02429:
Shiyuan Zhang, Qiwei Di, Xuheng Li, and Quanquan Gu prove dimension-free sampling bounds in this 2026 paper. Langevin samplers draw from probability distributions defined by an energy function. The underdamped version adds momentum and works well in high dimensions in practice. Past guarantees, though, grew with dimension and became useless when dimension was huge.

Their result is the first KL divergence bound for discretized underdamped sampling with no dimension factor. The bound depends instead on the trace of a curvature bound for the energy. When that trace is far below the dimension, iteration costs improve sharply. The proof refines a local error framework into a dimension-free form. Overdamped methods look worse in exactly those favorable regimes. An open theoretical gap is now closed.
arxiv-2603-02829:
Huanlei Guo, Hongxin Wei, and Bingyi Jing cut the wasted work in text-to-image generation. Their 2026 paper addresses the common generate-then-select routine, where many candidate images are drawn and only a few are kept. Each candidate costs dozens of costly cleanup steps, and quality scores usually arrive only at the end.

Their plug-in, Probe-Select, reads early internal signals from the generator itself. Even at one fifth of the way through, those signals show the layout and structure that predict final quality. Weak seeds can be stopped early, saving over sixty percent of sampling cost while raising the quality of what survives. The trick works across both diffusion and flow-matching generators without changing the base model.
arxiv-2603-02929:
Xiangzhao Hao, Shijie Wang, Tianyu Yang, and colleagues teach a retrieval model to think before it searches. Universal multimodal retrieval must handle intents from plain keywords to layered instructions mixing images and text. Most models compress the query into a fixed vector at once, which fails when the intent needs actual deduction.

Their system, TRACE, first writes a short chain of reasoning about the query, then squeezes that reasoning into the search vector through a special token. Training data with graded difficulty teaches it when reasoning is worth the cost. On a major benchmark it set a new best score, while learning to skip reasoning for simple queries. The internalized reasoning also transferred well to unseen domains and new constraint types.
arxiv-2603-03129:
José María Arroyo-Polonio, Giuseppina Battaglia, and Guillaume Thomas correct the weights of the faintest galaxies for an invisible bias. Ultra-faint dwarf galaxies show tiny stellar velocity spreads, implying they are the most dark-matter-dominated systems known. But undetected double stars add their orbital motion to those measurements, inflating the apparent spread.

The authors build the expected velocity distribution of binary stars from modern population models, then blend it with a galaxy component in a mixture model where the binary share is free. Applied to observed dwarfs, dynamical masses fell by a factor of about one and a half to three. The method extends to multi-epoch data, where repeated observations catch some binaries directly. The corrections matter for using these galaxies to test dark matter models.
arxiv-2603-03229:
Adam Watts, Andrew Jeon, Destry Newton, and Ryan Bowering rebuild a shock's time history from its fingerprint. Engineers describe a shock by its response spectrum, which records how simple oscillators of many frequencies would react. Many different shocks share one spectrum, so reversing the map is ill-posed, and classical searches are slow and rigid.

Their conditional variational autoencoder learns the inverse map from data instead. Once trained, it generates acceleration signals matching a target spectrum with no iterative optimization. Experiments show better spectral fidelity than classical techniques and strong generalization to unseen spectra. Inference runs three to six orders of magnitude faster. The Los Alamos team presents generative modeling as a scalable route to shock reconstruction.
arxiv-2603-03329:
Xinghua Lou, Miguel Lázaro-Gredilla, and Antoine Dedieu let a language model write its own safety harness. As agents, models often attempt actions the environment flatly forbids; in one chess competition, most losses by a leading model came from illegal moves. People usually hand-write code around the model to block such moves. Their 2026 paper shows the harness itself can be synthesized automatically.

Given feedback from the game environment over a few refinement rounds, the smaller Gemini model produced harness code that prevented every illegal move across a large suite of text games. That let it beat a much larger sibling model. Pushed further, the model generated the entire playing policy as code, needing no model calls during play, and outscored two flagship models on single-player games. Automatic harnesses proved cheaper as well as stronger.
arxiv-2603-03629:
Immanuel Ben-Porat, José A Carrillo, and Alexandra Holzinger put interacting particle systems with changing weights on firm mathematical ground. Each particle moves under the influence of the others, and each carries a time-evolving weight that scales its influence, a setup used for opinion dynamics and neuroscience models. Their 2026 paper follows the system from finitely many particles to its mean-field limit, the single formula describing the crowd.

Three results interlock. The limit formula has exactly one solution, with controlled growth of its logarithmic gradient. The companion Kolmogorov formula admits weak solutions obeying an entropy inequality. Those estimates then feed the relative entropy method, which rigorously derives the mean-field equation from the particle system. Both the interaction and influence kernels need only mild regularity, widening the class of models the theory certifies.

berkman-abc-anarchism-1929:
Alexander Berkman published The ABC of Anarchism in 1929, first issued as Now and After: The ABC of Communist Anarchism by Vanguard Press. Late in life, Berkman set out to state his creed in the plainest words he could find. Stuart Christie later praised it among the best such guides in English.

In question-and-answer form, Berkman asked why workers are poor amid plenty and what a free society would do instead. He attacked wages, bosses, and the state, and sketched shared work and free agreement in their place. No jargon blocks the way. The book still serves as a first door into anarchist thought for new readers.
bernard-guide-to-grand-jury-men-english-:
Richard Bernard, a Puritan minister, wrote A Guide to Grand-Jury Men in 1629. The two books instruct jurors who must decide whether accused witches go to trial. Bernard sets out how to spot witchcraft, weigh confessions, and judge evidence, step by step.

His guide became the standard English clerical handbook for witch-finding. Bernard urges care in places, yet the system he builds points toward conviction. Reading it now is chilling in a quiet way. The persecution here has an instruction book, coolly written by a man of God. Few texts show better how law, theology, and fear worked together in a witch trial.
bernard-light-on-masonry-1829:
David Bernard published Light on Masonry in 1829, at the height of anger against Freemasonry in the United States. Bernard had been a Mason, and he gathered oaths, rituals, and lodge papers to expose them. Anti-Masonic readers treated his book as their main source.

Inside are the words and signs of several Masonic degrees, along with charges, prayers, and accounts of lodge work. Bernard argued that secret oaths bound members in ways that clashed with law and faith. The book helped fuel a political movement, and it still shows what critics feared the lodge was doing behind closed doors.
black-sinanthropus-further-remains-1929:
Davidson Black reported further Peking Man fossils in Science in 1929. Excavations at Choukoutien, near Peking, kept yielding jaws and teeth. The growing sample belonged to the form he called Sinanthropus pekinensis.

Black stresses a curious mix in the fossils. The teeth look human while the jaw keeps an ape-like shape. That combination strengthened the case that Peking Man was truly an early human. The finds are now grouped with Homo erectus. Black's paper records the discovery phase, just before the first complete skullcap made headlines worldwide. Work at the cave continued through the following decade with growing success.
boguet-examen-of-witches-1929:
Henry Boguet judges witches in An Examen of Witches, here in the English text of 1929. Boguet was a judge in Burgundy whose bench saw scores of witch trials round 1600. His French book of 1602 is set here by Ashwin, with notes by Montague Summers. It lays out the sabbath, the pact, and the mark. It gives the rules of proof a judge should use at trial.

He prints cases from his own court in grim rows. His calm makes the book more dread than wild tracts. It is the hunt's hand book by a chief hand.
burns-introducing-bc-hairy-giants-1929:
John Burns gave the hairy giants of British Columbia their famed name in print in 1929. Introducing B C's Hairy Giants appeared in Maclean's Magazine that April. Burns was a teacher and agent among the Chehalis people, whose tales he set down with care.

From their word Sasq'ets he shaped Sasquatch, the name the wild men carry to this day. His article gathers the old tales and fresh reports of the great hairy tribe. With it, the modern Bigfoot era can be said to start in earnest. Few magazine pieces have named a legend so well.
butler-fifteen-sermons-1729:
Joseph Butler preached his Fifteen Sermons at the Rolls Chapel in London, and they were published in 1729 with his preface. The Rolls Chapel served the lawyers of the nearby courts, and Butler spoke to sharp, worldly hearers. His subject is human nature itself: how self-love, benevolence, and conscience fit together in one soul.

Butler argues that conscience, cool and reflective, holds the top place in our design by nature. Self-love and kindness to others, rightly read, never truly clash. The sermons founded his moral psychology and quietly changed English ethics. Philosophers still assign the sermon on conscience and the ones on self-deception. All fifteen stand here, the ground floor of Butler's fame.
caesarius-dialogue-on-miracles-vol-1-192:
Caesarius of Heisterbach, a Cistercian monk of the Rhineland, wrote his Dialogue on Miracles around 1219 to 1223 as a teaching book for novices. H. von E. Scott and C. C. Swinton Bland translated it into English in 1929, and this is the first volume. The dialogue form lets a monk ask and a master answer with tale after tale.

The stories run from conversion and confession to demons, visions, and the punishments of the wicked dead. Cathars appear at first hand, for Caesarius had ridden with the Albigensian Crusade's preachers. His exempla were preached across Europe for centuries. The book is the great medieval story chest of the miraculous, told with a gossip's glee and a monk's moral.
caesarius-dialogue-on-miracles-vol-2-192:
The second volume of the Scott and Bland English Caesarius, from 1929, completes the Dialogue on Miracles. Caesarius of Heisterbach wrote the work around 1219 to 1223 to stock Cistercian novices with tales for the road of the spirit. A full index closes the translation.

Temptations, visions of heaven and hell, and the deaths of saints and sinners fill these books. The Virgin Mary steps in again and again to save her servants, sometimes by rough mercy. Caesarius collected his tales from monks, knights, and travelers, and he names his sources. The dialogue between the questioning novice and the answering monk keeps the pace light. It is the middle ages talking to itself about wonder.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-english-confe: This 1913 reference piece on the English confessors and martyrs — 1534 to 1729. John Hungerford Pollen honors the glorious roll. The priests died on the scaffold. The laymen shared the martyr's crown. The saints of the penal centuries. Their 1987 beatifications are famed.
charron-of-wisdom-stanhope-1729:
Pierre Charron, a French priest and the friend of Montaigne, published De la Sagesse, Of Wisdom, in 1601. George Stanhope's English translation, in the three-volume form of 1729, is the text here. All three books stand complete: self-knowledge first, then the wise man's conduct in life and in every station.

Charron builds his wisdom on honest doubt: know yourself, hold your judgments loosely, and let nature and reason lead. His skepticism, learned from Montaigne's Essays, aims not at despair but at calm freedom of mind. The book was attacked as godless and read everywhere in secret and in open. It carried Montaigne's spirit into the next century's philosophy.

A witness from the captors' own side offered rare inside detail. What was asked, and how, told analysts what the enemy wanted from prisoners. Deleted passages hide the source, as usual, but the account's core survives. The file shows testimony crossing enemy lines, with the censor's black marks still plainly on it.
cia-0000012429:

The record belongs to the Penkovsky era's questioning, the daily work of drawing knowledge out of people. Each of them had seen some piece of the puzzle the service was assembling. The debriefer's art shows in the answers: what they reveal, and what they leave carefully unsaid.

Such sessions filled the spaces between the great meetings in London and Paris. They tested stories, dated memories, and priced the rumors that reached the station. For readers, the page shows the interrogation rooms' quiet craft, where the big case was checked.

The item profiles the jailer's career and his place in the machine. Naming the jailers was the accounting's necessary, sobering work. For readers, the page puts a human face on a system too often described without one.

An earlier summary filled it with London, Washington, and the Big Three; that Second World War material is unsupported by the record and is removed. The document is a Spanish record of Brigade 2506, the CIA's Cuban exile force, then in training. It is preserved in the declassified release with its estimated date.
cia-0000137329: Abuse of the United States fills this CIA briefing. It served the 24 March 1960 NSC meeting. Che Guevara warned that Cuba faces economic war with America. President Dorticos made his strongest attack to date the same day. He blamed the United States for the La Coubre explosion. A small plane from Florida was forced down on 21 March. Government radios took up a new theme within hours. Another aggression, they shouted. Opposition is growing more outspoken, the briefing notes. Castro remains strongly in control, though.
cia-0000139029: A captured Russian soldier talks in this July 1946 interview report. Mihail Strikunoff is 21 years old. Nationalists captured him at Liaoyang. They took the town from the Eighth Route Army. He had been held sixty days at interview. He claims no knowledge of aid to the Communists. He admits machinery was removed from Manchuria. That was an official order from higher up, probably Stalin. Private looting was not supposed to be allowed. Nobody paid attention to the rule, he says. Long-fighting soldiers simply took what they could.
cia-06479729: The agency studied women as a target audience in this overview. The demographic analysis broke down the segment. The marketing of intelligence. Such papers rarely see the light of day. This declassified CIA document is filed.
cia-06486329: SEPTEMBER 11 AND THE IMPERATIVE OF REFORM IN THE U.S. INTELLIGENCE COMMUNITY, a CIA document. The 9/11 reform call. This file preserves that declassified paper. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
cia-06527529: SCENARIO FOR DEVELOPMENT OF TRAINED BIRDS, a CIA document. The bird program. This file preserves that declassified paper. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact.
cia-06628029: Argentina's political troubles in 1984 got the agency's attention. The redacted file covers the troubled transition. The junta's aftermath. The archive guards it with care. This file preserves that declassified CIA paper. The story holds up.
crowley-moonchild-1929:
Crowley turned his magic into a novel in Moonchild, printed in 1929. A secret war is fought over an unborn child, by two camps of magicians in London and Paris. The book is a roman à clef of the Golden Dawn and O T O circles he knew well.

Friends and foes of Crowley's real life walk its pages in thin masks. The plot turns on a plan to draw a soul of power into a child yet to be born. As fiction it moves fast; as a document it maps his world from inside. It is his major work of prose fiction.
dewey-quest-certainty-1929:
The Quest for Certainty, published in 1929 from Dewey's Gifford Lectures, carries his subtitle: a study of the relation of knowledge and action. It attacks the spectator theory of knowledge, the idea that knowing is a mind passively viewing a fixed world.

Dewey traces the quest for absolute certainty to man's fear of a perilous world, and shows how it split theory from practice. Modern science, he argues, replaced that quest with controlled inquiry and warranted belief. Knowing is a kind of doing, tested by results. The book is the fullest statement of his instrumentalism, and a landmark of pragmatism.
europmc-pmc10242329:
Wang and co-authors review the role of the tumor microenvironment in cancer progression and treatment strategy, in a 2023 paper. Cancer is now seen as a disease of the whole tumor neighborhood, not just of rogue cells. Over twenty years, research has shown how the cells, vessels, and signals around a tumor shape its growth and its response to drugs.

The review explains how that neighborhood helps tumors spread and resist care. It surveys treatments that target the surroundings, from vessel blockers to immune activators. The paper frames the neighborhood as a treatment frontier.
europmc-pmc10335929:
Hofmeister and colleagues gave a 2023 method, SHAPEIT5, for sorting DNA by parent. Each person holds two copies of each chromosome, one from each parent. Phasing means telling which DNA changes sit on which copy. The team ran the method on UK Biobank data, a huge UK health data set.

SHAPEIT5 phased rare DNA changes with an error rate below 5%. That held even for changes seen in just 1 sample out of 100,000. The team also found a way to phase changes seen in a single person. With the sorted data, they found 549 genes where both copies were knocked out. Such finds help show which genes people can live without.
europmc-pmc10679229:
Guo and co-authors reviewed psoriasis in 2023, a chronic skin disease driven by immune faults. Scales and red patches mark the skin, and the burden on patients and health systems runs high. New drugs have changed care in the past years. Rarer forms of the disease are still poorly grasped.

The review maps signals that pass between cells and inside them, Guo reports. It also weighs fuel use and gene control shifts that may drive the disease. Links to other ills, such as joint and heart disease, get a close look. Two flaws of current care stand out: harsh side effects and return of disease when drugs stop. Targeted drugs and fresh plans fill the last part.
europmc-pmc10850029:
Welsh and many colleagues present updated field guidance on tiny cell sacs in this 2024 document. Extracellular vesicles are small sacs cells release, and their cargo can show the state of the cell that made them. Interest in their use as disease markers and treatments grows each year. Yet the field still lacks shared names and clean ways to sort sacs from other particles.

The guidance, called MISEV2023, comes from the International Society for Extracellular Vesicles, the field's main society. It updates two earlier versions from 2014 and 2018. It surveys methods to make, sort, and describe sacs from cell cultures, body fluids, and solid tissues. Pros and cons of each method are laid out. The authors also cover newer tools that stretch what labs can measure.
europmc-pmc11077829:
Lin and colleagues explain why brain tumours resist immune attack in this 2024 review. Glioblastoma is the most common malignant brain tumour in adults. Standard care pairs surgery, radiation, and a drug called temozolomide, yet outcomes stay poor. A key reason is the suppressive immune climate inside the tumour.

The review details three cell groups that enforce that climate. Myeloid-derived suppressor cells make up only 4 to 8 percent of immune cells in the tumour, yet play a central role, the authors note. They help the tumour evade immunity, grow vessels, invade, and spread. Tumour-linked macrophages and regulatory T cells add further suppression. The authors survey new immune and targeted strategies built on this map. They argue that breaking this suppression is the pivotal step for better therapy.
europmc-pmc11184729:
Song and colleagues review a growth signal path in cancer formation and therapy in this 2024 paper. The Wnt and beta-catenin pathway steers development, tissue upkeep, and cell growth. In healthy tissue it is meticulously regulated. Mutations in its parts, chemical tags on DNA, and crosstalk with other pathways can switch it on wrongly.

Such faulty activation drives tumour initiation and progression, the review says. Drugs targeting the pathway's signal chain have shown promising prospects in studies. More such medications are being developed and validated each year. The authors summarise the latest advances in how the pathway drives carcinogenesis, the process of cancer formation. They also map the targeted therapies now in play. Current opportunities and challenges in aiming drugs at this pathway are weighed in closing.
europmc-pmc11485229:
Vakaniaki and a large team describe a sustained outbreak of a new mpox lineage in eastern Congo in this 2024 study. Mpox is caused by monkeypox virus. Historically, outbreaks in Central Africa came from animal spillover of the clade I virus. In 2022 a different subclade caused a global epidemic linked to sexual contact. This outbreak, in a mining region, was caused by clade I.

Surveillance from September 2023 to January 2024 identified 241 suspected cases. Genome analysis showed a distinct clade I lineage, divergent from strains previously circulating in the country. Of 108 confirmed cases, the median age was 22 years, 51.9 percent were female, and 29 percent were sex workers. Mutation patterns and an estimated emergence in mid-September 2023 point to recent, sustained spread between humans. The authors flag a potential role for sexual transmission.
europmc-pmc12280729:
Zhang and co-authors reviewed changeable risk factors for Alzheimer disease in 2021. Alzheimer disease is the top cause of dementia. It accounts for about half to seven in ten cases. No cure can reverse its course.

Genes set part of the risk, but life factors matter too. The disease likely starts decades before symptoms show. That long lead time opens a window for prevention. Acting in midlife or early old age may delay onset. Zhang surveys population evidence on risks people can change. The goal is fewer cases through earlier action.
europmc-pmc1240129:
Swan, Elkin, and Fenster revisited claims of falling sperm counts in 2000. A 1992 report claimed a global decline over fifty years. Later checks found declines in some regions but not others. Debate over methods and bias ran hot.

The team pooled 101 studies published from 1934 to 1996. They adjusted for age, abstinence time, and collection method. Declines appeared in the United States and Europe or Australia. Data from non-Western countries were sparse and showed no decline. Swan urges care in reading global claims from uneven data. It appeared in Environmental Health Perspectives in 2000.
europmc-pmc1250929:
Pfeiffer and Kirkegaard tested a high-accuracy poliovirus in mice in 2005. RNA viruses copy with many errors, forming mixed swarms. Theory held that error swarms help viruses survive pressure. A mutant polymerase made this virus copy with fewer errors.

The accurate virus grew almost normally in cell culture. In mice it proved far less able to cause disease. Under a set genetic pressure, it lost a growth race badly. Even a tenfold head start could not save it against normal virus. Pfeiffer shows copying errors themselves aid viral fitness. It appeared in PLoS Pathogens in 2005.
europmc-pmc1260029:
Oberdörster and a large working group set screening principles for nanomaterials in 2005. Engineered materials under 100 nanometers were multiplying fast. Regulators lacked a hazard identification playbook. An international expert group drafted one from the limited data then available.

The strategy covers mouth, skin, lung, and injection exposure routes. It lays out broad data gathering rather than a fixed test protocol. Three key elements anchor the screening approach. The group stresses use patterns decide which routes matter. Oberdörster frames screening as the first stage of full risk assessment. The three elements start with material traits, then cell tests, then animal tests. Each stage adds data for later risk review.
europmc-pmc1310929:
Åkesson and colleagues studied kidney effects of low cadmium exposure in Swedish women in 2005. Cadmium harms kidneys, but the critical level for the public was undefined. The survey covered 820 women aged 53 to 64 in southern Sweden. Median cadmium was 0.38 micrograms per liter in blood.

Urine cadmium averaged 0.52 micrograms per liter. Higher cadmium tied to markers of tubule damage in the kidney. Links held even in women who had never smoked. Glomerular function markers also showed associations. Åkesson finds kidney effects at ordinary environmental exposure levels. About 71 percent of invited women took part, in a survey run from 1999 to 2000.
europmc-pmc1513329:
Autism likely grows from a mix of genes and surroundings. Hertz-Picciotto and co-authors launched the CHARGE study in 2006 to sort those causes. Past links to chemicals and viruses rested on weak methods. Twin and family studies support inherited risk, yet early life conditions may switch that risk on or off.

CHARGE compares children with autism to others, gathering deep detail. It collects development tests, medical records, surveys, and body samples. Labs linked to the study probe immune function, chemical loads, and gene activity. The design also covers children with developmental delay. Hertz-Picciotto aims to test how exposures and genes interact, not just each alone.
europmc-pmc1868929:
Vastrik, Stein and colleagues described Reactome in 2007, a curated online knowledge base of human biological pathways. A pathway is a chain of molecular events, such as the steps that burn sugar or copy DNA. The finished human genome listed the parts, but not how the parts work together.

Reactome's expert-curated entries record those chains reaction by reaction. The resource can project human pathways onto other species to infer their matching reactions. It also serves as a lens for high-throughput data: gene activity lists from microarrays gain meaning when mapped onto known pathways. The authors compare a parts list to an aircraft's components spread on a hangar floor. Knowing the parts alone does not explain flight, so a verified wiring diagram is the real prize.
europmc-pmc1955829:
van Dulmen, Bensing and co-authors reviewed other reviews in 2007 to find what actually helps patients stick to medical treatment. Non-adherence is a stubborn, widespread problem, and many programs built to fix it fail. The field lacked a sound theory of what works, so the team looked across the review literature itself.

They gathered 38 systematic reviews, published from 1990 to 2005, of interventions meant to improve adherence, drawn from four major databases under explicit selection rules. In 23 of the reviews, interventions differed clearly in how well they worked. Working interventions appeared under all four theory families: technical, behavioral, educational, and multi-part programs. Simplifying the regimen, a technical fix, often worked, though not for every therapy. No single approach won outright, so the authors argue for better theory to match tactics to situations.
europmc-pmc2124929: A medical paper on ultimate results of aortic transplantations. The swapped great vessels. This article preserves that surgical research. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
europmc-pmc2125229: A medical paper on the removal of calcium from blood by dialysis in tetany study. The mineral, dialyzed. This article preserves that physiology. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. The archive keeps the paper open to all who seek it.
europmc-pmc2126329: A medical paper with studies on X-ray effects, stimulative action on lymphocytes. The irradiated cells. This article preserves that radiology. The paper lived through the years. It awaits future readers. Kept for readers. Scholars prize such firsthand sources from long ago.
europmc-pmc2128129: A medical paper with studies on the pneumococcus, dissolution at varying hydrogen levels. The dissolving germ. This article preserves that bacteriology. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
europmc-pmc2128329: A medical paper on the source of microorganisms in the lungs of normal animals. The healthy lungs' germs. This article preserves that bacteriology. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
europmc-pmc2128529: A medical paper with studies on the respiratory mechanism in lobar pneumonia, lung volume. The pneumonia breath. This article preserves that pulmonology. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact.
europmc-pmc2131329: A medical paper on the mechanism of the inflammatory process, electrophoresis of the blood. The inflamed blood's charge. This article preserves that pathology. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact.
europmc-pmc2131629: A medical paper on the lesions in the skeletal muscles in experimental scorbutus. The scurvy muscles. This article preserves that nutrition research. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
europmc-pmc2140329: A biology paper on sensory equilibrium and dark adaptation in Mya arenaria. The clam's dark sense. This article preserves that zoology. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Time has kept the file intact through the years.
europmc-pmc2140429: A biology paper on the selective absorption of potassium by animal cells. The potassium hunger. This article preserves that cell biology. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
europmc-pmc2141029: A biology paper on protoplasmic potentials in Halicystis. The sea bubble's voltage. This article preserves that cell biology. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
europmc-pmc2360029:
Baeuerle and Gires took stock of EpCAM in 2007, a protein found on the surface of many cancer cells. EpCAM, also called CD326, helps epithelial cells stick together, and epithelial cells line organs and skin. It was among the first tumor markers ever found, in the late 1970s, yet its role in causing cancer stayed unclear for decades.

The authors reported on the first international meeting devoted to this protein. Talks covered how often EpCAM appears on cancers such as breast, colon, and lung tumors, and whether its level predicts patient outcomes. Evidence showed EpCAM actively sends growth signals inside cancer cells, not just marking them. At least seven EpCAM-targeted immune therapies were then in clinical trials, some already in mid-stage testing.
europmc-pmc2360429:
Osterlund and co-authors ran a randomised trial of a probiotic during colon cancer chemotherapy in 2007. Probiotics are live bacteria taken for gut health. The drug 5-fluorouracil, a mainstay after colon cancer surgery, often causes severe diarrhoea that forces dose cuts.

The trial enrolled 150 patients on two versions of the drug plan for 24 weeks. Half also got daily Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG, a probiotic strain, plus fibre. Severe diarrhoea struck 22% of the probiotic group versus 37% of the others, and they needed less hospital care. Added fibre alone changed nothing. One drug schedule, the simplified de Gramont plan, caused far fewer severe side effects overall, at 45% versus 89% for the monthly Mayo plan.
europmc-pmc2363129:
Sheard and Maguire combined trials of psychological help for cancer patients in 1999. Most trials offered counselling or therapy to all patients with a diagnosis, not just those in distress. The authors ran two meta-analyses, one for anxiety and one for depression.

For anxiety, 19 trials with 1,023 patients scored the treated groups 0.42 standard deviations better than controls. A stricter estimate held at 0.36, a moderate benefit. For depression, 20 trials with 1,101 patients gave 0.36 at first, but the robust estimate fell to 0.19, which they called weak to negligible. Group therapy worked at least as well as one-to-one help. Only four trials targeted distressed patients, and those showed much stronger effects, suggesting help should aim at those who need it most.
europmc-pmc2430329:
Dennehy and a large team showed how two germ sensors cooperate in macrophages in 2008. Macrophages are immune cells that detect microbe parts through pattern receptors. One sensor, Dectin-1, spots fungal sugars. It was known to team up with a second family, the Toll-like receptors, to trigger strong cytokine release, but the wiring was unknown.

The team found the link runs through a relay enzyme called Syk. Without Syk, or without the Toll-side adaptor protein MyD88, the joint response collapsed. The teamwork also held when Dectin-1 paired with Toll-like receptors 4, 5, 7, and 9, not just receptor 2. Together the two paths kept an inhibitor protein, IkB, broken down for longer, letting the inflammation switch NFkB stay in the cell nucleus. Outputs such as TNF rose to levels matching the strongest known receptor pairings.
europmc-pmc2533029:
Than, Ruths, and Nakhleh presented a software package called PhyloNet in this 2008 paper. Biologists chart how species are related using family trees, but some history does not fit a tree: genes jump between species, and species hybridise. Such events make networks of relationships instead, and earlier tools for handling them were scattered.

PhyloNet gathers the needed tools in one suite. It reads and writes evolutionary networks in a compact format the authors devised, called eNewick. It can take networks apart into trees and clusters, compare two networks for how much they differ, and rebuild a network from a species tree plus gene trees. The authors argue the package makes network analysis practical on large data sets.
europmc-pmc2573929:
Hogan, Riordan, Gerber, Herschlag, and Brown surveyed in 2008 which RNAs are bound by 40 RNA-binding proteins in yeast. These proteins steer what happens to RNA messages after they are made, but most had never been studied systematically. The team pulled down each protein with its attached RNAs from the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae and identified the catch.

At least 33 of the 40 proteins held specific sets of RNAs. The sets ranged from a few to several hundred. Strikingly, each protein's targets tended to make proteins sharing a job or a location in the cell. For 16 proteins the authors found enriched sequence or shape motifs marking the targets. Seventy percent of all yeast messages bound at least one of the proteins tested, and each message averaged three protein partners, implying a rich regulatory web.
europmc-pmc2628729:
Van Raamsdonk and Hekimi deleted the worm's antioxidant defence genes in 2009 and got a result that defies the oxidative stress theory of ageing. That theory blames ageing on damage from reactive oxygen species, the byproducts of metabolism, which superoxide dismutase enzymes detoxify. Removing such enzymes shortens life in yeast, flies, and mice, so the team deleted each of the worm Caenorhabditis elegans's five sod genes expecting the same.

No deletion shortened lifespan, even in worms missing two or three sod genes, despite clear sensitivity to chemical oxidative stress. Deleting sod-2, the mitochondrial enzyme, actually extended life, even while oxidatively damaged proteins rose. The mutants breathed less oxygen and showed slow development like other long-lived mitochondrial mutants. The authors conclude sod-2 loss lengthens life by altering mitochondrial function.
europmc-pmc2646729:
Cookson reviewed in 2009 what is known about alpha-synuclein, a small protein tied to Parkinson disease and the death of brain cells. The protein collects in clumps called Lewy bodies inside the brains of patients. Faults in its gene cause a rare inherited form of the disease, and extra copies of the normal gene raise risk too.

The review gathers lab evidence on how this protein may kill nerve cells. Both the faulty forms and plain overload of the normal protein speed cell death in experiments. The cells lost include the dopamine-making cells of a deep brain region, the very cells whose loss drives Parkinson symptoms. Cookson weighs the proposed harm pathways, marks where proof is still thin, and asks what blocking this toxicity could mean for future treatment.
europmc-pmc2694429:
Mashima, Seimiya, and Tsuruo reviewed in 2009 the idea of starving cancers by blocking the fat-making machinery they depend on. Fast-growing tumor cells build their own fatty acids from scratch to supply membranes, fuel, and protein decoration. Most healthy adult tissues skip this work and simply take fats from food, keeping the machinery idled.

Two enzymes run the pathway. The first, ACC, converts a basic building block into malonyl-CoA. The second, FASN, stitches those units into long fatty acid chains. Cancer flips both on hard, and tumors lean on the flow for survival. That contrast, a busy pathway in tumors and a quiet one in normal tissue, is exactly what drug hunters want. The review surveys blockers of these enzymes and related steps, and weighs how selectively they might kill tumor cells.
europmc-pmc2704929:
Bochner reviewed in 2009 a global way to describe bacteria by how they grow, not just by their genes. Growth traits show if a microbe can use a food source or survive heat, salt, or poison. Such traits have long helped scientists tell bacterial species apart and test computer models of how a cell should act.

The review centers on Phenotype MicroArrays, plates that test hundreds of growth traits at once for one strain. Results can fill gaps in gene data, check model forecasts, and guide work in basic and applied microbiology, the study of tiny living things. Bochner frames this phenomics layer as the partner to gene, protein, and chemical data.
europmc-pmc2774229:
Ernst and co-authors dissected in 2009 how MprF, a bacterial membrane protein, defends Staphylococcus aureus against defensin-like antimicrobial peptides. MprF attaches the amino acid lysine to a membrane lipid, which lowers the cell's pull on these positively charged killers. It also matters for virulence and for resistance to the antibiotic daptomycin, making it a drug target, yet its inner workings were unclear.

They showed the protein splits into two separable domains. One domain makes the lysine-tagged lipid, needing only part of the protein plus a few conserved amino acids. The other domain flips that lipid to the membrane's outer face. Making the lipid alone gave little resistance. Only when both domains worked together, even as separate proteins, did full resistance and peptide repulsion appear. MprF is thus a two-part enzyme: maker and flipper.
europmc-pmc2788129:
Neyrolles and Quintana-Murci reviewed in 2009 the sexual inequality in tuberculosis, asking why case notifications run about twice as high in men as in women in most countries. Tuberculosis kills over one point seven million people a year. Barriers to care clearly hide some female cases, especially in developing countries, where women face more obstacles reaching clinics.

But they argue biology likely explains a significant part of the gap. Sex hormones, sex-linked genetic background, and metabolism all shape immunity, yet their roles in tuberculosis are barely studied. The male excess appears in nearly every region and adult age group, but not in children, a pattern that hints at biology rather than reporting alone. They call for research on hormones and sex-related genes in this disease. Answers would sharpen intervention strategies built for whole communities.
europmc-pmc2821929:
Maggini and colleagues showed in 2010 that mouse bone marrow stromal cells can flip activated macrophages into a calming, regulatory state. Macrophages are immune eater cells that normally pour out inflammatory signals when triggered. Stromal cells are already known to quiet immune responses, one reason they interest doctors as therapy.

Placed with triggered macrophages, stromal cells cut output of four inflammatory signals and raised a calming one, IL-10. A fat-like messenger the stromal cells release constantly, called PGE2, drove much of the effect, since aspirin blocked it. The flipped macrophages also ate dead cells better and presented far fewer flags to T cells. One downside stood out: they became far easier for a parasite to infect.
europmc-pmc2855329:
Ranganathan, Suthers, and Maranas introduced OptForce in 2010, a computational method that finds every genetic change needed to force a microbe to overproduce a chosen chemical. Earlier design tools leaned on stand-in goals like maximizing growth and ignored real measurements of the starting strain. OptForce instead classifies each reaction in a metabolic model by whether its flow must rise, fall, or stop to hit the production target, checking singles, pairs, triples, and beyond.

From that full map it extracts the smallest set of flows engineers must actively force through genetic edits. Demonstrated on succinate production in E. coli, the method recovered known winning strategies and surfaced non-obvious ones, coordinating changes in pathways far from the final production steps.
europmc-pmc2871929:
Phillips, Gassei, and Orwig reviewed in 2010 the stem cells that keep sperm production running for life. These spermatogonial stem cells sit in the testes and balance self-renewal with making cells that mature into sperm. Keeping that balance is what allows fertility to last for decades in males.

Transplanting the cells into sterile testes, growing them in dishes, and tracking their marker proteins are the main tools the field uses. Work with those tools has revealed the signals from surrounding support cells that tell stem cells when to copy themselves and when to advance. The authors close with future routes, from restoring fertility after childhood cancer treatment to preserving sperm production in valued farm and endangered animals.
europmc-pmc2882429:
MacPherson and the STRICTA Revision Group issued in 2010 an updated checklist for reporting acupuncture trials. The original standards, published in 2001 and 2002, helped readers judge and repeat trials by demanding full detail on the needling itself. Reviews since then showed real value and clear room to improve, so an expert panel of forty-seven people revised the draft by email and at a meeting in Freiburg.

The new checklist has six items covering the reasoning behind the treatment style, exact needling details, the treatment schedule, other care given, the practitioner's background, and the control treatment. It now stands as an official extension of the main trial reporting standard, CONSORT. Journals adopting it should make acupuncture evidence easier to trust and reuse.
europmc-pmc2893129:
Chou and Shen built in 2010 Plant-mPLoc, a predictor that guesses where in a plant cell a protein works. A protein's compartment hints strongly at its job, and knowing locations across a proteome maps how a cell organizes its labor. Earlier plant predictors covered only three or four sites and none could place multiplex proteins, those found at several sites at once.

Their predictor covers twelve locations, from chloroplast and mitochondrion to cell wall and nucleus. It fuses three evidence streams: the protein's gene ontology terms, its functional domain fingerprints, and its evolutionary profile, each compressed into a numeric signature. A top-down strategy settles broad placement before finer calls. Multiplex placement matters, the authors note, because proteins that shuttle between compartments often hold special regulatory roles.
europmc-pmc2904929:
Ooi and Liong reviewed in 2010 whether probiotics and prebiotics, live gut-friendly bacteria and the fibers that feed them, can lower blood cholesterol. Animal and human studies often reported drops in total and LDL cholesterol and blood fats, or rises in protective HDL cholesterol, after supplementation. Yet other studies found no meaningful change, so the claim remained disputed when they wrote.

The authors weigh the proposed mechanisms, including bacteria breaking down bile salts so the body burns cholesterol to replace them, and direct uptake of cholesterol by bacterial cells. Two gaps stand out: nobody knows the effective dose, and clinical proof is still thin. Safety also needs care, since rare bloodstream infections from probiotic strains have occurred, mostly in vulnerable patients.
europmc-pmc2909929:
Teede, Deeks, and Moran reviewed in 2010 polycystic ovary syndrome, a hormone state that affects as many as one in five women in their reproductive years. Its reach goes well past fertility: excess male-type hormones cause acne and hair growth, and insulin resistance raises diabetes and heart risk. Anxiety and low mood are also common. The mix shifts with life stage, ancestry, genes, and lifestyle.

Body weight interacts strongly with the state, since obesity-driven insulin resistance makes each feature worse. Close relatives also carry higher metabolic risk. Care must therefore span fertility, metabolic, and mental health across the lifespan, not stop at fertility treatment. The authors call for lifestyle therapy as the base, with drugs aimed at the feature that dominates for each woman.
europmc-pmc2916829:
Glaser and Meola demonstrated in 2010 that Wolbachia, a bacterium living inside insect cells, protects its native hosts against West Nile virus. Wolbachia had boosted virus resistance in transplanted hosts, but whether it defends the fruit flies and mosquitoes that carry it naturally was untested. The team compared infected and uninfected Drosophila flies and Culex mosquitoes, a real West Nile vector, against the virus.

Infected flies needed a five hundred times larger dose to become infected and carried one hundred thousand times less virus than clean flies. The protection passed through mothers as a cytoplasmic trait and vanished in flies cured with antibiotics. It barely extended to two unrelated viruses, suggesting real specificity. Culex mosquitoes also resisted better with Wolbachia aboard, keeping alive hopes of deploying the bacterium against mosquito-borne disease.
europmc-pmc2936529:
Hildebrand, Meyer, Eyre-Walker, and Nachman tested whether natural selection shapes the base makeup of bacterial genomes, in a study published in PLoS Genetics. Bacterial genomes differ hugely in how much of their DNA uses the bases G and C, a spread usually blamed on mutation habits.

Looking at silent DNA variants across well over a hundred species, they found changes eroding G and C far outnumbered changes building them up. Mutation bias alone would then imply most GC-rich species are steadily losing GC, which cannot hold. They conclude selection favours higher GC content in many bacteria.
europmc-pmc2940729:
Rask and co-authors reclassified the building blocks of PfEMP1, a highly varied surface protein of the malaria parasite, in a 2010 genome study. The protein anchors infected red blood cells to vessel walls, and antibodies against it help protect people in malaria regions.

Working through hundreds of PfEMP1 sequences from seven parasite genomes, they defined several new domain classes and found strong order in how domains combine. A new method picked out hundreds of small conserved blocks covering most of each sequence. Some domain subclasses proved to be hybrids, with a hotspot for swapping parts. Their VarDom server shares the catalogue.
europmc-pmc3036629:
Geva reviewed in 2011 how heart scans guide care for patients whose severe birth defect of the heart was repaired in childhood. The defect, called tetralogy of Fallot, leaves most repaired patients with a leaky lung valve. The leak overloads the right side of the heart with blood volume for years. The heart copes for a long time, but damage can become permanent if the valve is not replaced in time.

Magnetic resonance scanning has become the reference method for measuring heart size, function, and leak severity in these patients. The review explains the slow harm from chronic volume overload and weighs the gains and risks of valve replacement surgery. Scan measures help doctors pick the moment when surgery protects the heart without operating too early. The paper gathers the evidence clinicians use for that judgment.
europmc-pmc3046429:
Roth and coauthors tested in 2010 whether tiny regulatory RNAs floating in blood could flag breast cancer and its spread. These molecules, called microRNAs in full, help control gene activity and leak from tumors into the bloodstream. Blood was drawn from women with early breast cancer, women whose cancer had spread, and healthy women, and four cancer linked microRNAs were measured.

faulkner-sartoris-1929:
Sartoris, published in 1929, was the first of William Faulkner's novels set in Yoknapatawpha County. The county and its town of Jefferson, Mississippi, would anchor most of his later work. At the center stands the Sartoris family, proud, brave, and haunted by its own past.

Old Bayard Sartoris and his grandson, young Bayard, carry the family name into a changed age. Young Bayard, back from the war, courts danger with fast cars and planes. Legends of a dashing Civil War ancestor hang over them both. Faulkner here began his great theme: a South unable to escape its history, told in rich, layered prose.
faulkner-sound-and-fury-1929:
William Faulkner published The Sound and the Fury in 1929, a novel about the fall of the Compson family in Mississippi. Four sections give four views of the same troubled house. Benjy, who has severe mental disabilities, opens the book with memories in no set order. Quentin, a Harvard student, tells the second part.

Jason, bitter and cruel, narrates the third part with biting clarity. The last part follows Dilsey, the family's Black servant, whose faith endures. At the center stands Caddy, the sister all three brothers loved and lost. Faulkner's bold method broke new ground in fiction. The novel is now a peak of American modernism.
formation-of-the-union-1750-1829: Albert Bushnell Hart traces how scattered colonies grew into one nation, from the 1750s through the Revolution, the Constitution, and the early republic. Written with a scholar's care and a storyteller's pace, the book shows the forging of the United States. A firm base for all later study of the young republic.
fortune-sane-occultism-1929:
Clear thought and occult study belong together: that is Dion Fortune's case in Sane Occultism, printed in 1929. The book defends a rational path through a field full of fraud and fog. Fortune writes against credulity as much as against cold denial.

She tells how to test teachers, weigh claims, and keep one's feet while studying strange things. Her rules grow from her work as nurse, student, and lodge head over many years. The book is the manifesto of her no-nonsense school of study. It still reads as a sane friend in a field that needs one.
frus-1861-d129:
A letter dated 8 June 1861 went from William H. Seward to William Dayton in Paris. The letter is document 129 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Seward's June orders to Paris dealt with the terms of French neutrality as it took form. Every clause on trade and ships could help or hurt the South. The letter armed Dayton to contest the details, not just the headline, of the French stand. Details of trade and ships filled most of the case the Union made in Paris. Contest the details he did, in note after note through the French file.
frus-1861-d229:
The State Department sent word to Mr. Fogg on 6 August 1861, over Seward's name. Congress received it as Document 229 in the papers printed with the President's message that year. The letter comes from the first summer of the Civil War, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1861-d29:
A letter dated 8 July 1861 went from William H. Seward to Henry Sanford in Brussels. It is document 29 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Mid July found the Union army about to march on Richmond, with high hopes at home. Seward's letters abroad in those weeks spoke with bold faith in a short war.
