Multi-spot disease is hard to spot because scans can look much like pancreatic cancer, so careful checks matter before treatment is chosen.
pmc-13315629:
Adrien Paschier and colleagues compared eye antiseptics in the lab in 2026 for killing germs tied to conjunctivitis and lid inflammation. Propamidine 0.1 percent was tested against hexamidine, cethexonium bromide, and picloxydine on five Gram-positive bacterial strains at set contact times from 2 to 15 minutes.

All products killed bacteria, with strength varying by strain and time. Propamidine acted fast, reaching its peak reduction within two minutes against Staphylococcus epidermidis, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and Propionibacterium acnes. A drop of more than five log units counted as bactericidal. Such speed data can guide choice of antiseptic before eye care or surgery.
pmc-13315729:
Mingjun Ma and a very large team show in 2026 how the gene regulator EZH2 creates a cholesterol weakness in ovarian cancer that a drug can hit. Ovarian cancer is the deadliest gynecologic cancer, mostly through spread, and EZH2 is often raised in tumors and tied to metabolic change.

High EZH2 levels marked both primary and spread tumors and tracked with poor outlook. Silencing EZH2 cut tumor growth and spread. The regulator switched on an NF-kappaB and Rap1A path and reset cholesterol handling through SREBP2 and TMED10. The team then identified napabucasin as a compound that exploits this metabolic dependence to suppress spread.
pmc-13316429:
Erhan Yarar sets out a 2026 framework paper on how cell membranes may shape joint signaling among three receptor families: cannabinoid receptors, smell receptors found outside the nose, and TRP channels. The core claim is cautious: shared presence in a membrane patch does not prove true higher-order teamwork.

His method, named MECS-BER, locks one membrane starting state, one near outcome, and one three-part assembly before any test begins. Gates check that each arm is engaged, and a statistic called kappa tests whether a three-way effect beats pair-only math. Practice matrices and simulations prove the logic works, but real biology verdicts await full datasets. Kidney niches are sketched as first test grounds, with no assembly claimed as proven.
pmc-13317029:
Érica Torres de Almeida Piovesan and co-authors link, in a 2026 Brazilian study, town-level dental service coverage with oral health in five-year-olds. Data came from the national oral health survey SB Brasil 2023, merged with town coverage records over time.

Towns fell into four coverage paths, from always-low to always-high. Children in towns with medium-high or medium-low coverage had lower odds of the painful fallout of untreated decay than those in always-low towns, with odds ratios of 0.59 and 0.63 in the adjusted models. Always-high towns showed the lowest odds of needing urgent care. About eighteen percent of child differences traced to town gaps, backing wider public dental coverage.
pmc-13320029:
Omer Mohammed and co-authors pool studies on a sugar lowering drug class after valve repair in a 2026 review. A new heart valve placed through a leg vessel fixes a tight valve, yet heart failure risk and other harms linger after the fix. Whether the drug class, first built for diabetes, also guards these patients was the question.

Six studies with 35075 patients in total, one trial and five records studies, were pooled with checks for bias. Drug use tracked with lower rates of major heart events, heart failure hospital stays, and death from any cause in the pooled counts. Proof grades stayed low, though, due to mixed study types. A firm trial is needed to settle whether the gain is real.
pmc-13320329:
Shohei Okusa and co-authors survey drooling in Parkinson disease at a Tokyo hospital in a 2026 study of body system burden. Extra saliva pooling is common in this illness yet poorly tied to gut, bladder, and swallow faults in past work, and few patients know shots exist that can dry the flow. Forms plus records for clinic patients over three months in late 2025 gave the data.

Among 208 patients, 116 met the study mark for drooling, and they skewed male with longer illness and higher drug doses. Drooling tracked solo with both body system scores and swallow scores after wide checks. Yet only about a third of droolers saw it as a problem, and very few knew of the shot option. Three drooler types split by burden level may guide tailored care.
pmc-13320429:
Yusuke Ota and co-authors grow slime films inside hospital waste water in place in a 2026 study of drug resistance. Hospital drains are feared as hot spots where germs trade drug proof genes, yet the live part those films play was ill defined. Films grown in real drain flow were read by gene scans, voice scans, and culture next to the free floating water crowd.

Films held more mass and more of a key drug proof gut germ than the water itself, and they packed a wider set of top tier proof genes. Transfer ready gene carriers ran hot in films and voiced more there too. Culture proof of a feared proof gene showed in four film strains and one water strain. Films act as stores that may seed spread.
pmc-13321029:
Valentina Mastrorilli and a large team test a paired treatment for long standing spinal cord injury in a 2026 animal study. Injury leaves lasting inflammation, scar glial growth, neuron loss, and myelin damage, causing weakness and nerve pain. Botulinum toxin type A eased harm in early injury, but its value in the chronic phase was untested.

Mice with severe chest level injury received electrical muscle stimulation on a set schedule, then a single spinal dose of toxin or salt water 15 days after injury. Recovery was tracked for up to 60 days, along with nerve pain and tissue measures for glial shape, neuron survival, and myelin proteins. Milder injury groups were also included to judge breadth.
pmc-13322829:
Siyuan Yang, Lei Wang and Jianyun Nie examine mitochondria as a treatment target in triple-negative breast cancer, in a 2026 article. This cancer type lacks the three usual receptors, spreads early and often resists standard drugs, leaving few targeted options.

Mitochondria help drive growth, spread and drug resistance by running several fuel pathways at once, covering oxygen use, fat burning and glutamine use. Their division, fusion and recycling also shape whether tumour cells live or die, and they influence immune responses and cell death routes. The authors weigh small drugs, nano-scale delivery and drug pairs against these weak points, while noting problems of selectivity, flexible metabolism and slow progress into clinic use.
pmc-13322929:
Haoran Gao and colleagues compare two endoscopic routes for broad-based lumbar disc herniation, in a 2026 retrospective study. Records cover 184 patients with single-level disease treated between June 2023 and October 2024, split between the transforaminal route and the interlaminar route, with the same mecobalamin regimen after surgery.

Pain scores at three months formed the main outcome, alongside disability scores, operating measures and complications. The interlaminar group had lower pain at three months and lower disability at three days, plus shorter operations, fewer X-ray checks and more disc material removed. Nerve function improved in both groups without a clear gap, and overall success and complication rates were alike.
pmc-13323029:
Yaoqiang Zhu and co-authors test treated fishpond sediment as a cleaner for metal-contaminated soil, in a 2026 plant study with spinach. Soil carried chromium, copper and zinc together, and amendments included plain sediment and sediment carrying zinc oxide or silica nanoparticles.

Both plain and treated sediments cut the share of each metal that plants could take up, with the zinc oxide version working best in their measures. Metal levels in roots and shoots fell, while photosynthesis and chlorophyll improved and stress signals eased. The authors infer that root uptake control linked to cytoskeleton-related processes may take part, though they relied on indirect signs rather than direct cell images.
pmc-13323229:
Jorge Robalino-Diaz and co-authors study how uneven data across sites weakens federated anomaly detection, in a 2026 analysis of Internet of Things and medical device networks. Training without centralising data protects privacy, yet sites differ strongly in what their sensors record.

Their hybrid dataset held 71,980 behaviour traces drawn from three public sources, with 22,698 traces used for testing. A central model scored near-perfect detection, while the federated version kept high overall discrimination but missed many true anomalies, with recall falling hardest in medical device data. Calibration also worsened. The authors warn that a strong headline score can hide failure where detection matters most, in clinical settings.
pmc-13323329:
Liping Li, Zhonghua Zhang and Lin Zong survey artificial intelligence in neurovascular surgery, in a 2026 narrative review spanning diagnosis, intervention and long-term prediction. Tools covered include machine learning, deep learning, computer vision and language processing applied to scans, records and operating room inputs.

Algorithms help spot large vessel blockages, describe aneurysm shape and separate bleeding types with speed and precision. Models also predict rupture risk, stroke recovery and complications after treatment. Surgical uses run from planning simulations to robot-assisted work and live guidance, though most operating room studies stay early or single-centre. Bias, weak general reach, opacity, privacy and regulation remain the main barriers the authors list.
pmc-13323929:
Christos Savvidis and Ioannis Ilias write a 2026 letter to the editor on clock and microbe misalignment in fatty liver disease. They respond to work by Rusman and others on gut microbes in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, published in the World Journal of Experimental Medicine.

Beyond which microbes live in the gut, timing matters: the gut-liver axis runs on daily rhythms shared between host clocks and microbes. Social jetlag scrambles metabolite timing, weakens the gut barrier and worsens liver injury in their account, with bile acid signalling knocked off rhythm. Time-restricted eating heads the clock-based fixes they cite, said to reprogramme liver gene activity and cut liver fat.
pmc-13324129:
Changhao Le and co-authors compare brain responses under two robot-assisted therapy modes after stroke, in a 2026 study using near-infrared brain imaging. The study enrolled 23 chronic stroke patients and the same number of matched healthy controls, who performed upper limb tasks in active movement mode and mirror therapy mode.

A 48-channel system tracked activation across frontal, motor and sensory areas, plus hemisphere balance and resting connections with eyes open and closed. Both groups activated widely under both modes in the reported tests, with task effects in the target regions. Activation levels were set against arm function scores to probe brain-behaviour links. The authors aim to guide which robot mode suits which stage of stroke recovery.
pmc-13326429:
Xu Zhu and co-authors simulate spine straightening surgery for severe ankylosing spondylitis kyphosis in a 2026 modeling study. Choosing which vertebra to cut changes the loads on screws and cages, and a wrong pick risks hardware failure.

Finite element models cut at T12, L1, L2, or L3, each with screw-rod fixation and a fusion cage. Total shift fell step by step down the spine, from 6.88 mm at T12 to 2.26 mm at L3 in the models. Peak screw stress peaked at L2, near 191.35 MPa, yet stayed under device limits throughout. The L3 cut gave the steadiest build with well-spread stress. One case fed the model, so wider checks are needed.
pmc-13326629:
Fabian Kerwagen, Maximilian Bauser, and Stefan Störk write a 2026 editorial on hearing congestion in heart failure through the voice. Fluid buildup drives hospital returns, yet symptoms and weight checks catch its shifts poorly.

The editorial discusses a pilot study by Riehle and colleagues on AI voice analysis in acute heart failure care. Across two centers in Germany and the United States, 79 patients gave daily voice samples until discharge. Their natriuretic peptide levels started high, at 9400 pg per mL, and they shed about 5 kg over a mean stay of 7 days. A learning model told admission from discharge voices. The editors weigh promise against proof still needed.
pmc-13328029:
Peng Dai and co-authors profile acute pancreatitis across three data layers in a 2026 study. The sudden pancreatic inflammation mixes immune turmoil, metabolic rewiring, and gut microbe shifts that single-method studies see only in part. Blood gene activity, plasma metabolites, and stool microbes were measured in 15 patients and 15 matched healthy controls.

Gene profiling found 4,776 altered genes, including 409 immune genes clustered in inflammatory pathways. Metabolite testing found 296 altered compounds. Nine of them separated patients from controls with AUC values above 0.75 in their screen. Microbe makeup and function also shifted clearly. Joint profiling may yield marker panels that sort patients earlier and more sharply.
pmc-13328629:
Taslima Khanam and co-authors examine privacy risks in shared brain-signal learning in a 2026 study. Brain-computer systems use EEG signals that can reveal personal traits. Federated learning trains models without gathering raw signals in one place, yet attackers may still guess who took part.

The team built a federated motor imagery system and tested four attack types, covering records, features, model updates, and client identity. Plain federated training gave weak protection on its own. Adding differential privacy cut attack success a lot, most of all for update and identity attacks. A strict setting protected best but hurt accuracy. A middle setting gave the best balance, the authors conclude.
pmc-13329229:
Sandeep Dey and co-authors reply in 2026 to a letter about their trial of pain relief for spine fusion surgery. The trial tested ropivacaine alone and with added dexmedetomidine or morphine in back muscles. The reply thanks the letter writer and answers two queries about rescue fentanyl use and pain scoring.

On rescue use, Dey clarifies that fentanyl ran only while pain scores stayed at or above the set limit, and stopped once pain fell below it. Nearly all patients needed rescue at some point, the reply states. On scoring, the authors give time-weighted average pain scores for the three groups and note group differences. The morphine mix group showed the lowest average among the values reported.
pmc-13329329:
Ke-Yun Chao and a large team compare three tools for Chinese to Japanese translation in clinic visits in a 2026 study. Language gaps can harm safety and fairness when skilled interpreters are scarce. The team recorded heart and lung outpatient visits between December 2024 and November 2025 and translated the spoken exchanges with ChatGPT, Google Translate, and UD Talk.

In total, 20 visits with 2,450 exchanges were checked. Skilled medical interpreters scored accuracy, and Japanese-speaking lay readers scored satisfaction. ChatGPT scored a median of 5.0 on both scales in the reported results, ahead of the other two tools at 2.0 in those summaries. The authors suggest such tools can aid multilingual care as a support, not a replacement.
pmc-13329729:
Neda Nikpour Rashidabad, Ashley D. Keiser, and Masoud Hashemi study perennial living mulches of clover and grass in a 2026 report. Mixes varied from pure clover to pure Kentucky bluegrass, with or without added root fungi. The team measured leaf traits, growth, carbon and nitrogen in shoots and roots, and forage quality.

A clover-heavy mix gave the most shoot growth and leaf colour in the reported results. With fungi added, that mix also held the most shoot carbon and nitrogen. Fungi lifted photosynthesis and root size across treatments. Clover gave more protein, fat, and calcium, while grass gave more dry matter and fibre traits. Pairing legume and grass with fungi balanced yield and quality best, the authors conclude.
pmc-13330629:
Mengqin Tao and colleagues trace how early lead exposure drives anxiety and low mood in mice in a 2026 study. Dams drank water with 100 ppm lead from pregnancy through weaning, and pups kept drinking it to day 60 after birth. Behaviour tests and brain checks focused on the medial prefrontal cortex.

Exposed offspring showed anxiety and depression-like behaviour plus neuron shape damage in that brain area in the reported results. Lead shut down a pathway where AMPK supports ACSS2, cutting a chemical tag on histones that keeps synapse genes on. Restoring the pathway with a supplement rescued synapse proteins and eased behaviour. The authors nominate boosting ACSS2 as a treatment idea.
pmc-13332429:
Flurina Staubli and co-authors tested freeze-storable cartilage modules for rebuilding jaw bone in a 2026 large-animal study. Their approach copies natural development: a soft cartilage template is placed in a defect and remodels into living, vessel-fed bone, a route barely tried in the face, where bone normally forms directly.

The modules are devitalized cartilage that keeps the instructive signals in its matrix without needing living donor cells. In ten goats with clefts on both sides of the upper jaw, one side received a module and the other the standard graft of the animal's own hip bone. Scans and tissue measures showed the module side regrew and remodeled bone no worse than the graft side early on. In rats, modules kept their bone-forming power after 9 months in frozen storage, supporting an off-the-shelf product for facial repair.
pmc-13333529:
Hao Zhou and colleagues review in 2026 whether the brain's daily rhythms can be harnessed to restore movement after stroke. Stroke leaves more survivors with motor disability than any other condition. Standard rehabilitation plateaus for many, because fatigue, thin intensity, and flagging motivation cap what practice can do.

The reviewers assemble evidence that circadian and ultradian rhythms govern neural plasticity and the feedback loops that rebuild motor control. So the same training may land differently depending on the brain's rhythmic state. They survey studies tying sensorimotor rhythms and motor-network connectivity after stroke to recovery trajectories. They examine neurofeedback and EEG-based modulation techniques that try to steer those rhythms. Gaps remain: the causal chain from rhythm to recovery is not fully mapped, and ward-ready protocols lag the laboratory findings. The authors pitch rhythm-aware rehabilitation as a layer on top of conventional therapy rather than a replacement.
pmc-13333629:
Qianxue Wei and co-authors looked back at a combined treatment for locally advanced cervical cancer in a 2026 retrospective study. They tested chemotherapy plus immunotherapy given before radical radiotherapy, a sequence meant to shrink tumors early and improve control.

The team reviewed 60 patients with stage IIIA to IVA cancer treated between June 2022 and July 2024. Thirty received the combined approach and thirty received radiotherapy with or without chemotherapy. Response in the combined group reached 93.3 percent before radiotherapy and 100 percent afterward. Two-year progression-free survival was higher with the combination, at 82.5 percent against 66.0 percent for the comparison group, and bowel side effects from radiation were less common. Immune side effects stayed mild, supporting further study of this sequence.
pmc-13334429:
Ohood Sallam and co-authors tested two bacteria-killing viruses as food safety tools in a 2026 study. Phage SW03 targets Salmonella enterica and phage CF03 targets Escherichia coli O157:H7, and the team checked how they perform inside real foods under storage conditions.

SW03 came from municipal sewage and CF03 from camel feces. Both were applied to artificially contaminated beef, chicken, and lettuce held at 4 and 21 degrees Celsius, with heavy starting loads for a stringent test. Antibacterial action showed within 4 hours and deepened by 24 hours. Lettuce at room temperature gave the largest cuts, around 4.0 log units for SW03 and 3.5 for CF03. Activity persisted in the cold, though weaker, and both phages also reduced biofilms. The work supports phage biocontrol for fresh foods.
pmc-13336229:
Emylly Lopes Theodoro and co-authors mapped oral problems linked to long COVID in a 2026 scoping review. Mouth symptoms receive little attention next to fatigue and breathlessness, yet they affect eating, speaking, and quality of life.

Following the JBI method, the team searched six databases for primary studies in Portuguese, English, and Spanish published between March 2020 and December 2024. Fifteen studies were analyzed descriptively. The most frequent findings were taste changes, dry mouth, chewing difficulty, gum bleeding, periodontitis, and changes in the teeth themselves. Age, other illnesses, and social inequality influenced how long symptoms persisted, and women were affected more often. The authors call for multiprofessional care and clearer dental guidelines for long COVID patients.
pmc-13337029:
Yeonsu Jeong and colleagues blend two ferroelectrics to strengthen memory films in a 2026 study. Pairing two-dimensional CIPS nanosheets with a ferroelectric polymer lets their dipoles reinforce each other. A balanced solvent mix spread the sheets evenly and helped the polymer form its active crystal phase.

The hybrid film gained nearly 75% more remnant polarization while needing a 15% lower switching field than the plain polymer in reported measures. Transistors using it as the gate layer kept data beyond 10,000 s and endured over 300 switching cycles in device tests. Light could also partly reset the filler, giving multi-level optical memory. Cooperative dipoles may power flexible, low-energy memory and logic.
pmc-13337429:
Jian Wang and colleagues untangle an infection that impersonated cancer in a 2026 case report and literature review. A 53-year-old Chinese man with untreated hepatitis B arrived with cough, chest pain, and back pain. Scans showed a lung mass, swollen lymph nodes, and widespread bone lesions glowing on PET imaging, a picture that screamed metastatic lung cancer.

Repeated biopsies found no cancer. Gene sequencing of lung wash fluid and spine tissue instead identified Mycobacterium kansasii, spread through lungs and bones. Immune testing then revealed autoantibodies against interferon-gamma, an acquired immune defect that invites such infections. Treatment was complicated by liver trouble and high hepatitis B levels. The case warns against anchoring on cancer when scans mislead.
pmc-13339029:
Jiho Shin and colleagues review new routes to zeolite pore structures once thought out of reach in a 2026 perspective. Zeolites serve in catalysis and capture, yet standard hot-water synthesis misses many feasible frameworks. Unusual chemistries are now opening those gaps.

Five routes are highlighted, from rebuilding crystals for tiny pores to phosphonium-guided ultra-open frameworks. One family holds fewer than 13.2 framework atoms per volume unit in the reported density measure, marking extreme openness. Uses include drying, carbon capture, and cleanup. Cost, scale-up, and guide chemical waste remain hurdles, but the expanded toolbox reshapes what zeolites can do.
pmc-13339629:
Sarah J. Madlener and colleagues shine light on sodium pyruvate clusters to mimic aged sea salt air particles in a 2026 study. Pyruvate gathers in such aerosols, and salt surroundings may change its light chemistry. Tiny clusters were made by electrospray and weighed with high precision.

Ultraviolet spectra, light-driven breakup rates, and collision tests mapped the paths. Clusters mainly shed whole sodium pyruvate units, while rarer breaks ran about a hundred times slower as reported. Light first cut a carbon bond, sometimes passing an electron to a neighbor and releasing carbon dioxide. Quantum calculations assigned the light bands behind each step.
pmc-13339829:
Evangelos Smith and a large team use liquid crystals to sense nitrogen dioxide on metal surfaces in a 2026 study. Nitrogen oxides harm air quality, and cheap optical detection at low levels is wanted. A common liquid crystal coated gold, silver, and copper films.

The crystal lay flat on gold and copper but stood upright on silver before exposure, as microscopy and infrared data showed. At 10 ppm nitrogen dioxide in nitrogen gas, alignment flipped in metal-specific ways as reported, with gold showing a reversible switch. Theory linked flips to gas binding. Crystal films could thus report invisible surface chemistry by eye.
pmc-13340129:
Jusail CP and colleagues profile immune responses in human leptospirosis using multi-omics in a 2026 study. This neglected waterborne disease varies widely, and blood immune signaling during acute illness was little known. White blood cells from confirmed patients and healthy controls were compared.

Gene profiling found over 5,800 changed genes, mostly raised, tied to inflammation paths such as TNF and interferon signaling as reported. Protein data and network analysis highlighted shared immune factors. Whole-blood and cell infection models checked key factors directly. The integrated picture names host signals that could become severity markers or treatment targets.
pmc-13341229:
Preparing a glide path before root canal shaping affects instrument damage, in a 2026 study by Merve Gökyar and colleagues. Sixty extracted lower molars were split into three groups of 20: rotary glide path, manual glide path with a steel K-file, or none.

Each canal was then shaped with a fresh nickel-titanium rotary file, imaged by scanning electron microscopy before and after. Tip bending was the commonest starting flaw everywhere. After shaping, canals without a glide path showed more microcracks, and blade distortion, surface pitting, and fractures also differed clearly between groups. A prepared glide path, by either method, appears to spare the shaping file.
pmc-13341429:
Sleep, body signals, and mood together separate depression from health in a 2026 cross-sectional study by Di Jiang's group. The 101 people fell into healthy (47), subthreshold depression (30), and major depression (24) groups, assessed by questionnaires, overnight sleep recording, heart rate checks, and eye tracking.

Groups differed on many symptom scales plus sleep timing scores and a rhythm index. After adjustment, anxiety score, a dream-related questionnaire score, and longer REM latency stayed tied on their own to depressive status. A combined model reached an AUC of 0.942, barely above the clinical-only model at 0.930, suggesting fancy measures add little beyond good symptom scales.
pmc-13341529:
A stubborn scarred esophagus is treated with a new combination in a 2026 case report by Xinhui He and colleagues. The 21-year-old man developed severe narrowing along the whole esophagus after accidentally swallowing acidic toilet cleaner, and 13 earlier endoscopic procedures had failed to hold it open.

Doctors paired balloon dilation with transplantation of acellular dermal matrix, a scaffold material, in a first reported use for this problem. The procedure succeeded and brought clear short-term relief with better quality of life. One case cannot prove a therapy, but it offers a fresh option where repeated dilation alone keeps failing.
pmc-13343529:
Prabhdeep Kaur and Jesús Rivera-Nieves set out a standardized stool transplant protocol in 2026 for triggering gut inflammation in mice that lack interleukin-10. Such mice develop colitis only through their microbes, but timing swings wildly between facilities, and drug tricks used to sync disease also injure the gut lining.

Recipient mice aged eight to ten weeks receive repeated oral doses over nine weeks from donor mice whose double gene knockout breeds a colitis-driving microbial community. Disease arrives evenly across cohorts without chemical triggers, keeping the mechanism purely microbial. The platform suits tissue, immune, and microbiome follow-ups and gives bowel disease researchers a steadier test bed for microbe-based treatments.
pmc-13343929:
Sharon K. Kuss-Duerkop and co-authors grade a targeted sequencing test for tuberculosis germs in 2026. Fast, accurate naming of mycobacteria and their drug resistance guides early care. The Deeplex Myc-TB assay reads many gene targets straight from sputum or grown isolates. The team benchmarked it against standard methods.

Across 78 isolates and 102 sputum samples, the test stayed fully specific, wrongly naming nothing. Sensitivity for the tuberculosis complex reached 92.7 percent in isolates and 97.6 percent in sputum, though rarer slow-growing species from sputum scored lower, and many sputum runs for those species came back invalid. Resistance calls matched reference results about 92 percent of the time, rising near 97 percent without unclear variants.
pmc-13346029:
John F Shepherd, Caroline W Maloney, and Paul L Linsky review robot-assisted chest surgery in children in 2026. Robots spread fast in adult thoracic work but slowly in pediatrics. Chest-center removals suit the robot's precise hands in tight spaces. The team gathered every study and case report on patients under 18.

Twelve reports made up the whole evidence base, a thin shelf, yet all pointed the same way: operations finished safely with few complications and rare switches to open surgery. Fans cite steadier vision, finer dexterity, and better surgeon ergonomics than camera-only surgery. The authors judge the approach feasible and safe while calling the literature too sparse for strong claims.
pmc-13348029:
Runjie Xia and colleagues hunt overlooked toxins in lake algal blooms. Their study came out in 2026. It uses a fragment-search method. Blooms in Muskegon, Michigan, supplied a fraction library. Two new micropeptins were isolated from it. One bears a stretched tyrosine unit. A known acid was also confirmed. Combined spectral tools did that work.

A network query language tagged whole peptide classes. It also tagged their tweaks across all fractions. Coverage widened beyond hand-picked isolates. One new compound slowed a human enzyme. That enzyme ties to exposure effects. Lake Erie field samples held recurring micropeptins. They held no microcystins, though. Toxin checks that watch microcystins alone are thus challenged.
pmc-13349929:
Julia Haldina and co-authors reviewed in 2026 a brain signal method for measuring vision without relying on a patient's own answers. Standard acuity testing needs cooperation, which fails in young children, people with cognitive problems, or suspected faking.

The P300 wave appears when a person consciously sorts a rare target from common stimuli, so tests can use ordinary eye-chart shapes such as Landolt Cs. Unlike earlier visual potentials that track only the first steps of seeing, this signal reflects conscious perception. It matched real acuity losses in lazy eye better than older methods. The authors present it as a useful partner to standard electrical vision testing.
pmc-13350129:
Kaizhi Wen and colleagues tested a six-herb traditional formula, Huyan-I, against kidney ageing and scarring in a 2026 study. The patented mix is used clinically for early chronic kidney disease, where cell ageing and the inflammatory signals aged cells release drive damage.

Chemical analysis found 211 ingredients, with dozens detected in the blood of treated mice. In naturally old mice and aged human kidney cells, the formula cut aged cell counts and ageing markers, calmed a STAT3 and NF-kB driven inflammatory chain, and eased tube injury and scarring. Computer predictions had pointed to exactly that pathway, giving the traditional remedy a defined mechanism to test further.
pmc-13351529:
Peng Jiang and co-authors present a 2026 case report with a literature review on hot spots in adaptive radiotherapy for cervical cancer. A patient treated on the Ethos system, version 2.0, developed areas of excess dose inside the target during daily adaptive sessions. The team links the problem to the target edge sitting near the collimator leaf boundary.

When the target sits that close, leaf movement is limited and dose shaping loses flexibility. Jiang and colleagues propose a revised online workflow that corrects the target shift before planning. The fix lowered the chance of hot spots and offers a practical reference for safer, more stable adaptive treatment.
pmc-13351929:
Mai Taguchi and co-authors build a high-throughput platform to mutate F1-ATPase, the rotary motor that makes ATP, and watch single molecules spin. Single-molecule rotation assays reveal how residues couple chemistry to motion, but testing mutants one by one is slow. Their 2026 study combines cell-free protein synthesis with a multiplexed rotation assay, completing the whole cycle within ten hours.

Two positions were mutated exhaustively. At the catalytic base position, almost every substitution destroyed activity; only aspartate, which keeps the crucial negative charge, worked partially. At a second conserved position near a proposed phosphate exit tunnel, variants were tolerated more broadly, with activity tracking side-chain size and water-avoidance. Smaller substitutions there increased the inactive fraction, suggesting the tunnel matters for occasional phosphate release linked to inhibition rather than routine turnover. The authors present the workflow for rapid mutational profiling of rotary enzymes.
pmc-13354029:
Abdulaziz Al Shaibani and colleagues report two pelvic kidneys paired with a two-horned womb in 2026. Both kidneys sitting in the pelvis is exceptionally rare, and shared developmental roots link kidney and womb anomalies. A 37-year-old woman with no urinary history presented with left flank pain.

Ultrasound showed both kidneys in the pelvis and a 5 mm non-blocking left kidney stone. Pain relief and fluids were advised, and a scan six months later confirmed the stone had passed. MRI during pregnancy mapped kidneys in the presacral and pouch spaces with unusual vessel origins. Kidney tests stayed normal throughout, and she delivered by planned caesarean at 37 weeks and 3 days without complications.
pmc-13355229:
Moshe Z Shapiro and co-authors studied in 2026 whether social factors shaped use of health monitoring among World Trade Center responders. The program offers regular checks to people who helped after the attacks, whose illness rates link to income, race, and other social factors. Records for 15,515 members from 2008 to 2024 were compared across groups.

Visit timing differed by less than a month across race, income, schooling, and other traits, which the authors call a strong result. Black and Hispanic members in fact came slightly sooner than white and non-Hispanic peers. The authors note the group still has fewer women, older people, and people of color than the wider public.
pmc-13355529:
Maria Ilyas and co-authors write a 2026 letter on low magnesium in patients taking oral EGFR blocker drugs for cancer. Low magnesium is a known effect of the injected forms of these drugs, but whether the pills cause the kidney to waste magnesium was unclear. The team reviewed 43 patients at one Florida center who started the pills from 2014 to 2024.

Eight patients developed low magnesium within a year, seven of them on one older drug. Yet on close review, every case had another cause, such as chemotherapy, water pills, gut losses, or acute illness. None met the bar for kidney wasting caused by the pill itself, which suggests other factors explain most cases.
pmc-13355729:
Christine M Pfeiffer and co-authors report in 2026 how blood folate forms changed in Ethiopian women given salt fortified with iodine and folic acid. Folate shortage causes anemia and raises the risk of spine birth defects, and Ethiopia has very high rates. Women got plain iodized salt or salt with a lower or higher folic acid dose for about six months.

All measured folate forms rose in step with dose, with the main form rising about fivefold at the higher dose and about threefold at the lower dose. No gaps appeared at the start. The pattern matched earlier supplement trials, backing double-fortified salt as a way to lift folate status.
pmc-13356729:
Álvaro Gimeno Peiró and co-authors present a 2026 clinical image case of a 55-year-old man diagnosed with pulmonary artery intimal sarcoma, an extremely rare cancer often mistaken for a lung blood clot. He had five months of chronic cough and general symptoms, and scans showed a large left lung mass pressing into the chest center and the pulmonary trunk, with tumor clot.

Instead of surgery, the team used an ultrasound-guided scope through the airway to take needle samples from the left upper lobe bronchus, with no complications. Cell tests showed a poorly differentiated high-grade sarcoma with a gene change that fit the diagnosis. The authors highlight the method for patients who cannot have surgery.
pmc-13358829:
Michael H Udin and co-authors study the scaffolding inside lung tumors in a 2026 paper. Some lung adenocarcinomas spread to lymph nodes while others, at the same stage, do not. The team asked whether the pattern of collagen, the tough protein that gives tissue its frame, differs between the two kinds.

They examined tissue from 120 patients treated at a Buffalo cancer center, using stains and a light-based imaging method to map fiber layout. Tumors that had spread showed collagen fibers lined up in one direction, while others crossed in a crisscross. Ordered fibers may give cancer cells a road out, a clue that could one day flag spread-prone tumors early.
pmc-13360429:
Charlotte E. J. Toomes and co-authors review new lab models of multiple myeloma in a 2026 paper. This blood cancer grows inside bone marrow, where the tissue around the cancer helps it spread and resist drugs, yet flat lab dishes copy that setting poorly. The disease is still incurable, so better models matter for testing treatments.

The review covers 3D and engineered platforms that mimic the marrow's mix of cells, bone, and blood flow more closely. In these settings, cancer cells act more as they do in a patient, including how they answer or resist drugs. The authors argue that such models can sharpen early drug screening and safety checks. They may also reveal new drug targets and speed the path to better care.
pmc-13363329:
Nursulu Nurpeissova and colleagues present a 2026 social study on national identity, gender roles, and state stability in Kazakhstan. Post-Soviet states face pressure to forge a shared identity while views on gender shift. The team surveyed 284 mostly young urban participants and ran three focus groups, then modeled which attitudes best predicted a sense of national stability.

A blended outlook, national uniqueness joined with gender integration, was the strongest predictor, and national identity alone also helped. Views on gender roles by themselves showed no direct link. Focus groups explained the pattern: equality framed as foreign import drew pushback, while equality woven into the national story won support. The authors advise reformers to root gender policy in the country's own narrative.
pmc-13363829:
Lan Ju and colleagues report a 2026 gene hunt for long mesocotyls in sorghum, the seedling stem that pushes shoots up through deep soil. Deep sowing helps sorghum reach moist ground, but only if seedlings can emerge. Scanning 232 varied sorghum lines genome-wide, joined with gene activity reads, the team singled out one switch gene, SbERF60, whose natural promoter variants raise its activity and lengthen the stem.

Tests that raised or lowered the gene confirmed it drives elongation, and moving it improved deep-sown emergence in rice as well. The authors offer the gene and its promoter variants as direct targets for breeding sorghum that stands up reliably from deep planting, a need that grows with machine sowing.
pmc-13365129:

After two days in intensive care she recovered well. Four rounds of drug plus antibody therapy brought a partial response at six months, with more rounds planned.
pmc-13404329:
Mohammed Alonazi and co-authors built a movement-reading system in 2026 that mixes wearable sensors with video to judge athlete form and rehab progress. Coaches and therapists need steady checks on how a body moves during training and recovery. Their system pays selective attention to the richest signals from each source.

Features such as paths, angles, and skeleton motion over time were drawn from both streams and fused. A tuned deep learning sorter then named the movement being done. Scores reached about 88.4 percent on one movement dataset and near 88.0 percent on another named set. Mixed sensing beat either stream alone for messy real-world motion.
pmc-13404629: A correction notice from BMJ Paediatrics Open in 2026 fixes one line in an article by M J Russell and colleagues. That article described work to prevent cardiac arrest in children whose heart disease kept them on an intensive care unit. The notice is a correction only. It changes the funding line, swapping the Hospital Cardiac Services Charitable fund for the Birmingham Children's Hospital Charity, Help A Heart Appeal. That charity paid for a part-time nurse post for arrest prevention. No findings or methods of the article change.
pmc-13405029:
Umar Rehman and co-authors set out the COPANOS trial, a 2026 protocol testing gabapentin for distorted smell after viral infection. Parosmia makes familiar smells seem foul, and cases rose after the COVID-19 pandemic. An estimated 637,836 people in the United Kingdom live with the post-viral form, with no licensed treatment.

Adults aged 18 to 65 whose distortion has lasted between six months and five years will join the phase 3 trial. Half receive gabapentin, raised to at most 600 milligrams daily, and half a matching placebo, for eight weeks. Small earlier studies hinted low doses might help, but only a blinded trial can separate drug effect from natural recovery.
pmc-13406729:
Yusuf Saleem Khan and colleagues trace a new anticancer route for thymoquinone, a compound from black seed, in a 2026 study. Lung cancer cells of two types, A549 and SHP-77, were used alongside computer predictions. Focus falls on a small RNA, miR-155-5p, and the proteins it controls.

The transcription factor BACH1 proved a direct target of that RNA in reporter tests. Thymoquinone suppressed both the RNA and BACH1 after interferon stimulation in the reported experiments. Downstream, the invasion promoter MMP-9 also fell. Blocking the RNA or BACH1 directly copied the compound's effect, supporting the proposed chain from plant compound to slower cancer spread.
pmc-13408129:
Philippe Hernigou and co-authors follow, in 2026, hip osteoarthritis patients for fifteen years after an injection of their own concentrated bone marrow into the thigh bone. The question was whether intraosseous marrow concentrate, rich in stem cells counted as colony-forming units, delays the otherwise common march to total hip replacement, compared with matched conservative care in 434 hips.

By fifteen years only 16.1 percent of treated hips had converted to replacement against 40.1 percent of controls, and survival curves favoured treatment overall, in mild disease, and increasingly with higher stem-cell dose, a dose-response pattern supporting a real effect. No adverse events were recorded, and none of the treated patients who did convert needed revision surgery, against 8 percent of converting controls. Early, higher-dose treatment looked best.
pmc-13409329:
Zenab Khan, Hamza Amir, Muhammad Uzair, and Astad Sidhwa chart in 2026 a quarter century of American deaths tied to hemochromatosis, the iron-loading disorder that quietly scars liver, heart, and pancreas. Earlier national analyses predated the modern coding era, leaving trend data stale. Death-certificate data from 1999 to 2024 were mined from the national WONDER system, with the iron disorder counted whether it caused the death or merely contributed.

Age-adjusted rates were sliced by sex, race and Hispanic origin, region, age band, state, and urbanisation, and joinpoint statistics hunted for the years when trends bent. The design gives public health readers a contemporary map of who dies with this treatable condition and where disparities persist. Because bloodletting prevents most damage when the disorder is caught, persistent mortality signals missed diagnoses more than failed therapy.
pmc-13409629:
Stacia Wyman and colleagues deliver an uncomfortable quality-control finding in 2026 for therapeutic gene editing. The synthetic DNA templates used to write corrections into the genome arrive from the factory already containing typos. These single-stranded templates guide repair of CRISPR cuts, and standard checks cannot read them letter by letter. Deep sequencing of templates from three manufacturers, and of blood stem cells edited with them, exposed the errors.

Every template batch carried mistakes, at rates differing more than twofold between suppliers and clustered by sequence context. The errors were copied into the genome at rates matching their abundance in the batch. In the team's sickle cell correction programme, common errors would create mostly harmless globin variants. Rarer one-letter deletions could create thalassemia-like alleles. The authors argue regulators should require deep sequencing of templates in clinical submissions.
pmc-13411329:
Rashida Batool and colleagues review in 2026 chemical sensors that learn as they work. Sensors guard factories, the environment, and patients, yet nearly all rely on fixed materials and settings, which dulls them in messy real conditions. Adding learning promises sensors that adapt, self-correct, and stay sharp longer.

The review follows intelligence through the whole sensing chain: materials that shift response, hybrid builds, and learning software that reads signals. Adaptive designs fight drift, a slow slide in readings that plagues field sensors. Worked examples show material, device, and algorithm acting as one system. Open problems include material stability, scarce training data, energy use, and explaining what the learned system thinks it smells.
pmc-13411629:
Seung-Jae Lee, Jaehoon Bae, and Sang Hoon Lee comment in 2026 on what monthly blood data from southwest China reveal about immunity to SARS-CoV-2 after the Omicron waves. Over three thousand samples collected from late 2022 into 2024 track antibody strength as variants rolled through. Two forces frame their reading: immune imprinting and viral drift.

Later variants, above all JN.1, dodged neutralization far better than early Omicron strains. Past exposure speeds recall of old defenses yet narrows the making of fresh, broad ones. Vaccine design must reckon with that bias, the authors argue, rather than simply boosting yesterday's targets.
pmc-13411729:
Jingjing Zhang leads a team showing in 2026 that removing one gut protein from the mouse intestine protects against obesity and fatty liver. The protein, Faf2, helps handle fat-carrying particles in gut cells, yet its whole-body role was untested. Mice lacking it only in the intestine were fed normal or high-fat diets.

Knockout mice stayed leaner on both diets, handled glucose better, and resisted liver fat buildup. Their gut cells hoarded fat droplets and held back a key particle protein, so fewer fat parcels reached the body. Oddly, blood fat spiked higher after meals in tolerance tests. Gut length and surface fingers also grew, painting a mixed picture of blocked absorption with compensating growth.
pmc-13412429:
Julia Umińska and co-authors set a large Polish heart registry beside randomized trial evidence in a 2026 structured review of blood-thinning drugs after acute coronary syndrome. Three oral P2Y12 inhibitors, clopidogrel, prasugrel, and ticagrelor, anchor dual therapy after stenting, and trial results have not always agreed. The review lined up eight trials covering 40,724 patients against the PL-ACS registry's 15,933 matched patients.

Registry findings pointed the same way as trials: prasugrel or ticagrelor regimens beat clopidogrel on ischemic outcomes. Direct registry comparison of the two stronger drugs, though, diverged from the one head-to-head trial on most endpoints. The authors say no winner between prasugrel and ticagrelor is established, and bleeding differences demand care.
pmc-13413529:
Yonggang Xue and colleagues devise in 2026 a laminate trick that keeps curved satellite antenna ribs from warping as temperatures swing in orbit. Carbon-fibre ribs bend when heated because their arc turns in-plane expansion into out-of-plane lift, and standard theory mispredicts that expansion badly, causing errors up to 79.4 percent in symmetric designs. Their asymmetric stack uses nine plies on top and seven below from the same material batch, creating a deliberate expansion mismatch.

The mismatch generates a thermal moment that fights the curvature-driven lift directly. Against the symmetric design, thermal deformation fell by 50.4 percent, from 210 to 104 micrometres, in the tests reported. Prediction accuracy improved to under five percent error, and the method needs only ordinary materials and processing.
pmc-13414529:
Wong and colleagues pooled trial data in 2026 to test whether advanced ulcerative colitis therapies work as well and as safely in older adults as in younger patients. Older patients are often denied biologics and JAK blockers over safety fears, which may leave them undertreated. The post hoc analysis covered 2,841 participants from thirteen induction trials of eight therapies, comparing patients aged sixty and over with those under sixty.

Response, remission, and endoscopic improvement rates were similar across the age split, as were overall safety outcomes, with only minor variation between specific drugs. Hospitalization ran numerically higher in the older group, the one clear caution in the results. The authors conclude that age alone should not bar patients from advanced therapy. That withholding effective treatment from older adults on blanket safety grounds is not supported by the trial record.
pmc-13414629:
Marcia A. Docherty, Andrea L. Taylor, and Josh T. Duncan describe a refreshed transition program for new nurses at Island Health, evaluated in 2026. The health system has run the program since 2005 and rebuilt it for graduates entering practice during pandemic recovery, covering cohorts from 2022 to 2024.

Evaluation followed repeated Look, Think, Act cycles with graduates and other users shaping each round. Engagement, once scattered between almost zero and 36 percent, rose to between 14 and 61 percent. Graduates leaving within a year fell from 7 percent in 2021 to 4 percent in 2023. Casual positions also dropped sharply by 2024, which the authors credit to deliberate relationship building.
pmc-13415429:
Hiroyuki Tokue and co-authors build a planning framework for bleeding from the inferior epigastric artery, an abdominal wall vessel, in 2026. They reviewed sixty-two patients treated with catheter embolization, sorting cases into four types by the collateral route feeding the bleed. Types covered isolated wall bleeds, postpartum cases, pelvic fracture cases, and puncture injuries.

Embolization stopped bleeding on imaging in every case, yet clinical success averaged about 82 percent. Pelvic fracture cases fared worst, near 56 percent, and supplied all three rebleeds. A simple score using fracture type, a clotting disorder, and very low blood pressure tracked failure risk in steps.
pmc-13415529:
Zijuan Wang and a large team uncover a repair module built around the small protein tag UFM1, in 2026. Cells fix double strand DNA breaks by several routes, and non-homologous end joining is a fast, direct one. The team built a light activated UFM1 probe to catch its weak binding partners.

Mapping showed UFM1 touching core repair factors, including a floppy tail of the XRCC4 protein. A partner protein, Ku70, carries the UFM1 tag and helps XRCC4 lock the repair complex onto damaged DNA. Patient cells with defects in this tagging system repaired breaks poorly. The work links a little studied tag to genome protection and disease.
pmc-13416829:
Bingqing Wang and colleagues mine insect genomes for piggyBac transposons in the order Hymenoptera, in a study published in 2027. These mobile DNA pieces can cut and paste themselves, and labs use them as tools to move genes. Bees, wasps, and ants matter for farming and nature, yet their transposons were little explored.

Across 287 species, elements appeared in 137 genomes and fell into four groups. Tests showed two transposons, from a cuckoo bee and a mason bee, moved DNA about as well as a top engineered version. Attempts to boost them further gave mixed results. The pair adds strong new tools for genome work.
pmc-13418429:
Melis Selamoglu and colleagues survey family physicians in Istanbul about e-cigarettes as quit smoking aids, in a 2026 cross sectional study. Responses came from 243 doctors, collected online between August and October 2022. Most felt responsible for helping patients quit and trusted current medicines, yet views on vaping were strongly negative.

About four fifths rejected e-cigarettes as cessation aids or as safer than cigarettes. Worries centred on addictiveness, gateway effects, and health harm. Over half lacked confidence in their knowledge or in answering patient questions. Most would not recommend vaping even after other methods failed. Training and guidance are the authors' prescription.
pmc-13418929:
Alisha Dhiman and colleagues show that one part of a chromatin-opening machine is required for breast cancer cells to change form and spread. The machine, called SWI/SNF, comes in three forms, and the team focused on the PBRM1 part found only in the PBAF form. A growth signal normally pushes breast lining cells toward a loose, mobile state that seeds spread.

Cells missing PBRM1 could not finish that shape change in lab tests. Mouse breast tumors without the part also failed to spread to distant sites. The same pattern held across several mouse models of the disease. Blocking the PBAF form could therefore offer a new line of attack against metastatic breast cancer, the stage that drives most deaths from the disease.
pmc-13419929:
Hallas and colleagues propose widening drug safety watch: beyond side effects, to the way medicines are used. Side effect reporting misses misuse that no single clinician can see, such as odd doses, strange treatment lengths, or relapse patterns spread across a system. Their 2026 concept paper names the practice DU-Vigilance, drug utilization vigilance. It models the practice on signal detection. Real world datasets are screened without a prior suspicion, and anomalies surface for expert review.

The data would come from prescription registries, health records, and insurance claims, scanned continuously, since misuse patterns shift over time. The tools are borrowed from drug use research, but the stance is new: hypothesis generating rather than checking known worries. An anomaly is a question, not a verdict, and subject experts judge which ones matter. Folding this watch into pharmacovigilance, the authors argue, could catch prescribing problems years earlier and lift the quality of care.
pmc-13421129:
The Pan American Health Organization issued this 2026 outlook on the El Niño climate pattern expected during 2026 and 2027 and the health risks it brings across the Americas. Warm ocean conditions can drive both drought and flooding in different places at once.

The outlook divides the region into two broad patterns. Northern South America, Central America, the Caribbean, and the Amazon face hotter, drier conditions. Those conditions raise risks of drought, water shortage, food insecurity, wildfires, heat illness, and mosquito-borne disease. Parts of Ecuador, Peru, southern Brazil, Colombia, Paraguay, Argentina, and the southern United States face heavier rain, with flooding, landslides, displacement, and waterborne disease. Because the worst health effects often arrive in the year after onset, the organization urges sustained monitoring and early preparation, especially where poverty and weak services already strain health systems.
pmc-13421229:
Gao-Feng Liu leads a ten-author team investigating, in a 2026 study, a long non-coding RNA called MNX1-AS1 in non-small cell lung cancer. Long non-coding RNAs do not build proteins, yet they can steer gene activity, and earlier work had left this one's role in lung cancer unclear.

The team measured MNX1-AS1 in 40 paired tumour and healthy lung samples and found it raised in tumours, where higher levels tracked with poorer outlook. Silencing it in two lung cancer cell lines reduced growth, migration and invasion. The RNA works by soaking up a small regulatory RNA, miR-218-5p, which frees a gene named COMMD8 to act. Tumour growth in mice confirmed the chain, marking the pathway as a possible treatment target.
pmc-13421329:
Rima Baalbaki leads a very large collaboration reporting, in 2026, experiments on how new particles form in the atmosphere from gases released by ocean plankton. At CERN's CLOUD chamber, which simulates atmospheric conditions, they tested methanesulfonic acid — a breakdown product of a marine sulfur gas — whose role in particle birth was unclear.

Below minus ten degrees Celsius, the acid formed new particles with ammonia as effectively as sulfuric acid does, and the two acids together formed mixed clusters that nucleated faster still. It also drove particle growth at near-maximum rates in cool, humid air. Global simulations suggest the process boosts cloud-forming particles, especially over polar oceans, and may have mattered in the pre-industrial atmosphere.
pmc-13422329:
Taco Jan Prins leads a five-author case report, published in 2026, of a pregnant Karen woman on the Thailand-Myanmar border who arrived unable to walk, sit or drink unaided. Wilson's disease, an inherited failure to clear copper, was destroying her liver and brain; untreated, it is fatal, and successful pregnancies with symptoms this advanced are rare.

Her year-long decline, with the tell-tale copper rings in her eyes, pointed clinicians to the diagnosis despite scarce tests. Zinc treatment began at once, switching later to a copper-binding drug once it could be sourced. She delivered a healthy full-term girl, and after a year of treatment most symptoms had melted away while the baby thrived. The authors champion careful physical examination where laboratories are few.
pmc-13422829:
Jiaying Li leads an eight-author team surveying China, in a 2026 study, on whether the public would accept large language models in healthcare — and whether acceptance is fairly shared. Nearly thirty-six thousand adults across one hundred fifty cities rated their acceptance after a standard explanation of what these systems can do.

Average acceptance sat near sixty-four on a hundred-point scale, lower among people with chronic conditions and falling with age. Higher social status, prior digital-health use, self-confidence, warm neighbourhood ties and digital health literacy all nudged acceptance up, while loneliness and financial strain pulled it down. Tree analysis profiled the groups likeliest to refuse. The authors warn that uneven acceptance could widen health inequities as the tools spread.
pmc-13422929:
Mohamed and colleagues gather in 2026 what patients and clinicians actually think of virtual hospital care, hospital treatment delivered to patients at home through digital links. They drew only on qualitative studies, which record experiences in people's own words.

From more than fifteen thousand initial records, nineteen studies survived screening, covering 514 clinicians and 215 patients, mostly in high-income countries. Five themes shaped experience: whether the care felt valuable, confidence and readiness to use it, and digital and health literacy. The therapeutic relationship at a distance and the infrastructure behind it completed the five. The reviewers conclude that acceptance depends on tailoring the service to each person's needs, training clinicians properly, and designing the model together with its users. They flag a near absence of evidence from poorer countries.
pmc-13423029:
Ivan Bivolarski, Martin Dimitrov, and Hristo Dechev review how daily body-clock gene networks shape prostate cancer, drawing on RNA sequencing studies published through 2026. Their article links disrupted circadian rhythms with androgen receptor signaling, shifts in transcript forms, and pathways tied to metabolism and drug resistance.

Sequencing data, the authors argue, can reveal time-based gene patterns even in tumor samples collected without timing records, thanks to newer computing methods. They close by weighing chronotherapy, the idea of timing treatment to match biological rhythms, as a route toward more personal care. Clinical use remains limited, so the review frames circadian transcript patterns mainly as a guide for future trials and biomarker work.
pmc-13424029:
Henry Bair, Molly Orlick, and Zeba A Syed review how GLP-1 receptor agonists, the widely used diabetes and weight-loss drugs, affect the surface of the eye. Most eye reviews of these drugs focus on the retina, so the authors instead treat the tear system, lids, and cornea as one metabolic surface unit and weigh repair against unwanted reshaping.

Human evidence is still thin and observational, with diabetic cohorts showing less dry eye among users. Reports from weight-loss patients hint at tissue changes around the eye that need watching, the authors caution.
pmc-13424529:
Huang and colleagues report a 2026 lab study of naringin, a citrus compound, as a helper for chemotherapy in nasopharyngeal carcinoma, a cancer of the upper throat. They tested whether naringin makes cancer cells more sensitive to the drug paclitaxel.

Forcing the enzyme up or blocking it with a drug shifted the paclitaxel response, which supports its role. A food compound that sharpens one drug, through a named enzyme, is a focused research lead.
pmc-13425029:
Shraddha Uprety and colleagues published a 2026 letter describing itching as an overlooked sign of leprosy. Their patient was a 57-year-old woman with a severely itchy red plaque on her forehead that had lasted six months. Biopsy showed granulomas around skin structures and nerves, while stains for acid-fast bacilli stayed negative, and the team diagnosed tuberculoid leprosy from the combined clinical and tissue findings.

Readers learn why itch can mislead clinicians toward other skin conditions and delay care in areas where leprosy remains common. The authors link the symptom to nerve injury and inflammatory mediators, note dry skin from sweat gland damage, and describe starting multidrug therapy planned for six months.
pmc-13425529:
Wang and co-authors widen the job description of a small brain nucleus in this 2026 narrative review. The review argues it equally integrates emotion, mood, and sleep.

Its projections to the lateral habenula, a disappointment-processing center, regulate aversion, addiction-related behavior, and mood, while specific cell circuits govern anxiety. Its disruption is tied to depression, anxiety, and Parkinson's movement problems, and the authors nominate the nucleus as a target for neuromodulation.
pmc-13426029:
De Roy and colleagues published a 2026 study on how spine facet cartilage is built and behaves. Facet joints guide spine motion, and their cartilage wears in patterned ways. The team mapped one sheep joint surface point by point for this work. They paired squeeze tests with measures of thickness and key tissue parts.

Upper facet cartilage proved thicker and richer in a water-holding tissue part. Strength measures matched between upper and lower facets despite those build gaps. At lower facets, thicker spots relaxed under load in a distinct pattern. At upper facets, the water-holding part tracked the same relaxing behavior closely. Such maps may show which joint zones face the highest wear risk. Sheep joints served as the test model for these detailed maps.
pmc-13426229:
Yonne Peters and colleagues tested a probiotic milk drink in Barrett's esophagus in a 2026 single-arm pilot study of 23 patients. Barrett's tissue and its cancer successor are linked with an inflamed esophageal microbiome dominated by Gram-negative bacteria. Participants drank a fermented milk product containing Lactobacillus casei strain Shirota twice daily for four weeks.

Afterward, metaplastic lining showed significantly more Gram-positive Firmicutes without a change in total bacterial amount, and the Gram-positive to Gram-negative ratio rose as Proteobacteria fell. Shifting the esophageal community toward a friendlier profile could, with further testing, become a low-risk adjunct in Barrett's care. A drink a day is a light ask for most sick men and women, so a clear win here could spread fast in real wards and clinics.
pmc-13426729:
Dharmendra Kumar Pipal and colleagues report a woman whose large kidney cyst came back after a simpler needle treatment, and review similar published cases. Her cyst, a fluid-filled sac, measured about 8 by 10 centimetres and pressed on her left kidney.

The 46-year-old had six months of dull back pain and a swollen belly, and scans showed her kidney working at only 30 percent strength. Doctors first drained a litre of fluid and treated the sac lining, yet the cyst returned within about a month. Surgeons then removed the cyst wall through small cuts using ultrasonic scissors, finishing in 60 minutes with no complications. Pipal presents this keyhole approach as safe and effective for large cysts that return.
pmc-13427229:
Jiapeng Zhang and colleagues describe a molten salt method that recovers palladium, a scarce metal used in car catalysts and electronics, without acid baths. The route first locks palladium into a calcium compound, then uses molten calcium iodide to free the metal.

Computer calculations showed charge moving from calcium to palladium, giving the compound a stable, partly ionic bond structure. The compound barely lost mass when heated to very high temperatures, confirming its heat stability. In the molten salt at high heat, iodine attacked the calcium and left pure metal behind within one hour. The recovered palladium reached about 99.5 percent purity by weight, pointing to cleaner recycling of spent catalysts.
pmc-13427529:
Pooja Kushwaha and Sangita Mukhopadhyay show a tuberculosis protein fragment easing experimental colitis by removing mast cells in a 2026 mouse study. pmc-13428029:
Robert Rauschkolb and colleagues grew five long-lived herb species in gardens at five Central European sites to see how leaf and root traits shift within one species. Traits are measurable features, such as height or leaf dryness, that hint at how a plant grows.

After up to four growing seasons, the team measured shoots and roots and compared them with local weather and soil data. Taller plants tended to have less branched roots, and dry leaves matched dry roots, linking above- and belowground parts. Soil nutrient levels, more than weather, drove most of the shifts seen within each species. Rauschkolb warns that leaf traits cannot stand in for root traits, so studies should measure both on site.
pmc-13428229:
Dadson and colleagues report a case in which a new kind of PET scan helped decide whether joint inflammation after Lyme disease had turned into true autoimmune arthritis.
