The team scanned her with a tracer that targets VAP-1, a vessel molecule that guides white cells into inflamed tissue. Uptake lit up the same joints and persisted after antibiotics, which pointed to ongoing immune activity rather than leftover infection. The diagnosis became seronegative rheumatoid arthritis triggered by the Lyme bacterium. The scan backed stepping up to disease modifying therapy. The tracer also exposes patients to less radiation than the glucose scan, suiting repeat checks.
pmc-13428429:
Herr and colleagues published a 2026 study on spotting immune therapy effects early with ultrasound. Some cancer drugs free the immune system but work slowly and unevenly. The team tested bubbles that stick to a blood-vessel growth marker in tumors. They used a mouse model of bowel cancer for the test.

Mice on dual immune therapy showed far lower tumor blood flow by week one. Bubble binding to the vessel marker also dropped sharply under therapy. Tissue checks confirmed more tumor cell death and more immune cells inside. Treated tumors also grew fewer and smaller blood vessels over time. The scans flagged response well before size changes alone would show it. A blood-free scan like this could spare patients repeated biopsies.
pmc-13429129:
Yun-Qiang Yue and colleagues test, in a 2026 study, nanoparticles harvested from a magnolia flower remedy against ulcerative colitis in mice. The flower buds, called Xinyi in Chinese medicine, yield tiny exosome-like particles when boiled into a decoction. Such plant particles survive digestion and carry active compounds. The team isolated and profiled the particles, then ran dish tests and a mouse colitis experiment with daily oral dosing for two weeks.

The particles carried flavonoids and other plant chemicals known for calming inflammation. In dishes they mopped up damaging molecules and pushed immune cells toward a healing mode. In mice they eased weight loss, protected colon length, lowered disease scores, and shifted gut microbe mixes. Computer docking and protein checks pointed to the pathways involved. A traditional remedy gains a modern, testable form here.
pmc-13429729:
Melisa E. Gülseren and colleagues build, in a 2026 study, an infrared sensor that listens to radio waves instead of light. Tiny vibrating radio-frequency devices, called RF MEMS, can be tuned to absorb specific infrared colors when paired with patterned surfaces. Earlier designs tracked shifts in vibration frequency. The new design watches changes in electrical impedance, the resistance a circuit presents, and ties them by formula to sensing strength.

The detector reached very high responsivity at room conditions, responding to infrared power down near a trillionth of a watt. It picked out a narrow color band around a chosen wavelength in the mid-infrared. Response time sat under a millisecond. Because a matching network can retune it, one chip could serve many sensing jobs. On-chip chemical fingerprinting for medicine and environment checks is the stated direction.
pmc-13430529:
Debora Freitas Silva and a large team packed an essential oil from an Amazon tree into tiny capsules in 2026, then tuned the recipe with a planned set of tests. The oil comes from breu branco, a plant valued in local use. Bare oil can break down fast, so the shell aims to keep it stable and active longer.

The capsules came out round and small, with a tight size spread, a strong load of oil held inside, and steady form over time. Skin cell tests showed good match with living tissue at most doses. Free oil failed to stop a common skin germ, while the capsules held it back at a low dose. The capsules also sped skin cell movement in a scratch test and calmed one key swelling signal, which supports wound care use.
pmc-13430829:
Afnan Sultan and co-authors asked in 2026 how much vast pre-training helps transformer models that forecast traits of new drug-like molecules. Such models often learn first from millions of unmarked molecules held in large public banks. The team tested whether a bigger first diet truly lifts scores on lab traits that govern how a drug moves through the body.

Across seven data sets, growing the first diet past a few hundred thousand molecules brought no gain. A small second step worked far better: tuning on at most four thousand molecules close to the task, with side targets drawn from basic chemical traits, lifted scores on every set. A mid-sized model tuned this way matched or beat far larger rivals. Plain chemical feature sets stayed strong as a base for fair checks.
pmc-13432729:
Frank Hülsemann and co-authors compared lab routes in 2026 for spotting fake urine used to cheat doping and forensic tests. Fake products mimic real urine, and cheats may blend the two. The team ran three routes blind: a steroid scan, an atom-weight method for carbon and nitrogen, and a marker-based liquid scan.

All routes caught pure fake samples. The steroid scan flagged fakes by their lack of body-made steroids. The atom-weight route shone on blends: fake urine's atom marks sat far outside the human band, and half-and-half blends still read as off. The marker scan caught blends rich in fake share. The authors pitch atom weights as a strong partner when steroid reads leave doubt.
pmc-13432929:
Jia-Xin Wang and co-authors set out a trial plan in 2026 to test a classic Chinese herbal drink against lasting fatigue after COVID. Fatigue ranks among the most common tails of the illness. Old books record the drink, and fresh lab work backs its power to ease tiredness. The trial will run at one Beijing hospital.

One hundred patients with post-COVID fatigue will draw by lot into drink or fake-drink groups for eight weeks of care, with a month of watch after. Score keepers and math hands stay blind to who got what. A fatigue impact scale leads the reads, joined by mood, worry, sleep, life quality, and a timed walk test. The plan hews to care-as-planned math. The team frames the trial as firm proof on short-term gain and safety.
pmc-13434129:
Prabhat Tiwari led a 2026 field study in Bundelkhand, India, on farms that mix fruit trees, timber trees, and grass for animal feed. Two tree mixes were grown at two spacings during 2024 and 2025. The work asks which mix gives more feed, better feed quality, and more stored carbon.

The mix with custard apple gave taller grass, more green feed, and more dry feed than the mix with pomegranate. It also gave more crude protein in the grass. Wider spacing helped grass growth, while close spacing raised tree mass and stored carbon. The results point to a farm plan that feeds stock well in dry years.
pmc-13436429:
Xiangru Cheng and coauthors chart how intermittent fasting rewires jumping genes in mouse tissues in 2026. Mice fasted sixteen hours daily for four months. Gene reads cover liver, skeletal muscle, and cortex, with locus level counts for transposable elements.

The liver answered loudest, with 5,359 jumping genes shifted. Muscle shifted 620, while cortex barely stirred. Modules link jumping genes to nearby host genes that move in step. Liver modules center on metabolism and protein making, while muscle modules center on contraction and chromatin. Jumping genes may act as local dials for fasting gains.
pmc-13437629:
Suye Sun, writing alone in 2026, examined whether university counselors' guidance of student values can lower psychological crisis risk. Chinese campuses face rising student distress, and most research maps risk rather than protection. The first surveyed 800 undergraduates on counselor guidance, sense of meaning, resilience, and crisis vulnerability. The second ran a six-week workshop in sixteen classes, with 319 students completing it, against ordinary mental health lectures.

In the survey, stronger guidance tied to lower vulnerability, through two channels of similar size: students built more meaning in life, and more resilience. In the workshop, the guided group improved more than the lecture group, with gains in meaning and resilience again carrying the change. Sun is frank about limits: the trial was logged internally but not publicly registered ahead of time, so its tests count as exploratory. Registered repeats with longer follow-up must confirm the pattern.
pmc-13438729:
Aradhana Chhabra, Riya Kalra, and Kanu Goyal write to qualify a study of hippotherapy, therapy on horseback, that varied the sitting surface under children with special needs. They welcome the question as practical and unexplored. Their 2026 letter then raises five cautions about how the original findings should be read, starting with a classic statistical trap.

The textured surface group improved its own ten-meter walk scores, yet the change did not beat the other groups' changes, so comparative benefit is unproven. One thirty-minute session also cannot show what repeated practice and motor learning would do. Balance, a headline outcome, improved in no group at all, a null the letter says deserved more weight. The children ranged from three to eighteen with mixed conditions, which blurs who exactly benefits. The authors close constructively: bigger, tighter, longer studies can settle whether the horse-rider interface truly shapes rehabilitation gains.
pmc-13439029:
Xin Huang and Jie V Zhao use genetics in a 2026 study to test whether alanine, an amino acid found in meat, plays a causal part in mental illness. Alanine helps move energy between muscle and brain and feeds into brain chemicals tied to mood and thought. Early work gave mixed signals, with some small studies hinting at help for schizophrenia and others raising worry for mood disorders.

The pair applied Mendelian randomisation, a method that uses genes fixed at birth as a stand-in for lifetime alanine levels. They drew gene data from large genome studies covering more than 115,000 people in the UK Biobank. Outcomes covered major depression, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, anxiety, and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, with checks split by sex. Readers can follow how gene-based tests sidestep many traps of small observational studies.
pmc-13439629:
You and colleagues examine healthy lifestyle and survival in a modern combined syndrome in this 2026 analysis of two large cohorts. Cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic syndrome describes the intertwined burden of heart, kidney, and metabolic disease. The team scored lifestyle across seven factors, from smoking and diet to sleep and social connection. They covered over 300,000 affected people in the UK Biobank, plus about 9,800 in a United States cohort.

Each step up the lifestyle score was tied to roughly a fifth lower risk of death in the British cohort. That held overall and for cardiovascular death, with hazard ratios near 0.81 in the fitted models. The United States data showed smaller but similar protection. Physical activity and low sedentary time stood out as the strongest individual factors in both cohorts, and the benefit was greatest when the syndrome was still at an early stage.
pmc-13439829:
Zimmermann and colleagues studied in 2026 how a blood protein called resistin interacts with smoking and sex in depression risk. Resistin is a hormone-like protein from fat tissue linked to inflammation and insulin resistance. The team assessed depressed patients with two symptom scales, one standard and one designed for men.

Higher resistin levels went with a higher risk of major depressive disorder, but the pattern depended on sex and smoking. The link was strongest in women who smoked or had quit smoking. Resistin did not track how severe depression was once present. Alcohol use, in contrast, was the strongest predictor of masculine depression symptoms on the men's scale. The authors argue that prevention should pay special attention to women who smoke and carry metabolic risk.
pmc-13441029:
Hussein Biganeh and colleagues isolate phenolic compounds from the plant Diarthron lessertii and test them against cervical cancer cells, reporting in 2026. Plant phenolics are a rich hunting ground for cancer drug leads. Chromatography pulled nine compounds from shoot extract, spanning lignans, a biflavonoid, a bicoumarin, and five flavonoids, each identified by magnetic resonance and mass readings. A standard viability assay graded their killing of HeLa cells.

One lignan, epinortrachelogenin, hit hardest, halving cell growth at a moderate dose. Reporter tests showed the same compound selectively switching on FOXO3a, a forkhead protein that can order cancer cells to die or stall. Computer docking placed the lignan snugly in the protein's binding pocket, matching the laboratory signal. The authors nominate the compound as a lead for FOXO3a-targeted drug design, pending wider testing.
pmc-13442629:
Sayada Momotaz Akther and colleagues study root-zone microbes in two bermudagrass types under drought in a 2026 paper. One grass type bears drought well, while its twin wilts fast. The team joined chemical scans of root leaks with full gene reads of soil microbes to see how the two halves talk.

Drought reshaped what roots leaked into the soil, and microbe jobs shifted in reply, with toxin and contact-weapon systems among the movers. Broad microbe group counts barely moved, which points to job shifts over cast shifts. Two leak goods, riboflavin and a carboline compound, tracked with a microbe called Massilia putida near tolerant roots. The authors read the pattern as grass-led tuning of its soil crew through chemical signals, a route seed breeders may exploit.
pmc-13443129:
Shikuma and colleagues investigate RIOK2, a protein that helps build ribosomes, the cell's protein factories, as a driver of clear cell renal cell carcinoma, the commonest kidney cancer. Their 2026 study stains 166 tumor samples for the protein, checks gene data, and silences RIOK2 in lab cancer cells. They also test a drug that blocks the protein, checking whether it mimics silencing.

Tumors rich in RIOK2 were of higher stage and grade. Their patients had shorter cancer specific and progression free survival. That means less time until death or until the disease advanced. Silencing RIOK2 cut cell growth, invasion, and movement, and froze cells at the first stage of the division cycle, with less of a key cycle protein. Gene profiles after silencing showed cell cycle programs switched down. The blocking drug slowed cell growth in proportion to dose, backing RIOK2 as a drug target.
pmc-13443329:
Yingchun Shao and colleagues review USP25, a tag-trimming enzyme, in heart and brain vessel disease in a 2026 paper. The enzyme trims ubiquitin tags off proteins, which keeps cell protein balance in tune. Faulty tuning feeds vessel and brain ills, from stiff arteries to stroke harm.

The review lays out the enzyme's build, its upstream switches, and the proteins it trims. Each disease chapter ties the enzyme to a harm path in cells. Blocker drugs against the enzyme have reached lab and early clinic stages, a sign of translational pull. Gaps span thin human data and off-target risks. The authors set ranked research aims, from better blockers to clearer maps of who gains most from the drugs.
pmc-13445429:
Han Gong and colleagues review how the body's stress hormone system goes off track after ischemic stroke and drives later harm, in a 2026 narrative review. The system, run from brain to adrenal glands, shapes metabolism, immunity, and mood. Its role in stroke after-effects has drawn less notice than the brain injury itself.

In the first days, hormone surges and a broken daily rhythm can upset blood sugar, weaken the brain's barrier, and blunt immunity enough to invite pneumonia. Over months, a system stuck on high can reshape circuits for feeling and thought, feeding depression, anxiety, and poor memory. The review ties these threads into one frame and points to hormone control as a care target.
pmc-13445529:
Hari Shankar Meshram and colleagues model how many organ transplants India needs each year, now and by 2040, in a 2026 study. Transplant is the surest cure for end-stage organ failure, and India runs the world's third largest program, yet no one had sized the unmet need across organs. The team joined disease counts, world transplant data, and population forecasts.

For 2021 they put yearly need near one hundred twenty-six thousand kidneys and one hundred eighty-five thousand livers, with far smaller supply meeting each need. Supply covered only about seven in a hundred kidney cases and under two in a hundred liver cases. By 2040 need climbs for every organ, and even brisk reform leaves most liver, heart, and lung need unmet. Five states supply the bulk of transplants today.
pmc-13446329:
Xiaoqing Yuan and colleagues build a diagnostic model for limited mouth opening in jaw joint disorders, joining two scan types, in a 2026 study. A jaw that will not open past a set span wrecks chewing, speech, and daily comfort. Records covered two hundred twenty-six patients, most of them women in their mid-twenties, with four hundred fifty-two joints scanned in all.

Four signs carried the model: age, flattening of the jaw condyle, head height, and a jaw disc slipped forward and stuck. Split into training and test groups, the model sorted limited opening from normal with fair accuracy in both. Fit checks and benefit curves also looked sound. The authors offer the tool for sorting each patient's risk and shaping care to the joint's own state.
pmc-13448129:
Kwang Nam Jin introduces a July 2026 special issue on essential thoracic trauma imaging for a Korean radiology journal. Chest trauma demands fast, accurate image reading, since early severity sorting shapes survival. Earlier special issues from the journal covered lung cancer screening, general chest advances and artificial intelligence in daily practice, and trauma imaging now takes its turn as the fourth theme.

Four reviews make up the issue, covering air and blood in the chest cavity, lung and airway injury, chest wall and diaphragm injury, and aortic injury with blood around the heart. Each was planned for immediate practical use by residents and general clinicians alike. Checklists of key findings and sample structured reports aim to prevent missed injuries. Clear grasp of injury mechanism plus anatomy-based systematic reading underpin the guidance offered.
pmc-13449329:
Robert and co-authors review hair as a double record of environmental chemical exposure. The shaft stores pollutants built up over time. The living follicle offers cells in which body damage can be read. Proving which exposures cause disease is hard. Illnesses emerge decades later, making fast working biomarkers in exposed people valuable.

Chemicals stored in the hair matrix reflect total internal exposure over defined growth periods. Each person's exposure profiles differ between people in the monitoring studies surveyed. Plucked follicles contain fast-growing and stem-like cells suited to spotting genome changes. Those include DNA breaks and epigenetic changes linked to cancer and nerve disease. The authors propose a joined design mixing social and income measures, hair chemical makeup, and follicle biology. The aim is to map the exposome and its effects. They close by surveying the state of the art, current limits, and prospects.
pmc-13450229:
Hanne Sagsveen Hjorthaug and colleagues map in 2026 the cell types of the thymus lining, the tissue that teaches T cells to tolerate the body's own proteins. Using single-cell profiling that reads genes and open chromatin together, plus microscope imaging, they charted epithelial cells from children's thymuses. These cells display fragments of proteins from across the body, tissue-restricted antigens, so developing T cells that react too strongly can be culled.

The survey uncovered an undescribed cortical population marked by NEURL2. The team suggests it shepherds T cell maturation. It includes both progenitor cells and the nurse cells that cradle developing cells. Two flavors of a late medullary population separated by location and shape. Chromatin opened and closed in waves along the maturation paths. The authors propose that distinct chromatin landscapes switch self-antigen display between modes, with implications for immune disease and thymus-based therapies.
pmc-13450529:
Bell and co-authors tracked a regional Australian clinical trials unit in Victoria from 2011 to 2022 to learn what drives growth outside metropolitan centers, where trial access for remote patients lags. They scored the unit yearly against a published capability framework and compared those scores with hard counts of trials, patients, and investigators.

Active trials grew from just 4 in 2011 to 70 in 2022 at the Grampians Health unit studied. Its framework rating climbed from established to high performing over the same decade of expansion. The capability score correlated at 0.9 with both principal investigators per year and open trials per year, and at 0.8 with patient numbers enrolled annually. Organizational support and infrastructure were the key growth contributors identified, and oncology trials drove most of the expansion, validating the framework as a planning tool.
pmc-13450629:
Nan Ding and co-authors track in 2026 how a targeted breast cancer drug spread through Dutch care over a decade. The drug, pertuzumab, is used for cancers that carry the HER2 mark and have already spread at first find. Registry data covered 1,982 such patients who got drug treatment between 2013 and 2023.

Use climbed from under a tenth of patients in the first year to about four fifths by 2018, then held flat. Older patients and those with lower incomes or hormone-linked tumors got the drug less often in the flat years. The authors say the gaps point policy makers to where equal access still fails.
pmc-13451629:
Ferreira and Stocker build a new rat model to separate the jobs of one hormone receptor in thirst and blood pressure. The hormone angiotensin II acts through its type 1a receptor to drive drinking when blood volume falls. The 2026 study uses CRISPR gene editing, a method that cuts DNA at a chosen site. With it, the team deletes that receptor in rats, since mice respond oddly to the hormone.

The knockout rats ran a resting blood pressure about ten points lower than normal, at the same heart rate. Given angiotensin II, normal rats drank and raised their pressure, but knockout rats did neither. A drug that drops pressure also made only normal rats thirsty. Yet both strains drank alike after salty blood or a night without water. The receptor, they conclude, is key for thirst from low pressure, not from salt or plain deprivation.
pmc-13451929:
Huang and colleagues describe three new species of the congrid eel genus Gnathophis from deep waters off Taiwan in 2026, based on 130 specimens. Only two species of the genus were reliably known from Taiwan before, and one past record proved to be a misidentification. The team therefore checked fin colors, vertebra counts, and sensory pore patterns closely.

Each new species carries a distinct mix of traits. One has dark rear fins and the highest pore counts near the head. Another pairs pale side fins with a black tail fin and fewer vertebrae. The third is pale-finned throughout, with the most vertebrae of the three. DNA barcoding of a standard gene supported two of the new species. The authors dedicate the work to a late colleague who shaped eel taxonomy.
pmc-13452229:
Ting Peng and a large team map in 2026 how early birth reshapes a newborn's brain networks by the due-date age. Resting brain scans came from a large Chinese cohort, 107 babies born early and 62 born on time. The team read the webs both as still maps and as shifting ones, at whole-brain and node levels.

Early-born babies showed weaker web unity and clumping, with longer paths between nodes. Set nodes and modules shifted across many webs, and one memory-zone link set stood out in the shifting reads. Web scores also tracked age at scan, twin or shared pregnancy, and surgical birth. The work frames birth timing as a web-level event, not a local one.
pmc-13452629:
Lian and colleagues pool the evidence on pairing dupilumab, a lab made antibody drug, with house dust mite immunotherapy for atopic dermatitis, a long lasting itchy skin disease. Immunotherapy trains the immune system with tiny doses of the mite allergen, the trigger found in house dust. Their 2026 review searched four databases for trials and comparison studies that tested the pair against dupilumab alone, judging skin severity, quality of life, and side effects.

Only four studies with 138 patients met the bar, and just one was a randomized trial. The pair showed no clear gain in skin severity at 6 or 12 months. A hint of benefit appeared at 18 months, but the authors rate that evidence as very low in certainty. Quality of life and side effects, including eye problems, did not differ between groups, so the added value of the pairing stays unproven.
pmc-13453029:
Lei Xu, Shuang Peng, Zhongjun Huo, Zhixiong Fang, and Yuqing Chen report a case of severe chickenpox pneumonia where the airway itself showed the disease. Their 2026 case report follows a 35 year old man with diabetes whose breathing worsened five days after his rash began. By then most of his skin spots had crusted over, hiding the usual clue.

A camera passed into his airways found scattered blister like spots in the lower windpipe and both main bronchi. Washing fluid from the lung, checked with a targeted gene test, found the chickenpox virus and no other germ. He improved fast on intravenous acyclovir plus breathing support, and a scan five days later showed the lung shadows largely gone. The authors argue that looking inside the airway can crack the diagnosis once the rash has faded.
pmc-13453729:
Seok Hyun Kim, Soo Yong Lee, Min Ku Chon, and Kook Jin Chun report a heart attack in a transplanted heart that resisted every standard fix. Their 2026 case report follows a 38 year old transplant recipient whose front heart artery had blocked fully. Balloon work and clot suction failed to restore flow, a failure called no reflow, and his heart stopped and needed a support machine.

The team turned to a bailout trick called the Marinade technique: a balloon seals the artery's far end while clot busting drug soaks the trapped segment. Repeated rounds plus a final dose through a suction tube reopened the vessel, using 25 milligrams of alteplase in all. His pain eased and his circulation steadied, which opened the path to a second heart transplant. No major bleeding hit despite the support machine.
pmc-13453829:
Tamoghna Chattopadhyay and twelve co-authors build AI models that read brain scans to guess which dementia linked pathologies a living person carries. Brains often hold several of these changes at once, from amyloid plaques to TDP-43 deposits, and the usual proof needs spinal fluid, costly scans, or autopsy. Their 2026 framework joins 3D MRI scans with age, clinical, and genetic data.

Training used scans from people whose brains were later checked at autopsy, the hard ground truth. Two model types compete: a 3D neural network built for images and an automated learning platform. Extra tools highlight which brain regions drive each guess, and those maps are checked against classic brain shrinkage analysis. The authors present the setup as groundwork for cheap, needle free profiling of mixed dementia in life, with full results still to come.
pmc-13454029:
Sudip Prasad Jena and seven co-authors design, on a computer, a two part molecule meant to hunt cells infected by Nipah virus. Nipah kills a large share of those it infects and has no licensed vaccine or drug. Their 2026 study targets the viral protein that grips host cells, using modeling to test how candidate parts bind.

The design joins a targeting ligand to a peptide stitched with short pieces of measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine proteins. People in Nipah prone regions already carry long lived immunity to those vaccines, and the plan borrows that memory to mark infected cells for clearing. A sturdy oxime link holds the parts together. The model showed selective binding to a protein on infected cells. All proof so far is computational, and the authors call for lab and animal tests next.
pmc-13454229:
Qian Zhang and six co-authors map how the coronavirus spike protein and its parts move inside cells and leak out, hunting for better vaccine parts. Their 2026 study expresses the full spike and its subunits in mammalian cells and tracks each one's address. The full spike spread widely: surface, cytoplasm, nucleus, and outside the cell.

The S1 subunit piled up inside cells and secreted more than the full spike, yet showed less on the surface. The binding domain and S2 parts mostly stuck to the cell's inner scaffolding. Adding a stronger signal tag flipped the binding domain into a secretion star, reaching about 100 times the full spike's outside level. A proximity assay read these levels far more sensitively than standard methods. The authors back the tagged binding domain as a vaccine candidate.
pmc-13454329:
Glenn A. Harris, Lymor Barnhard, Jennifer Brummet, and Kristophe Diaz review, in 2026, new tests for progressive supranuclear palsy, a brain disease caused by clumped tau protein. Doctors once relied on one classic syndrome, yet the disease mimics Parkinson disease and other disorders. That overlap has slowed both diagnosis and drug trials.

The review weighs brain imaging first. Standard scans and a midbrain shrinkage index still help, while new tau PET tracers can now picture tau buildup in living patients. Blood markers get equal attention. One Alzheimer-linked marker, p-tau217, serves mainly to rule out mixed Alzheimer changes in these patients. The authors argue that pairing imaging with fluid tests can sharpen early diagnosis and open the way to tau-targeted trials.
pmc-13454529:
Jin-Ying Lu and thirteen colleagues compare, in a 2026 hospital study, three treatments for insulinoma, a rare pancreatic tumor that floods the body with insulin and crashes blood sugar. Surgery is the standard cure, yet some patients cannot face it. The team reviewed 19 patients treated at a Taiwan hospital between 2011 and 2025.

Thirteen patients ended with surgery, and all thirteen reached complete remission. Their hospital stays averaged about 13 days, and two developed new diabetes. Three patients had alcohol ablation guided by ultrasound endoscopy, with two remissions. Three relied on medicines alone, which eased symptoms yet cured none. A quarter of patients tested with one drug, octreotide, suffered paradoxical sugar crashes. Higher starting glucose predicted remission. The authors frame surgery as most reliable, with ablation as a middle path.
pmc-13454829:
Hao Wang and four colleagues investigate, in a 2026 study, a gene called FAM122B as a warning marker in low-grade glioma, a slow-growing brain tumor. The team merged public tumor databases from three sources to map where the gene runs high and what it tracks with. Lab tests then silenced the gene in glioma cells to watch the effect.

The gene ran far higher in tumor tissue than in healthy brain, and high levels paired with worse clinical features. Patients with high levels fared poorer overall, and the gene held up as an independent sign of bad outlook. Silencing it in two glioma cell lines sharply slowed cell growth and movement. The authors propose FAM122B as both a prognostic marker and a possible drug target, while noting that animal and patient studies must come next.
pmc-13457729: Human milk and galacto-oligosaccharides — their impact on early-life pathogenic gut bacteria growth. Job T. S. Schlösser, Wendy W. J. Unger, Ad C. J. M. de Bruijn, and others grow the bacteria. The 2026 Europe PMC paper is infant nutrition. It oligosaccharides baby gut pathogens.
pmc-13457829:
Uzma Faridi and co-authors review how obesity helps cancers start and grow, focusing on the disturbed fat metabolism that comes with excess weight. Their 2026 paper pulls together laboratory and clinical evidence on the mechanisms involved. Enlarged fat tissue produces chronic low-level inflammation, oxygen shortage, and scarring, which switch on growth pathways inside nearby cells, while insulin resistance and high insulin levels add further tumor-promoting signals.

The review also covers fat-derived hormones: leptin rises and adiponectin falls in obesity, and that imbalance encourages cell growth, new blood vessels, and escape from immune attack. Obesity additionally reshapes the tissue around tumors in ways that blunt anti-tumor immunity, and may reprogram genes and gut microbes. The authors end with a treatment roadmap spanning metabolic drugs, cytokine blockade, hormone modulation, immune therapy tuning, and microbe-directed strategies for obese patients.
pmc-13458029:
Zhao and colleagues reviewed in 2026 strict trials of mind craft nudges in the care chain for sex and blood spread germs. Nudges steer picks without bans: cash, gifts, set picks, and frames. The chain runs from guard steps, to tests, to pills kept up. Five banks gave the hunt, refreshed in 2025. Forty trials of twelve nudge kinds made the cut, and each was graded for trust.

Cash and gift card nudges won most rounds. They lifted safe sex, male cuts, germ tests, and care stays. Set pick nudges, where a test comes unless refused, held strong gains for two germ screens. A pay it on scheme, where one gift funds the next man's test, lifted dual tests and paid its way. Two in three trials scored weak on trust marks. Worth shifts by step and place, the team warns.
pmc-13458929:
Panteleimon E Papakonstantinou comments on a large Japanese registry study of patients whose leaking mitral valves were repaired with a catheter clip procedure called mitral TEER. The editorial, published in 2026, focuses on atrial fibrillation, the chaotic heart rhythm that often accompanies mitral regurgitation, the backward leak the procedure fixes. The underlying analysis covered 3,764 repaired patients, and atrial fibrillation was present in 61.7 percent of them across all causes of valve leakage.

The rhythm problem predicted worse outcomes only in one group. Among patients whose valves had degenerated structurally, atrial fibrillation was independently tied to higher two-year death rates after repair. In patients whose leak came from a failing ventricle or an enlarged atrium, the rhythm carried no independent link to mortality. Papakonstantinou argues the rhythm is a context-dependent marker rather than a uniform risk, and urges earlier rhythm control before atrial damage becomes irreversible.
pmc-13459329:
Mengyu Li and co-authors traced how a medicinal fritillary plant shifts its sugar storage strategy as its underground bulb ages year by year. Fritillaria unibracteata bulbs are a valuable traditional Chinese medicine, and their active compounds track with carbon storage. Their 2026 study sampled bulbs from the first through the fifth year of growth. It measured starch and sucrose, the two main stored carbohydrates, and sequenced gene activity to find which storage program dominates at each age.

Starch rose steadily through the fourth year, peaked, then fell in the fifth year. Sucrose moved the other way, dipping in year four and rising sharply in year five, a clear late stage switch. Sequencing found 21,964 genes changing across ages, and starch building genes peaked in expression exactly when starch peaked. Sucrose building genes, especially the enzyme sucrose phosphate synthase, switched on strongly from the fourth to the fifth year.
pmc-13459429:
Yong Jiang and co-authors modeled how feeling that one belongs at school supports college students' mental health, and which habits carry that benefit. Their 2026 survey collected questionnaires from 600 college students and tested a chain mediation model. In that layout, belonging flows through physical exercise and then a growth mindset, the belief that abilities can develop, before reaching mental health. The analysis used five thousand bootstrap resamples to build confidence intervals for each pathway in the chain.

School belonging showed a total effect of 0.589 on the mental health indicator used. About half arrived indirectly: the pathway through exercise alone contributed 0.111, the pathway through growth mindset alone contributed 0.160, and the chained route through both contributed 0.057 in the reported effects. The remaining direct effect was 0.260, still significant. The authors caution that cross sectional mediation shows statistical patterns, not proven causation over time.
pmc-13459629:
Wenfang Wang and co-authors tested a digitally designed jaw splint against a conventional one for teenagers whose jaw joint disc slips forward but pops back, a disorder causing clicking and pain. The digital splint is shaped from the patient's own scans for exact anatomical fit, while the conventional version follows standard fabrication. In their 2026 trial, eighty two adolescents aged twelve to sixteen received one splint or the other. Outcomes at six months combined MRI checks of disc position, jaw bone volume measures, and comfort questionnaires.

The digital splint recaptured the slipped disc in 94.44 percent of cases versus 79.63 percent with the conventional splint, a significant advantage. Both groups gained jaw condyle volume, by roughly 202 and 209 cubic millimeters respectively, so bone growth proceeded either way. Comfort scores were also collected to weigh the patient experience. Precision fit matters most for holding the disc in place during growth.
pmc-13460329:
Shahin Ayazi and colleagues analyzed in 2026 antireflux surgery outcomes for 2,388 patients, asking whether obesity undermines the operation as tradition assumes. Patients treated between 2011 and 2024 received either a fundoplication wrap or a magnetic sphincter device, and were split at a body mass index of thirty-five. The obese group numbered 309 and arrived with larger hiatal hernias and worse measured reflux.

One year after surgery, symptom scores, satisfaction, and freedom from acid-suppressing pills all matched between groups, and the picture held at three years. Five-year anatomical integrity and revision rates were also similar. One exception stood out: obese patients with the magnetic device normalized their acid exposure far less often. The authors argue body mass alone should not bar patients from antireflux surgery.
pmc-13461029:
Mukti Nath Sankhi and co-authors report in 2026 a 28-year-old man whose sudden weakness in all four limbs after a carbohydrate-heavy meal turned out to be thyrotoxic periodic paralysis. Blood tests showed dangerously low potassium alongside an overactive thyroid, and a thyroid scan pointed to Graves disease as the cause. Excess thyroid hormone drives potassium into cells, starving the blood of it and paralyzing muscle, a pattern seen most often in Asian men.

Treatment paired cautious potassium replacement, since overcorrecting can rebound into excess, with propranolol and carbimazole to control the thyroid. Definitive radioactive iodine treatment followed to destroy the overactive gland tissue. The authors warn that an overactive thyroid hides behind many paralysis presentations and must be treated itself to stop attacks returning.
pmc-13461329:
Niezi Wang, Wei Sun, Yang Chen, Shuyuan Cong, and Yixin Zhan pooled in 2026 randomized trials asking whether exercise reverses sarcopenia, the muscle wasting that shadows liver cirrhosis and raises death risk. Sixteen studies with 942 patients were combined. They measured walking distance in six minutes, thigh size and muscle thickness, knee strength, walking speed, grip strength, quality of life scores, and a liver severity score.

Exercise delivered clear gains: patients walked roughly fifty-four meters farther, thighs grew thicker and stronger, walking speed rose, and quality of life improved noticeably. Grip strength and liver severity scores, however, did not budge, hinting that leg-focused training misses the hands and cannot undo liver damage itself. The authors back structured exercise as part of cirrhosis care while noting variation among programs.
pmc-13461729:
Athanasia Pataka wrote an editorial introducing a journal collection on women in neurology, focused on sleep disorders. Women are often underdiagnosed in sleep medicine and underrepresented in its research leadership, a gap the collection sets out to close.

Women often show atypical sleep apnea symptoms, such as fatigue, low mood, and insomnia, rather than the classic signs seen in men. Missing those patterns delays diagnosis and treatment, Pataka warns, citing a review of sex differences across major sleep disorders. Animal studies in the collection link hormones and brain mechanisms to women's distinct sleep regulation. The editorial also urges early diagnosis from childhood and teamwork across dentistry, paediatrics, and primary care.
pmc-13461929:
Andrew Jacques, Giuliano Testa, and Anji Wall comment, in a 2026 article, on differing practice for a donor organ method called thoracoabdominal normothermic regional perfusion. The method restores warm blood flow to a donor's chest and belly organs after circulatory death, while blocking flow to the brain. It keeps organs viable until removal. A companion report compared programs in Colorado, Spain, and the United Kingdom.

Practice varies widely. Teams differ on when and how to place the tubes, how to control the vessels to the head, and how to prove the brain gets no flow. Laws on steps allowed before death, definitions of death, and ethics oversight all differ, shaping what each team may do. The commentators argue such variety is not wrong, yet it complicates training and public trust. They call for shared standards, open reporting, and ethical safeguards that still leave room for local rules.
pmc-13462029:
Xuezhong Zhang and co-authors profiled MEX3C, an RNA binding protein, across the full landscape of human cancers to judge its worth as a biomarker or drug target. RNA binding proteins steer which messages a cell reads, and MEX3C had been implicated in cancer growth piecemeal. In their 2026 pan cancer analysis, the team mined national tumor and normal tissue atlases for MEX3C levels, mutations, survival links, and immune ties.

MEX3C ran high in several cancers, including breast and lung squamous tumors, but low in others such as adrenocortical tumors. pmc-13462229:

That lens widens care beyond treating disease, toward building health, giving people a voice, and centering the person. Relationships, workplaces, and community resources all shape how health is lived.

Together they show how psychological insight can shape clinical work, health service design, and public health planning. The editors stress that modern health systems are complex and needs keep shifting across the lifespan. They call for care models that are joined-up and sensitive to context, serving individuals, professionals, and whole communities alike.
pmc-13462429:
Rui-Zhi He, Min Zhou, Yong-Jun Chen, and Xing-Jun Guo compare, in a 2026 records study, three drug plans meant to shrink advanced pancreatic cancer enough for surgery. The authors recommend it for fit patients and flag a normalized tumor marker and good nutrition as good signs.
pmc-13462529:
Chunkai Li and colleagues study, in a 2026 analysis, how dryness reshapes soil microbes' abilities by changing the balance of carbon, nitrogen, and phosphorus in soil. As sites grew drier, the ratios between those elements shifted downward consistently. Gene pools shifted with them, in a coordinated move.

Genes for building cell material, copying RNA, making proteins, and moving cargo inside cells became more common. The pattern reads as a switch from a tearing-down lifestyle to a building-up, drought-resistant one. The authors link element ratios to microbe function across biomes, offering a frame for predicting how drying will reorganize soil life. Such reorganization carries consequences for how carbon and nutrients cycle through ecosystems.
pmc-13463229:
Caminero and Oreja-Guevara reviewed in 2026 a testing problem in multiple sclerosis care that affects safety decisions for the drug natalizumab. Many weak positive results on the newer test also faded or flipped back over time. The authors advise reading clashes in context, using antibody strength, persistence over time, and the patient's full picture, not binary cut-offs alone.
pmc-13463629:
Filipa Godoy-Vitorino reports on the first Puerto Rico and Caribbean Microbiome Symposium, held in San Juan in February 2026. More than two hundred researchers, trainees, and partners attended. Talks covered microbes in human health, cancer, infection, diet and immunity, wild ecosystems, and data methods.

The meeting launched the Puerto Rico Center for Microbiome Sciences as a regional hub for multiomics work, meaning studies that read genes, proteins, and small molecules together. Student talks and mentor links sat at the center of the program, alongside plans for shared training across the islands. Readers get a record of a new network tying Caribbean labs to partners worldwide.
pmc-13463929:
Alshahrani and colleagues audited Saudi Red Crescent records in 2026 to measure how often bystanders start CPR. CPR means the chest compressions that can keep a person alive after the heart stops outside a hospital. Each extra minute of ambulance response slightly lowered the odds. Wide regional gaps persisted after adjustment. The authors call for dispatcher coaching, wider public training, and cleaner registry forms.
pmc-13464329:
Candelario and colleagues evaluated in 2026 a Los Angeles County experiment in who gets heard in policy. It kept attention on root causes and tailored services to real community conditions. Members described gains in motivation, peer support, and leadership skill. Respondents urged earlier involvement in pivotal decisions and steadier grassroots engagement.
pmc-13464729:
Greta Romano leads a team that reads whole genomes of RSV from Italy's 2024-5 season, the first under a national baby protection program. The antibody shot nirsevimab now shields newborns, so tracking virus change matters early. Eighty-eight positive airway checks from two regions went to full sequencing.

Within type A, one lineage led with about two thirds of strains, while all type B strains shared one lineage. Genes for surface and copying parts varied most across the set. No changes known to blunt the antibody shot appeared anywhere, a reassuring first-season read.
pmc-13465329:
Nikhil Raj Selvaraj and eight co-authors craft a family of thiazolone compounds and test them against Alzheimer's-like damage in cells and fruit flies. Oxidative stress and amyloid clumps drive the disease's neuron loss. Their microwave-fast chemistry yielded a series built on a sulfur ring core.

In flies bred to make human amyloid, 3n eased movement and behavior faults. Computer fits placed the compounds inside the acetylcholinesterase pocket, and lab tests confirmed dose-linked blocking of that enzyme. Drug-likeness scores looked clean across the set.
pmc-13465729:
Cong and colleagues published a 2026 study on keeping Sichuan pepper fresh in storage. The spice is prized for its numbing heat and bright scent, both quick to fade. The team tested cold rooms, nitrogen gas, yellow LED light, and all three together. Storage ran for 60 days, with checks on flavor and health-linked plant compounds.

Cold air at five degrees and zero oxygen slowed losses the most in early screening. Yellow light best protected the numbing compound on its own. The three methods combined beat every single method by a wide margin. Losses of two key plant compound groups fell by about half versus plain storage. The combined setup needs no chemical sprays, which suits food sellers well.
pmc-13466129:
Piotr Zawadzki and Łukasz Pierzchała tune a light-driven cleaning process that strips color from the dye methylene blue, in a 2026 water treatment study. Their method activates persulfate salts with visible light, helped by glucose, to create aggressive radicals that attack the dye. A statistical design tested how acidity, glucose dose, salt level, and starting dye strength interact.

Best results came at a fairly acidic setting with set doses of each ingredient, reaching about sixty-three percent color removal at the middle dye level. Reaction speed followed a simple first-order pattern across runs. Scavenger tests showed both sulfate and hydroxyl radicals at work, and the process stayed effective across a tenfold range of dye strengths.
pmc-13466229:
Zheng and colleagues search biopsy tissue taken before treatment for a gene pattern predicting whether ulcerative colitis patients will respond to anti-TNF therapy, in 2026 gastroenterology research. Ulcerative colitis is chronic bowel inflammation, and anti-TNF drugs such as infliximab fail many patients. When each dataset was held out in turn, the signature still separated non-responders, with a pooled effect size of 1.36 in standardized units. Pathways for inflammation, TNF signaling, and tissue remodeling dominated the non-responder pattern, while energy-production pathways marked responders. Zheng presents the tissue state, measured before any drug, as a reproducible guide for choosing therapy.
pmc-13466329:
Iftikhar ud Din, Daud Khan, and Tayeb Denidni design a flat patterned surface that soaks up microwaves in three separate bands, in a 2026 engineering study. The pattern pairs a square metal ring with two nested ten-sided resonators on a common circuit board material backed by metal. Target bands sit inside the S, C, and X ranges used by communication systems.

Simulations tuned the shape until absorption topped ninety-nine percent at each of the three peaks. Field maps and current patterns showed the coupled metal parts trapping energy inside the structure, where it fades as heat. Symmetry keeps performance nearly equal for either wave orientation, and absorption held steady for signals arriving at angles up to sixty degrees.
pmc-13466529:
Karumbi and colleagues built a core outcome set for newborn research in Kenya in 2026, testing whether a rich-country set could be adapted instead of starting fresh. A core outcome set is the agreed minimum every trial should measure. None existed for sub-Saharan Africa, where newborn deaths remain high. The team reviewed outcomes used in regional trials, interviewed 17 stakeholders, and ran discussion groups with 15 mothers. A workshop of 13 experts then voted on sixteen candidate outcomes.

Seven more were endorsed after debate, including family impact, costs to mothers, pain, and infection. Seven outcomes overlapped the rich-country set, though with definitions reshaped for Kenya. Five were Kenya-specific, reflecting local costs and family burdens. The study shows adaptation works, but only with genuine local reshaping.
pmc-13466729:
Shun Nakahara, Bradley Fujiuchi, Toru Nakata, and Lorrance Majewski describe a fungal brain infection hidden behind low blood sodium in an older man, in a 2026 case report. The seventy-seven-year-old had taken the immune-damping drug fingolimod for multiple sclerosis for fifteen years. He arrived after four weeks of growing confusion, with no fever and no classic neck stiffness signs.

Blood tests showed severe low sodium and a shortage of lymphocytes, and a head scan looked normal. Spinal fluid held only mild inflammation signs, which made the cryptococcal meningitis easy to miss. The authors warn that in patients on such drugs, low sodium and muddled thinking may be the infection's main mask.
pmc-13466829:
Huang and Li reviewed a 2026 account of small cell carcinoma of the cervix, a rare but highly aggressive cervical cancer making up only one to two percent of cases. It invades early, spreads readily, and returns often despite treatment. High risk human papillomavirus, especially type 18, is recognised as a core driver.

Huang also describes a virus independent route driven mainly by mutations in the TP53 and RB1 guardian genes. Tumour diversity, treatment resistance, and spread are tied back to those molecular features throughout. The authors propose a closed loop model where laboratory research answers clinical questions and clinical practice feeds questions back.
pmc-13467129:
Rizwan Barkat and colleagues check two suspects for clots forming inside a graft after planned aortic arch replacement, in a 2026 records study. The frozen elephant trunk operation leaves a fabric tube where clots appear in about a tenth of patients. Transfused blood products and the choice of clot-preserving drug were the suspects, since both shift clotting balance.

Every non-emergency arch replacement at their center from 2017 to mid-2025 entered the analysis, with clots defined on follow-up scans. Neither transfusion volumes during or after surgery nor the choice between aprotinin and tranexamic acid tracked with clot formation. Known drivers such as aneurysm disease and graft position remain the likelier explanations, which refocuses prevention efforts.
pmc-13468129:
Samuel Haeuser and co-authors image in 2026 the protected edge channels of the topological material ZrTe5 at the nanoscale, using a cryogenic near-field infrared microscope of their own design. Such helical edge modes promise charge transport without the usual energy loss, but watching them directly at high frequencies has been difficult. The experiment ran at 1.8 kelvin under magnetic fields up to 5 tesla while scanning the crystal surface.

Remarkably, that high-frequency response survived magnetic conditions that normally shut down edge conduction at low frequencies. The images also showed a two-lane reorganization of the edge channels. Direct views of how these edges behave in real use help teams judge them for low-loss electronics.
pmc-13468329:

The authors describe the route as reliable, simple, economical, and environmentally friendly, with room to scale up. Optimizing area and transport together matters most in flow-through uses such as biosensing, biofiltration, and catalysis, which are the applications they name.
pmc-13468429:

pmc-13468529:

pmc-13468929:

Tests on six materials, powdered solids and liquids, confirmed the device could measure dielectric constants accurately. Shi calls the sensor a simpler, more precise alternative.
pmc-13469729:

pmc-13469829:

Parents and staff sometimes weighted features differently, which the mapping process made visible. The authors say these user insights will guide building and refining the program. Later studies are planned to test usability, feasibility, and effects.
pmc-13470029:
Xu and colleagues in the United States asked in 2026 what deep space rays do to blood vessels more than a year after the dose. Moon and Mars crews will soak in mixed rays that Earth's shield blocks. pmc-13471329:

pmc-13471429:

pmc-13472729:

pmc-13472929:

pmc-13473129:

pmc-13474829:

pmc-13476229:

pmc-13476729:

Newborn admissions numbered 227, spanning extremely early births to full-term babies, and child admissions numbered 173. pmc-13477129:

pmc-13479929:

pmc-13480029:

pmc-13480229:

pmc-13480529:

pmc-13480729:

pmc-13483229:

pmc-13483529:

pmc-13488129:

pmc-13489629:

Satisfaction also ran higher on all ten survey items, with the biggest gaps in creativity, clinical thinking, interest, and communication. Attendance tracked strongly with exam success in both groups. The authors back wider adoption in competency-based training.
pmc-13493829:
Zalewski and co-authors examine whether narrow-spectrum LEDs could light roads more cheaply at night. After dark, drivers' vision sits in the mesopic range between daylight and darkness. Standards are written for brighter, daylight-like vision, so lamps are judged by rules that may waste energy at night. In the 2026 laboratory work, the team tested LED chips emitting single colours from blue-green to orange-red and computed how much light vision actually gets from each at low brightness.

For chips between green and yellow-green, useful light output rose as the scene got dimmer, the opposite of what standard ratings suggest. A yellow-green lamp and one blended spectrum each promised up to a fifth better energy efficiency than old sodium streetlights at the lowest levels modelled. The authors call the option worth developing, not yet proven on real roads.
pmc-13495229:
Chaofan Zhang and a large team chart, in a 2026 study, how quinoa and its wild kin adapted to high altitude in the Chenopodium genus. Quinoa splits into highland and lowland forms, yet the genetic and regulatory roots of that split were hazy. The team re-read the genomes of 558 samples from twenty species and added gene activity data from 295 of them.

The data showed rich diversity, uneven change in the crop's two subgenomes, and gene flow between species. A wild relative had fed helpful variation into farm quinoa, above all in stress and defense genes. Both farm and wild forms bore matching marks of selection for altitude, hitting shared genes for nutrient transport and flowering time. A huge map of gene control switches tied one switch, near a clock gene, to deletions common in highland plants. The authors offer the resource for breeding tougher quinoa.
pmc-13495429:
Annalisa Maraone and colleagues measure, in a 2026 study from Rome, demoralization in people with obsessive-compulsive disorder. Demoralization is a state of helplessness and lost hope. It overlaps with depression yet is not the same, and it may call for different care. The team recruited 43 adults from a clinic and scored how severe the illness was, plus demoralization and depression, with standard scales.

A subgroup showed strong demoralization without matching depression, proof the two can part ways. It deepened as obsessions grew worse. The authors argue that spotting this state can sharpen the picture and tailor therapy beside standard treatment. They call for longer studies on how it steers the course of the illness.
pmc-13498429:
Joerg Klepper, Lucia Kiesel, and Eva Runkel report in 2026 that movement episodes in a rare glucose transport disorder can last far longer than textbooks describe. The condition limits how glucose reaches the brain, and exertion can trigger sudden muscle tightening, mainly in the legs. Published episodes usually run 20 to 30 minutes, yet families increasingly described attacks lasting hours.

Among 60 patients seen at one centre over four years, 26 experienced exertion-triggered episodes despite a special high-fat diet used as treatment. Eighteen had episodes under an hour, while eight had prolonged attacks lasting from over an hour up to a full day. The authors stress that these long episodes resist diet treatment and place a heavy burden on patients and families.
pmc-13499729:
Matthew Todd and co-authors summarise in 2026 the landmark cardiology trials of 2025, drawn from the year's major international heart conferences. Heart medicine moves quickly, and clinicians need a filtered view of which results should change practice or shape future guidelines. The team screened trials presented at leading cardiology meetings and kept those with the highest likely impact and broad relevance across the field.

More than 80 key trials were identified in total. Highlights included challenges to the standard year of dual blood-thinning therapy after stenting, plus new drug-coated balloon data. Valve replacement and closure device updates featured too, alongside advances in heart failure, muscle disease of the heart, and prevention. Trial names and designs are catalogued by subspecialty, giving clinicians a single map of a crowded year and researchers a guide to where evidence shifted most.
pmc-13500429:
Akihiro Usui leads a 2026 multicentre Japanese analysis of whether free cancer cells found in wash fluid during bowel cancer surgery predict return of disease differently by tumour side. Data came from a prospective observational study of stage II and III colorectal cancers removed with curative intent, now reanalysed by right-sided versus left-sided origin and by wash cytology result. A total of 1,500 patients qualified, split between right and left sides.

Fewer than one patient in twenty-five had positive wash cytology in the reported share. Among those who relapsed, positive cytology, deep tumour stage, and right-sided location each independently predicted spread within the abdomen. Cytology-negative patients on the left fared worse on relapse-free survival than those on the right, while overall survival matched. Once relapse occurred after positive cytology, right-sided patients survived for a shorter time.
pmc-13500629:
Shunshun Liu and Prasanna V Balachandran build in 2026 an active learning workflow that predicts a key strength descriptor in refractory high-entropy alloys, exotic mixes of several heat-resistant metals in equal shares. The descriptor, misfit volume, captures how much each atom's size and electronic character distorts the crystal, and crude averaging rules miss the local relaxation that matters. Their loop couples quantum-level calculations with ensemble machine learning across 126 five-element alloys, choosing which compositions to calculate next for maximum information gain.

Analysis plots showed atomic size mismatch driving the descriptor directly, while differences in electronegativity, the pull atoms exert on electrons, partly compensated electronically. Feeding the learned values into a mechanistic strength model reproduced measured yield strengths well across diverse compositions in the reported checks. The workflow promises cheaper screening of alloys for jet engines, nuclear systems, and power plants.
pmc-13500829:
Aparna Chaudhuri leads an eight-author team with a 2026 computational design of a peptide vaccine meant to cover all four dengue virus serotypes. Candidate fragments between 45 and 65 amino acids were checked for immune visibility, allergy risk, and toxicity before assembly into one construct.

Docking showed it binding strongly to immune receptors TLR2 and TLR3 and to antibody chains, with energies near minus 13.9 to minus 11.3 kilocalories per mole. Simulated immune responses showed raised B-cell and T-cell activity, and codon optimization suggested the construct could be produced in E. coli. Laboratory and animal testing remain ahead.
pmc-13501629:
Barış Baydemir leads a four-author team reporting a 2026 biomechanical study of what makes freestyle swimmers fast over a short sprint. Twelve licensed male swimmers aged 18 to 25, each with at least three years of competitive experience, had their body measurements recorded and their best 25-metre freestyle times documented. Stroke count, stroke length, stroke frequency, and glide time were extracted from recordings with Kinovea, a two-dimensional motion analysis program.

Swim time correlated significantly with all three technique measures. Higher stroke frequency and longer glide time went with faster times, showing negative correlations. Longer stroke length, by contrast, went with slower times in this group, a positive correlation the authors flag for individual technical review rather than a general rule. They recommend that training programmes develop stroke rate, stroke length, and glide use in balance instead of chasing any single parameter.
pmc-13501729:
Mira Miraturrofi'ah leads a four-author team with a 2026 protocol for a systematic review of family-centered communication for parents of premature babies. Babies born early face high risks, above all in low-resource settings, and coaching families to talk and take part in care may help families care better and improve outcomes. Evidence so far is scattered, so the team lays out its full plan in advance, following PRISMA-P guidance. The review is registered in PROSPERO.

Eligible studies will test communication programmes delivered by health staff to parents or caregivers of preterm babies without major conditions. Designs range from randomized trials to observational studies. Five databases will be searched using a Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcome framework, with two reviewers screening, appraising, and extracting data separately. Results will be combined in narrative form under SWiM guidance, with meta-analysis where the data allow and GRADE ratings.
pmc-13501829:
Lili Zhu leads a nine-author team reporting a 2026 comparison of two childhood lung viruses in Wenzhou, China. Human metapneumovirus and respiratory syncytial virus both cause acute lower respiratory infections, a leading killer of young children. Hospitals there tested 15,772 admitted children during 2021 and 2022 with a multiplex PCR panel. Some 889 children, 5.6 percent, carried the metapneumovirus, while 2,196, or 13.9 percent of those screened, carried RSV in the same testing round.

The two infections looked different at the bedside. Metapneumovirus patients were older, with a median age of 2.5 years against 1.6 years, and more often had underlying conditions. Their fevers ran longer and hotter, and blood markers of inflammation, including C-reactive protein at 14.18 against 7.80 milligrams per litre, ran higher. RSV patients showed more breathing distress signs. Chest imaging in the metapneumovirus group showed more consolidation and collapsed lung segments.
pmc-13503829:
Damodharan Palaniappan leads a team that built a screening tool for diabetic eye disease, in a 2026 paper. The disease is a top cause of sight loss that can be prevented if caught early. Screening must work across cameras and clinics, yet past models often fail on new data sets and miss rare severe stages.

Their tool builds on a transformer design that reads images in patches at several scales. Prep steps boost contrast so faint lesions stand out. Training weighs the rare classes more, so severe stages are not swamped by mild ones. Across three public data sets the tool scored accuracy near 97 percent, with strong recall of advanced disease. The code is shared in public for checks by others.
pmc-13503929:
Jianjun Zeng, Ziyang Cheng, and Yanqiang Cui track four ecosystem services in China's Shule River Basin from 1980 to 2020, in a 2026 study. The services are water yield, soil keeping, carbon storage, and habitat quality. A standard model suite simulated each service across the basin.

Water yield and carbon storage rose over the four decades, while soil keeping slipped slightly and habitat quality dipped a touch. Rich service zones cluster in high mountains at the basin's south edges; poor zones sit in the dry northwest. Rain, water loss to air, and height best explained where water yield was high. Slope ruled soil keeping. Land use, climate, and terrain mattered far more than people or wealth in shaping the patterns.
pmc-13505029:
Naema Ibrahim, Abdiqani Abdikadir Mohamoud, and Abdirahman Omer Ali study why patients start dialysis at the main hospital in Hargeisa, Somaliland, in a 2026 paper. Rich countries often start dialysis on lab numbers found in routine care. The team expected Somaliland starts to be driven by symptoms, given late presentation and thin early care.

Records covered 123 new dialysis patients over two years. Poisoning symptoms from kidney failure led: a stomach form of uremic illness in about 44 percent, and a brain form in about 29 percent. Nearly all patients came from the home region of the hospital. Men more often showed the stomach form, women the brain form. The authors call the pattern a sign of crash-landing starts and urge wider early screening.
pmc-13507129:
Jingwen Zhang leads a 2026 team that adds transcript awareness to rare variant hunting in heart and lung traits. Genes can make several transcript versions, and standard tests that use one version can miss real effects. Their method tests each version, then combines results into one gene score while keeping false alarms in check.

Simulations showed power close to knowing the best version in advance. Applied to whole-genome data from over 240000 people in the All of Us program across 129 traits, the method found eleven new gene links and recovered forty-seven known ones. For the TTN gene, it pinpointed the N2B version as the strongest tie to heart muscle disease.
pmc-13507229:
Carlos M Vallez, David Contreras, and Mario Castro build, in 2026 work, an interpretable probability framework for demand in BiciMad, Madrid's dock-based bike share system. Demand swings with hour, weather, station, and day type, yet records show only part of true demand. Their model generates synthetic trips under stated assumptions so planners can test ideas safely.

Trip distances follow one standard curve family, while hourly counts use another that allows extra spread and responds to rain and day type. Checks against 2018 data showed well-calibrated uncertainty bands. A 2019 consistency check even exposed systematic timestamp errors, later confirmed by the provider. The tool serves demand study and data auditing, not full operations simulation.
pmc-13508229:
Rajdeep Jajoriya and six co-authors hunt gene regions that shape rice straw quality, aiming to make straw better feed and industrial material, in 2026 work. Rice straw is produced in huge amounts, but its fiber and silica make it hard for animals to digest. The team measured straw parts in 207 diverse rice lines plus 25 farm varieties. Traits covered silica, lignin, cellulose, plant size, and lab digestibility. A genome scan on a subset of lines used dense DNA markers.

High silica tracked strongly with poor digestibility, while lignin effects shifted with other components. The scan found 33 marker links spread across the genome for these traits. Several landed near known genes for silica uptake and fiber building. Certain gene versions cut silica by up to about one sixth and lignin by about one quarter. Breeders could use those versions to raise straw value without harming the grain crop.
pmc-13509229:
Zeng and colleagues compare tiny parcels released by the back of the human eye in 2026 research on retinal disease. These parcels, called extracellular vesicles, carry proteins between cells and reflect the state of the tissue that made them. The team collected vesicles from the macula, the central region used for sharp vision, and from the peripheral retina of donor eyes, asking whether their cargo differs by region.

Explants from four non-diseased donor eyes were cultured, and vesicles were isolated and checked by electron microscopy and particle tracking. The particles measured between 119 and 140 nanometers across, confirming they were small vesicles in both regions. Protein profiling then showed a clear regional split: macular and peripheral samples separated in both the vesicle data and the surrounding fluid. Pathway analysis linked macular vesicle proteins to functions that may explain why the macula is prone to disease.
pmc-13510829:
Raymundo A. Munoz and colleagues review a simpler urine diversion used after bladder removal for muscle-invasive bladder cancer. The method, single-stoma cutaneous ureterostomy, brings both urine tubes to one skin opening and skips any bowel surgery.

The standard alternative, an ileal conduit, uses a piece of bowel and carries more surgical burden, the review notes. Newer refinements of the older method show shorter operations and faster recovery than the conduit in early data. The option appeals most for older or frail patients, where cutting operative burden matters most. Problems still needing watch include narrowing of the opening, catheter dependence, infections, and long-term kidney health. Munoz stresses that randomised trials are lacking, so most evidence comes from small backward-looking studies.
pmc-13512829:
Martinez-Zujeros and colleagues published a 2026 study on recovery paths of older hospital patients. Rehab wards treat elders whose daily abilities vary wildly at admission. The team clustered 957 patients by how their independence scores moved over time. Records came from one geriatric rehab unit between 2019 and 2025.

Four recovery profiles emerged from the machine-learning grouping in the study. Two groups regained independence well and showed strong bounce-back overall. The other two stayed limited by chronic damage or severe impairment. Walking ability and muscle strength traced the same split across profiles. Stable groups could guide tailored rehab plans for each new arrival. Check methods agreed, which supports the profiles' stability over resampling. Walking category and muscle testing joined independence scores in the records.
pmc-13514729:
Li and colleagues fed young pigeons in 2026 to learn how the energy and protein mix in feed shapes meat and gut health. The birds were gray-feathered King pigeon squabs weaned early, a stage when chicks shift from crop milk to solid feed and react strongly to diet. The team varied both feed factors at once.

In a trial with 216 squabs, the team crossed three energy levels with three protein levels, giving nine diets. More energy raised belly fat, while protein level changed carcass traits and gut enzyme strength, which shows how well food is broken down. The two factors often acted together rather than alone. Gut microbe samples also split by diet: the richest, lowest-protein feed favored Lactobacillus types, while the leanest, highest-protein feed held a wider mix of microbes.
pmc-13516229:
Nicolò Bisi and Abdallah Hamze compare two ways of attacking cancer with one molecule in a 2026 medicinal chemistry review. Tumours dodge single drugs through backup pathways and resistance. Dual inhibitors block two proteins at once by sitting in their active sites. Dual PROTACs instead tag both proteins for the cell's shredding machinery, destroying them outright. The authors walk through cancer target pairs where both designs exist.

Across the paired examples, switching from blocking to destroying improved tumour killing in more than eighty-five percent of cases, lengthened action, and beat resistance mutations. The catch is the linker, the strap joining the molecule's two ends: its length and shape decide whether both proteins can be dragged to the shredder together. Bisi and Hamze distil practical linker strategies, offering chemists a working entry point for designing multi-target degraders.
pmc-13517129:
Maria Michailou and seven colleagues audit vaccine coverage among kidney patients and their families in a 2026 hospital study. Chronic kidney disease raises infection risk, yet vaccination lags, and the cocooning idea, shielding patients by vaccinating their households, is barely studied here. The team recorded coverage for sixty-three dialysis patients, fifty-three children with kidney disease, and their relatives at one Greek university hospital.

Coverage was thin almost everywhere. Dialysis patients reached sixty-two percent for flu but only a quarter for pneumococcal vaccine and almost none for tetanus-pertussis boosters. Children with kidney disease managed just twenty-one percent for flu and zero for COVID-19, though their flu rate still beat healthy controls. Relatives fared little better, leaving the cocoon full of holes. Michailou's team calls for targeted catch-up drives and for teaching families that their own shots protect the patient.
pmc-13517629:

Metal levels ran higher in glacier meltwater than in downstream rivers, which the authors attribute to local geology plus air pollution carried in from surrounding regions. Statistical source analysis grouped the metals into three associations pointing to mixed natural and human-made origins. Ecological risk came out low, and non-cancer health risk stayed within safe limits, though children were more susceptible than adults and arsenic contributed most of the risk. The authors offer the results as a baseline for water management on the plateau.
pmc-13517829:
Sartore and colleagues reviewed in 2026 what makes domestic cats aggressive, weighing inherited causes against environmental ones. The team gathered the current evidence on inherited roots of feline aggression and on the life conditions that interact with that inheritance.

Comparing studies is hard because teams define types of aggression in different ways and measure behaviour with varied tools. Sharper shared definitions, the authors argue, would help vets and owners prevent problems earlier, manage cases better, and improve cat welfare. pmc-13518829:

Blocking it in brain slices woke up receptor-bearing neurons, and in living animals the blocker curbed food intake and caused weight loss. Peisley and co-authors also confirm the channel and receptor sit close together on the cell surface.
pmc-13518929:

pmc-13519029:

Hormone surges appeared in some ovulating females but matched neither smears nor scores in time. pmc-13520529:

pmc-13521529:

Both groups gained root length and wall thickness over twelve months, with no clear difference between them. The injectable form, however, healed the area around the root tip better: every case succeeded, against about nine in ten for the standard form, and infection scores fell further. Most roots showed ongoing maturation without yet closing at the tip. An injectable scaffold is easier to place in narrow young roots.
pmc-13521929:

pmc-13522429:

Twenty-four survivors aged thirty to fifty took part, with one group doing bilateral arm training alone and the other adding rhythmic sound cues from a metronome. Sessions lasted thirty-five minutes, five days a week, for four weeks.

The authors present cued training as a low-cost option that clinics could add to usual stroke rehabilitation, while noting the small size of the trial.
pmc-13522529:

pmc-13523229:

Split by sex, the association was clear in men and absent in women. The authors highlight accessible urban green space as a possible support for mental resilience, with attention to gender differences in how that benefit appears.
pmc-13523529:

pmc-13525929:

In this rare form, the appendix sits inside a groin hernia sac. His right groin and scrotum hernia had gone untreated for ten years. He presented with swelling and dark skin. His bowel was blocked.

Surgeons removed damaged bowel and made an ileostomy. One testicle was removed. The scrotum was cleaned repeatedly over a 33-day hospital stay. The patient survived. Bowel continuity was later restored.
pmc-13527129:

Water first sticks to sulfur-rich spots, then oxygen swaps in for sulfur and migrates below the surface. The surface ends as an oxygen-rich layer that breaks into several lithium compounds and turns porous. That layer failed to protect the material, and ion conductivity fell by 36 percent within three days.
pmc-13528029:
M. Ndu and five colleagues explore how research institutes can practice solidarity in global health in a 2026 paper. Global research still leans on uneven funding, credit, and data control. pmc-13528129:

Across the studies, students trained faster with the new tools. Procedures took less time once learned. Errors dropped as well. Knowledge and skill scores improved versus traditional teaching. Gains showed most clearly for complex tasks like oral surgery and extractions. The authors call immersive tools a strong support for engagement and skill building. They still want bigger trials with shared measures. Dental schools weighing the cost get a mostly positive verdict here.
pmc-13528229:

pmc-13530229:
