Half the group needed more than one session, averaging under two sessions per person. Prior bleeding was less common among staged cases, while supply from certain deep arteries and a location in the parietal lobe appeared more often. Small lesion size sharply lowered the odds of staging, while parietal location raised them, supporting anatomy-led planning.
pmc-13531829:
Habibollah Mahmoodzadeh and Sayyed Mohammad Reza Hakimian test in 2026 a budget-friendly way to support breast implants using the patient own skin layer. Minor skin wound problems appeared in ten breasts and healed with simple care. Two implants were lost, both in patients exposed to radiation around the surgery window. The series shows the technique can be done, while flagging wound burden and radiation as concerns needing bigger studies.
pmc-13532429:

The study enrolled 749 people in hospital with a heart attack who had at least two risk factors.

More risk factors meant more heart attacks, strokes, and deaths over one year. Within each risk group the platelet test still split people into higher and lower risk groups. Readers see how a blood mark could help doctors weigh clot risk against bleed risk when they choose care.
pmc-13532529:

Surface tension holds a stable oil and gel border inside a narrow channel.

Ultraviolet light sets one ring at a time, and stacked rings form a tube whose width follows the light position. Straight, curved, and branching tubes were made, plus tubes with more than one material. Readers get a flexible route toward vessel networks for grown tissue.
pmc-13534429:
Changshu Pan and colleagues run in 2026 sixteen model tests on how reinforced embankments fail under rainfall. Extreme rain is growing more common and damages such earthworks used for roads and water projects. Tests varied rain strength, slope, and the number of reinforcing layers in a custom rig.

Pressure in soil water and soil stress both showed depth and slope effects, though in opposite ways for water pressure. Failure grew step by step from water entry and softening through gully growth to full collapse. Loss of soil suction, not a pressure spike, drove the breakdown, guiding safer designs.
pmc-13534629:
Samarth Godara and colleagues present in 2026 AgriTrack, a framework that tracks farm pest movement using farmer helpline data in India. Manual pest surveys are costly and slow, which limits large-scale watch. Fourteen years of call centre data held over 36 million farmer queries from across the country.

The system tracks pest movement within and across seasons, extracts key date shifts, and forecasts farmer information demand with deep learning. A case study followed termite pests in wheat across India and matched real patterns well. Stakeholders gain timely, low-cost insight for targeted pest action.
pmc-13534729:
Muhammad Arsalan, Xiaojun Yu, and Muhammad Tariq Sadiq develop in 2026 a reinforcement learning optimiser that slows tumour growth with combined radiation and chemotherapy while easing toxicity. Many dosing plans chase short-term shrinkage alone and ignore patient comfort. Their model joins tumour, immune, and healthy cell dynamics in one system.

A smoothed control method paired with a policy learning algorithm adjusted doses in simulation. The hybrid plan cut chemo and radiation doses sharply versus baselines while holding tumour suppression and speeding it slightly. Total treatment intensity fell by over nine tenths in model runs.
pmc-13536529:
Herman G van de Werfhorst argues in 2026 that sociogenomics, the study of genes and social rank, must face core theories of inequality directly. Findings on gene-environment interplay and parental genetic nurturing are often read in unlike ways. One view stresses efficient sorting of people into roles, while another stresses how society builds which traits get rewarded.

Simulations that split context-linked from context-free genetic variation show the field cannot separate these views with current methods. Some starting assumptions about genetic differences can never be tested, yet they are always required. Scholars should state those assumptions plainly when they interpret genetic links to schooling or earnings.
pmc-13536629:
Fatemeh Ahmadinia and colleagues test in 2026 whether bitter orange flower capsules ease anxiety around childbirth and postpartum blues. The plant is used traditionally as a calming agent in Iran. One hundred anxious pregnant women were split into capsule and placebo groups for six weeks spanning delivery.

Anxiety scores fell in the capsule group both at delivery and two weeks after, unlike the control pattern. Blues at two weeks were also less frequent with the capsules than with placebo. The authors recommend the capsules for anxious mothers, within this trial setting.
pmc-13536729:
Yu Gao and colleagues build a computer model to predict low blood pressure after surgery in people with type 2 diabetes in a 2026 study. Low pressure during recovery can cause serious harm, yet tools tailored to this group are scarce. Records from more than 44,000 past and recent surgical patients supplied training data, narrowed to 13 key predictors. Fourteen model types were trained and compared, with explanations for each prediction.

A random forest model performed best across training, internal, and later patient groups, and held up in an outside hospital check. Blood loss during surgery, age, heart failure, sleep apnea, and body weight ranked as top predictors. The authors present the tool as a practical aid for sorting risk before surgery and tailoring watchful care afterward.
pmc-13538529:
Raju Vidap and colleagues present a brain-inspired spiking network for edge gesture reading from muscle signals in a 2026 study. Standard deep models need offline training and heavy power, blocking tiny wearable devices. The design uses memory-like synapses with self-adjusting updates, ongoing learning that guards old gestures, and short-horizon prediction from spike timing. Muscle-surface signals from hand movements supplied the test stream.

Sorting accuracy ran high, with a matching strong combined score and very low forgetting of earlier gestures. Short-ahead prediction also scored well. Average energy per decision stayed tiny, suiting low-power edge hardware. The authors argue that unifying adaptation, retention, and prediction in one spiking design answers the drift of personal muscle patterns over time.
pmc-13540229:
John Robert White and five colleagues argue, in a 2026 ethnobotanical study, that crop research should look at whole plant genera rather than single species. Indigenous growers often manage several related plants together, and those shared practices can shape the gene pools of all of them.

Fieldwork with the Runa community of Mondayacu in Ecuador combined interviews, observation, and walks focused on the genus Xanthosoma, whose starchy roots are eaten widely. One historically important species is no longer grown there. Another, called lalu, draws responses from destruction to careful keeping for medicine, animal care, and ritual. Herbarium records and literature place these local habits in a national frame.
pmc-13540829:
Jian-hang Xue and four colleagues measure, in a 2026 survey in Xiamen, China, how much four groups at high risk of hepatitis C actually know about the virus. Reaching the global goal of eliminating viral hepatitis by 2030 depends on such groups understanding transmission and cure.

A standard national questionnaire reached 1,621 people across men who have sex with men, drug users, female sex workers, and patients facing invasive procedures. Overall awareness reached about seventy-seven percent, highest among men who have sex with men and lowest, near half, among procedure patients. College education strongly predicted adequate knowledge in most groups. Gaps centred on curability, hidden infection, and new drug risks.
pmc-13540929:
Libo Zhu and seven colleagues hunt, in a 2026 study, for microbial signatures in the uterus that mark endometriosis, a painful inflammatory condition affecting about one in ten women of reproductive age. Diagnosis is often delayed for years, and a non-invasive test would help.

Gene sequencing profiled bacteria in 266 uterine tissue samples taken in two phases of the menstrual cycle. No single microbe survived strict correction as a biomarker, and the well-known Lactobacillus varied widely among individuals. A combined feature set, merging faint signals with machine learning picks and a dysbiosis score, classified proliferative-phase samples moderately well. Secretory-phase models did worse, so the authors stress cycle-aware sampling.
pmc-13542129:
Zhiming Guo and colleagues build a scoring framework in 2026. The field is engineering evaluation. The framework judges how well a process can evolve over time. Car door stamping served as the test case. Older methods handle shifting, uncertain data poorly. That gap motivates the design.

Three parts string together in the system. An indicator set rests on the plan-do-check-act cycle. A weighting scheme mixes entropy weights with a cloud model. The cloud model captures fuzziness and randomness together. An improved ranking method then orders the options. A divergence measure separates options near the ideal. Five real stamping schemes scored across a wide range. Their order matched production logic.
pmc-13542229:
Anna Szymczak-Graczyk and colleagues report a 2026 study, part laboratory work and part computer modelling, on how layered perlite concrete beams respond when one face is heated. Perlite is a light volcanic material valued for insulation, and such beams are increasingly used in energy-saving buildings. Their model links heat flow through the beam thickness to bending behaviour, using a shear-deformable beam formulation with an added axial term.

In the laboratory, a concrete and perlite sandwich beam was warmed on its upper surface to 35 degrees, and measured midspan deflections over time matched the model well. The match shows the calculation captures the delayed bending that slow heat conduction causes in mixed materials. A further purely numerical example, with stiffness falling as temperature rises, shows the framework can extend beyond the simple linear case, though that extension was not tested in the laboratory.
pmc-13545229:
Mei Yi and colleagues build in this 2026 study a risk score for prostate cancer based on genes from cancer-associated fibroblasts, the support cells that surround a tumor and help it grow. Such scores aim to predict which patients will relapse and how they might respond to immune therapy.

Using single-cell and bulk gene data from public databases, the team found two fibroblast types tied to patient outcomes. Five genes survived statistical screening and formed the final signature. Patients scored low risk lived longer, while high-risk patients relapsed more often in outside datasets. High-risk tumors also showed heavier immune cell infiltration and more activity in growth and spread pathways. The authors propose the score as a guide for prognosis and treatment planning.
pmc-13547329:
Aliakbar Dehno Khalaji and Kasim Sakran Abass synthesized in 2026 a new composite material for pulling dye pollution out of wastewater, combining chitosan from crustacean shells, starch, and iron oxide particles. They tested it in batch experiments against two common industrial dyes, the orange methyl orange and the blue methylene blue, tuning conditions for the best removal.

At its best the material removed about 99 percent of the orange dye and about 98 percent of the blue one. The capture pattern fit models describing a single layer of chemically bound dye on the surface. After five rounds of washing and reuse, removal still stayed above 92 percent for both dyes. The authors present the composite as a cheap, repeatable cleaner for dye-laden water.
pmc-13547629:
Hye Mi Lee and colleagues described in 2026 a Merkel cell carcinoma, an aggressive skin-related neuroendocrine cancer, that appeared as a large mass under the jaw with no skin lesion at all. The tumor almost always starts in sun-exposed skin, so a primary growth in the submandibular region is exceptionally unusual. Their patient, an 86-year-old man, had a painful neck mass that grew over three months to roughly seven by five centimeters.

Imaging placed the mass at the submandibular gland with no lymph node spread, and a needle biopsy confirmed the cancer type. The report walks through the diagnosis, surgical handling, and early recovery. The authors urge doctors to keep this cancer on the list for fast-growing submandibular masses even when the skin looks clean.
pmc-13548529:
Rudy Celeghin and colleagues examine gene changes that disrupt RNA splicing in arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy, a heart muscle disease, in a 2026 study. Many such changes sit outside the usual splice sites and stay labeled as variants of uncertain significance, which limits what doctors can tell families. The team gathered candidate variants from 200 affected people and tested them several ways.

Computer prediction, heart tissue data, and laboratory minigene tests were combined, then matched against family segregation records and standard classification rules. Faulty splicing was confirmed for nine of twenty variants, and sixteen of the twenty could be reclassified once all evidence was joined. Certain heart genes, including DSP and DSG2, carried an excess of these variants. The work shows how pairing prediction with bench testing can turn uncertain findings into clinically usable answers.
pmc-13548629:
Xin Zhang and colleagues look for a blood marker that separates better from worse outlooks among pancreatic cancer patients whose scans show stable disease, in a 2026 retrospective study. Scan categories judge chemotherapy response crudely, and stable disease hides wide variation. Among 182 patients on first-line chemotherapy, the team tracked the tumor marker CA19-9 every eight weeks alongside imaging, focusing on those whose marker started high and whose scans stayed stable.

Most patients landed in the stable group, and their survival resembled that of patients whose tumors had visibly shrunk. Inside the stable group, patients whose marker fell by at least thirty percent from its starting level lived longer without progression and longer overall than those without such a fall. The authors propose the thirty percent cut as a cheap extra layer for judging prognosis when scans look unchanged.
pmc-13550029:
Cécile Pinault and colleagues show that umbilical cord jelly stem cells can make fat after all, if the metabolic menu is right, in a 2026 study pairing a literature review with experiments. Wharton's jelly stem cells had a reputation for poor fat formation compared with marrow stem cells. Reviewing forty-one papers exposed a tangle of differing recipes with no shared standard, suggesting the verdict might reflect conditions rather than the cells.

The team tested four induction mixes varying sugar and insulin, reading fat buildup with machine learning assisted imaging. Marrow cells fattened readily under the standard recipe, while cord cells lagged. Extending the induction and enriching metabolic support unlocked a delayed but clear fat response in cord cells, with sugar and insulin reinforcing each other. The authors propose a standardized yardstick for comparing fat potential across cell sources.
pmc-13550429:
Shivendra Verma and colleagues chart the hormone response to sugar in a rare diabetes caused by a calcified, stone-filled pancreas, in a 2026 physiology study. Fibrocalculous pancreatic diabetes destroys insulin production, but its effects on glucagon and gut incretin hormones were murky. Nine patients and six healthy volunteers each took glucose by mouth and, on another occasion, by vein at a rate matched to copy the same blood sugar curve.

Patients ran high glucagon at rest and after oral glucose, and glucagon exposure was larger by mouth than by vein, a route difference absent in controls. Two hormones from the lower gut surged, while the upper-gut hormone GIP lagged. Insulin-linked C-peptide and pancreatic polypeptide stayed deeply suppressed by both routes, confirming severe gland failure. The authors describe a distinctive hormonal fingerprint for this diabetes type.
pmc-13550529:
Jiraporn Sirison and colleagues blast two green microalgae species with ultraviolet-C light to make them richer for food and fuel at once, in a 2026 cultivation study. Stress can push algae to stockpile valuable compounds. Cultures of Desmodesmus quadricauda and Scenedesmus dimorphus received up to three hours of UV-C, then grew for fourteen days while the team tracked biomass, pigments, protein, and fats.

Both species grew more biomass after irradiation, peaking at different doses. Cancer-fighting carotenoid pigments and protein rose, protein by up to about a third. Fat content and productivity crested at one hour of exposure, reaching up to nearly double the untreated level. The fat mix shifted toward oleic acid. The prized omega-3 DHA also appeared for the first time. Biodiesel from the fats met the cetane standard but failed cold-flow requirements, so the authors call for more tuning.
pmc-13554129:
A Andres F Ramirez and L Alberto J Lamadrid forecast air pollution from New York power plants in 2030 as green energy grows, in a 2026 study. They built their method on hourly records from 2019 across the state grid. Federal pollution archives and forecast tools from a national energy programme filled the gaps. The aim was a method that grid planners can reuse in running studies.

Future cases vary how much wind and solar power joins the mix. Swings in that green supply change how hard fossil plants must run, and thus what they emit. The authors lay out steps linking past plant behaviour to future cases. Planners can use the output to weigh climate goals against local air quality before choices are locked in.
pmc-13554229:
Yulong Chen leads a five-author team breaking tunnel models to learn how rock bolts hold layered stone together in a 2026 study. Blocks of rock-like material held a round hole crossed by bedding layers, laid flat or upright. Seven support schemes were fitted, from sprayed concrete to steel arches and bolt patterns. Cameras watched the hole walls fail under squeezing, and CT scans mapped cracks afterward.

Full bolt patterns and slotted steel pipes gave the biggest strength gains. Sprayed concrete and arches pressed the walls and stopped flakes from spalling off. Upright bedding gained more strength from support than flat bedding. Scans showed bolts compacting cracked zones, halting cracks, and bending their paths. That grip lifts the load the broken rock can still bear.
pmc-13555629:
Kai Ye leads a six-author team crafting an injectable corn-protein gel to mend torn shoulder tendons in brittle bone in a 2026 study. Rotator cuff repairs often fail when osteoporosis weakens the tendon-to-bone joint. Their gel carries niacin, a vitamin, inside tiny carbon spheres that also convert light to gentle heat. Gel extracts pushed bone-forming cells toward bone and tendon stem cells toward tendon in dishes. Signs of cell aging fell, and harmful oxygen species dropped inside cells. In rats with brittle bones, gel plus near-infrared light rebuilt the joint's cartilage zone and strengthened the repair. Skin wounds also healed faster with richer blood vessel growth and calmer inflammation.
pmc-13555929:
Ruth B Mbwambo leads a sixteen-author team mapping variation in a malaria parasite gene eyed as a vaccine candidate in a 2026 study. The gene, called phistb, helps the parasite survive inside red blood cells. Genomes from more than fourteen hundred samples across Tanzania, Kenya, Uganda, and Ethiopia were drawn from a public database. Filtering left 1,312 samples for analysis.

Two thirds of infections carried a single parasite strain, with Ethiopia highest on that measure. Among single-strain samples, eighty-eight gene versions appeared, two of them dominating. Kenya showed the richest diversity of the four countries. Populations barely differed from each other overall, with no clear geographic structure. Rare variants ran in excess in most countries, hinting at recent expansion.
pmc-13556029:
Veethika Nayak and four colleagues mapped in 2026 what research connects hospital falls to the wellbeing of the staff who work there. Burnout, low professional fulfilment, poor work settings, and weak organisational culture can all erode care, yet their link to falls had not been gathered in one place. Following established scoping methods, the team searched five databases and also checked whether fall-prevention trials measured staff wellbeing at all.

Seventy-eight studies qualified from more than eleven thousand records, most of them observational and focused on nurses in acute hospitals. Burnout tracked with more falls, job satisfaction with fewer, and better work environments also helped. Culture findings were mixed, with supportive leadership protective and toxic leadership harmful. No fall-prevention trial in the Cochrane set had built staff wellbeing into its design, a gap the authors highlight.
pmc-13556229:
Liu and colleagues report a 2026 study of a tiny viral protein that blocks plant immunity in two separate ways.  Cucumber mosaic virus fights back with its 2b protein. The team built virus versions with shortened 2b proteins to separate the protein's skills.

One shortened protein could still grip small RNAs and long viral RNA, and it blocked the amplification route run by the host enzyme RDR6, but not the RDR1 route. The other shortened protein could not grip RNA, yet it blocked the RDR1 route by binding that enzyme directly. pmc-13558329:
Wei Li and four colleagues reviewed in 2026 how minimally invasive tension band methods for kneecap fractures have evolved. The classic operation wires the broken patella so that muscle pull presses the fragments together, and newer versions do the same job through small incisions. Their review searched three databases to December 2023 for clinical studies of these percutaneous techniques, with or without camera assistance.

Four families of technique emerged: plain tension band, wire-based, screw-based, and strong suture versions. Against open surgery, the gentler methods generally won on operating time, hospital stay, pain, joint recovery, and scar appearance. Two questions stay open: many patients still need a second operation to remove hardware, and whether adding a joint camera helps enough to justify it remains disputed. The authors warn that most studies are small and retrospective, so enthusiasm should stay measured.
pmc-13558529:
Valentin Herber and six colleagues measured in 2026 how accurately a dynamic navigation system places dental implants. Their prospective study covered 109 implants in 76 patients placed by five experienced surgeons at four centres, with deviations checked by matching scans taken after surgery to the plan.

Average angular error came to just over three degrees, and the implant tip landed about a millimetre from its planned spot on average. Every deviation measure beat freehand benchmark goals drawn from the literature by a clear margin. No serious device-related harm occurred, and surgeons rated the system highly for satisfaction. The authors conclude that navigation delivers true-to-plan, safe placement in experienced hands.
pmc-13558629:
Jing Zhang and Siti Zuraidah Md Osman tested in 2026 a game-based language module in vocational education, a setting where game learning is rarely studied. Their quasi-experimental design taught sixty students with the game module for six weeks. Sixty-six peers followed ordinary instruction. The team then compared achievement, enjoyment of the foreign language, and learner autonomy, with interviews adding texture. Flow theory, the psychology of full absorption, framed the module's design.

The game group finished with clearly higher achievement and enjoyment scores. Autonomy, the habit of directing one's own learning, did not differ between groups. Students praised the module for building language skill and allowing flexible, personal pacing, while criticising thin game features and technical glitches. The authors conclude that well-built games lift results and mood in vocational language classes, even if self-direction must be taught apart.
pmc-13559129:
Wenting Wang and colleagues examined whether the volume of red blood cells transfused during children's heart surgery predicts harm afterward. Their 2026 retrospective study covered 19,081 patients aged 14 or younger who had operations with cardiopulmonary bypass. Children were grouped by weight-adjusted transfusion volume, from none up to more than 34.5 mL/kg.

About 44.5 percent of the children received red cells during surgery. After adjustment, the team found no steady linear rise in risk with volume; a threshold pattern fit better instead. Volumes above the top cutoff were tied to longer mechanical ventilation, more acute kidney injury, and more combined complications. Small volumes, curiously, were linked to fewer of those outcomes than no transfusion at all. The authors suggest a workable transfusion range may exist and that volume per kilogram deserves attention in surgical planning.
pmc-13559629:
Jinzi Liang and six colleagues published this 2026 study on whether adding radiation, with or without chemotherapy, after surgery helps patients with head and neck adenoid cystic carcinoma. That is a rare salivary-type cancer that has not spread. Guidelines recommend postoperative radiation for high-risk cases, but evidence is mixed. The cohort held 114 patients, 35 surgery-only, 42 radiation and 37 chemoradiation, followed for a median of 51.0 months across the study. No significant differences appeared between the groups in overall survival, progression-free survival, local control or distant spread. Nerve invasion by the tumour predicted worse survival, with a hazard ratio of 3.425 for death. Within that subgroup, radiation did improve local control over surgery alone. Adding chemotherapy showed no clear advantage over radiation alone.
pmc-13560129:
Xin Li and colleagues model poor prognosis in invasive aspergillosis, a dangerous fungal infection, using records from a general hospital in Anhui. Their 2026 retrospective study covers 307 patients diagnosed between January 2019 and March 2024. Thirty-nine patients had unfavorable outcomes, against 268 with favorable ones, and detection of the infection had climbed in the last two years.

Four factors survived selection as independent risks: longer intensive care stay, higher C-reactive protein, higher blood glucose, and kidney failure. A nomogram built from them predicted poor outcomes with an area under the curve of 0.810 in the group's analysis, and bootstrap checks kept the figure close. Calibration agreed well between predicted and observed risk. The team also released the tool as an interactive web application. The authors present it for early risk sorting and faster intervention in high-risk patients.
pmc-13569529:
Hana Amer and colleagues survey, in a 2026 cross-sectional study across four South Australian hospitals, how inpatients feel about collaborative pharmacist prescribing. In that model, pharmacists and doctors build medicine plans together and pharmacists then prescribe. Two hundred patients answered, half served by the joint model and half by doctor-only prescribing.

Feelings and views were compared between the groups, with written notes analyzed for themes and rating scales summed side by side. Shared decision-making sits at the center of the model, so patient views are the test that matters. Hospital managers weighing wider pharmacist prescribing get direct evidence on whether patients feel involved and respected under the newer arrangement.
pmc-13570429:
Haihang Ao and colleagues pilot, in a 2026 animal study, patches made from processed human skin tissue to rebuild narrowed ureters in three miniature pigs. Ureters are the tubes carrying urine from kidney to bladder. Long narrowings are hard to repair by joining cut ends, so the team replaced a two-centimeter segment with a rolled tube of the material over a stent.

At forty-five days all three pigs showed open channels on imaging and scope checks, with new lining, organized collagen, fresh blood vessels, and early muscle regrowth. Gene data supported repair activity. Only three animals and short follow-up limit the claim, yet the approach could one day free patients from needing their own tissue grafts.
pmc-13572529:
Xiaofan Yu, with ten colleagues, reports a 2026 study of gene activity behind eggshell formation in laying hens. Gene reads from the uterus, the organ where the shell forms, were grouped by stage and network pattern. Early on, a protein called ovalbumin ran high and may stop crystals from forming too soon. In the fast phase, shell matrix proteins plus calcium pumps and carriers worked together to hold calcium steady. Calcium in uterine fluid rose over time, then held flat through the fast phase. The gene map offers targets for breeding and feed plans.
pmc-13573329:

A wall motion score also improved in the cell group. Chamber sizes and scar size showed trends toward gain, but none reached clear proof. Major bad heart events did not rise with cell treatment. The authors say long-term gains in heart shape remain open and need stronger trials.
pmc-13575929:
Anna M Newen leads a 2026 immunology study on how the body deletes self-reactive B cells before they cause autoimmune disease. B cells that target the body's own tissues arise during development. Blocking it after activation raised self-reactive cells and antibodies yet caused little tissue harm. The authors propose a model of deletion spread across stages, where early checkpoints carry the main protective weight.
pmc-13576129:

LigaSure patients faced a lower recurrence risk, with a gap of 12 percentage points. Rates of bleeding, infection, urine retention, and clotting were similar. The authors rate certainty in the pooled results as very low and ask for stronger trials.
pmc-13578329:
Hamid Reza Roosta, Sajad Azizabadi, and Seyed Hossein Mirdehghan grow three bell pepper types in a soil free film system. Their 2026 greenhouse study, set in Iran, tests which feed mix suits each type. Roots sat in a thin stream of liquid feed, a setup called nutrient film technique. Three feeds were tried: a classic standard, a Dutch mix, and a mix advised by a United States agency.

Plant type and feed both shaped growth, yield, and fruit quality. One pepper paired with the agency mix piled up the most growth and the heaviest fruit. A second type kept the richest green color on the standard feed. A third used light most ably under every feed. Fruit firmness and vitamin C also rose on the agency mix.
pmc-13578529:
Christopher W Roy and colleagues test a free running heart scan that needs no breath holds or heart wires, in a 2026 study of 45 patients born with heart defects. Standard scans split the heart check into flat movies and still three dimensional views, each with its own setup. Their five dimensional method records the whole heart while sorting beats and breaths after the fact, using a standard contrast dye.

The new scan ran faster than both older methods. Its measures of heart chamber size tracked the standard movie method closely, though small offsets appeared. Graders scored its overall quality above the still three dimensional scan, and longer bits of the heart arteries stayed visible. Sharpness on those arteries still favored the older still scan, a trade the authors note.
pmc-13579829:
Brototo Deb, Timothy Lim, Ian K Everitt, and Carl G Streed audit how clinical calculator tools handle sex and gender, in a 2026 review of the MDCalc site. Such tools guide daily care, and a muddled sex or gender input can skew their advice. The team screened eight hundred twenty one tools in May 2025 and kept those asking for sex, gender, or both.

Eighty four tools qualified, and nearly all forced a two way answer. Most labeled the input as sex, the rest as gender. One in five mixed the two up, pairing a label with answer choices that meant the other thing. Source papers showed the same mix up in a quarter of cases that stated how data were gathered. Most tools carried medium or high weight for care decisions, raising the stakes of the muddle.
pmc-13582129:
Sammy J S Wrede, Ines-Maria Gärtner, and Achim Mortsiefer scan workplace health programs for how much they build health, not just dodge risk, in a 2026 scoping review. The lens is salutogenesis, a frame that asks what makes people thrive: feeling life makes sense, joining in, setting goals, having variety, and gaining power over one's work. Five databases gave up 128 intervention studies from 2014 to 2024.

Each program was scored on how many of the five principles it wove in. Overall uptake landed mid range. Empowerment, variety, and sense of coherence appeared most, while taking part and goal setting lagged far behind. Programs with personal coaching or self management tools scored highest, and mixed programs aligned best overall.
pmc-13586029:
Roshan Kumar, Babak Pakbin, Mona Roshan Singh, and Bharathi Muruganantham introduce a journal collection on the microbiome in cancer therapy. Another builds stool and spit classifiers that can flag bowel cancer without a scope. Liver and bile duct cancers also feature, where microbe and chemical profiles together may sharpen forecasts. The editors frame microbes as both markers and levers for future care.
pmc-13589929:
Jing Zhang leads a 2026 study of liver scarring, a slow harm that can lead to liver failure and liver cancer. The work centers on SNX3, a protein that sorts cargo inside cells. Levels of SNX3 were high in scarred liver from both patients and mice. Zhang and the team used mice bred so the gene could be cut or raised in liver cells.

That signal wakes nearby star shaped cells, which lay down scar tissue and make yet more signal. Blocking the signal path eased the harm, marking SNX3 as a drug target.
pmc-13592629:

The group therapy targets thinking biases behind delusions and related symptoms, and men and women often present differently. Harmonized records from an international consortium covered 573 people with schizophrenia spectrum disorders who took the training in clinics or studies. Symptom scales tracked positive, negative, general, and total scores over time.

Symptoms fell across every domain for the whole group. Yet the pace and size of gains matched between men and women, despite different starting profiles. Sex did not steer the trajectory of change on any scale. Lamarca and the team read the training as broadly usable, while urging finer study of sex linked factors beyond the simple male female split.

Peto, Pike, Armitage, and co-authors set out how to design long randomised trials in cancer and other diseases. The Medical Research Council had backed joint trials in leukaemia and other cancers for years, reporting results in journals. Less visible was the craft of designing such trials well.

In this first part, the authors cover introduction and design for trials where each patient must be followed for a long time. They stress sound planning, fair random assignment, and patience in watching outcomes. Their approach shaped modern trial design, where careful setup protects results from bias.
pmc-3319429:
Lorenz, Bernhart, Honer Zu Siederdissen, and co-authors present version two of the ViennaRNA Package. Secondary structure is a key level for describing nucleic acids such as RNA. It captures most of a molecule's folding energy, is often conserved through evolution, and routinely explains experimental findings.

The package predicts and analyses those folded shapes from sequence, based on carefully measured energy rules. Researchers use it to design experiments and interpret how RNA works. ViennaRNA became core infrastructure for RNA science, taught in courses and built into many other tools.  Virus and ribosome studies both depend on predictions from this software family.
pmc-3626529:
Luo, Liu, Xie, and co-authors present SOAPdenovo2, an improved assembler for building genomes from short sequencing reads. Assembly of new genomes from next-generation short reads was growing rapidly. Big challenges remained in making that process efficient and accurate, since reads must be pieced together without a guide.

The earlier SOAPdenovo had already assembled many published genomes. Version two improves memory use empirically, so larger genomes fit on ordinary hardware. Cheaper, lighter assembly widened genome projects to species and labs that could not afford massive computing clusters.  Human and plant genome projects both used the assembler during its peak years.
pmc-4196729:
Moons, de Groot, Bouwmeester, and their colleagues published the CHARMS checklist in 2014. The checklist guides people who review studies that build prediction models for diagnosis or prognosis. Such reviews need care, since weak methods can make a model look better than it is.

CHARMS tells reviewers what to extract from each study and how to judge its quality. It covers the source of data, the outcome predicted, and how the model was built and tested. A shared checklist makes reviews of prediction studies more complete and more alike across teams. That in turn helps clinicians know which risk models deserve trust.
pmc-4315529:
Boellaard, Delgado-Bolton, Oyen, and their colleagues wrote procedure guidelines in 2014 for FDG PET/CT tumor imaging. This scan combines a sugar-based tracer with CT imaging to find cancers in adults. The guidelines aim to help doctors recommend, perform, read, and report the scan in a consistent way.

PET is a quantitative method, so it needs common quality control and quality assurance across centers. The European guidelines set out standards for patient preparation, scanning, and measurement. Shared practice means a scan in one hospital can be compared with a scan in another. That consistency matters when scans decide whether a cancer treatment is working.
pmc-5433529:
Thursby and Juge introduced the human gut microbiota in 2017. The human gut is home to a dense, ever-shifting community of microbes, the gut microbiota. Their influence on the host is strong, in health and in disease alike.

Many forces shape the founding of this community in infancy, among them birth mode, diet, and antibiotics. Once set, the community helps digest food, trains the immune system, and blocks invaders. Disturbances in it are linked to conditions from bowel disease to obesity. The introduction gives new readers the core concepts of a field that has reshaped medicine's view of the body.
pmc-7046529:
Erik Sahai, Igor Astsaturov, Edna Cukierman, and coauthors set out a framework for cancer-associated fibroblasts in 2020. Fibroblasts inside tumors help build the matrix tumors sit in. They swap signals with cancer cells and with immune cells constantly.

The field had grown messy, with rival names for overlapping cell states. The authors propose shared definitions and experiments to sort helper from harmful fibroblast types. Some types restrain tumors while others feed them, so blanket targeting is risky. Their framework gave a fragmented field a common language and research agenda. A proposed naming scheme for fibroblast states is offered for community testing and revision.
pmc-7078829:
Kenji Mizumoto, Katsushi Kagaya, Alexander Zarebski, and coauthors estimated silent COVID-19 cases on the Diamond Princess in 2020. The cruise ship was quarantined in Yokohama with thousands aboard after a former passenger tested positive. Hundreds on board later tested positive as well.

Because nearly everyone aboard was tested, the ship offered a rare full picture. Modeling the timing of tests and symptoms, the team estimates a substantial share of infections never caused symptoms. That share matters, since silent carriers can spread the virus. The estimate shaped early debate on screening and quarantine policy.
propertius-elegies-butler-loeb-1929:
Sextus Propertius poured his stormy love for a woman he calls Cynthia into four books of elegies in the age of Augustus. H. E. Butler translated the poems into plain prose for the Loeb series. His version gives the complete Cynthia cycle, from first sight to bitter end.

Propertius is the most allusive voice of Augustan poetry: every love scene drags in gods, myths, and old wars. The last book turns to Rome itself, its rites, its dead heroes, and a ghost who speaks from the tomb. Butler's prose lets English readers follow the dense Latin line by line. The poems set the mold for love elegy after him.
proust-captive-moncrieff-1929:
The Captive, fifth volume of In Search of Lost Time, was published in French in 1923, after Marcel Proust's death. C. K. Scott Moncrieff's English translation came out in 1929. The narrator now keeps Albertine in his Paris rooms, half guest and half prisoner, while jealousy eats at him daily.

He watches her sleep, questions her friends, and fears her secret past. Albertine, bored and trapped, plans her escape from his control. Their locked rooms become a study of love turned into surveillance. Proust stretches single days across hundreds of pages of fine attention. The volume is his fullest study of jealousy as a form of knowledge.
razi-de-aluminibus-et-salibus-steele-192:
The Book of Alums and Salts bears the name of al-Razi, the Persian doctor and alchemist who died in 925. Gerard of Cremona turned it into Latin in the twelfth century, and Robert Steele gave it English form in the journal Isis in 1929. It is the first Western work on making chemical substances ready for use.

Salt by salt and alum by alum, the book tells how to clean, roast, dissolve, and test each material. The tone is that of a workshop bench book, not a book of secrets. Such plain craft writing carried Arabic chemistry into Latin Europe. Steele's version keeps the matter close for students of the early craft.
remarque-all-quiet-1929: Remarque's 1929 All Quiet on the Western Front follows German soldiers in the trenches. It exposed war's lie. The Tower library holds the full text. It showed the mud. Boys died. Myths broke. Truth bled. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
remy-demonolatry-1929:
Nicolas Remy feeds the flames with law in Demonolatry, here in the English text of 1929. Remy was a high law man in Lorraine who boasted he had sent scores on scores of witches to death: nine score in all, by the lore of his book of 1595. Ashwin turned the Latin to English, with notes by Montague Summers, for this late print of the grim work.

Remy sets out the sabbath, the pact, and wolf turns as points of law. His pride in the count is the book's true horror. It is the hunt's creed.
rise-of-the-new-west-1819-1829: Frederick Jackson Turner's Rise of the New West covers America from 1819 to 1829. The rough frontier democracy of Andrew Jackson's age takes shape in these pages. Sectional quarrels, new states, and western settlement fill the stirring story. A true classic of American historical writing.
roosevelt-trailing-the-giant-panda-1929:
Theodore Roosevelt the younger and his brother Kermit rode into China in 1929 to fetch a fabled bear. Trailing the Giant Panda tells of the hunt for the giant panda, the mystery bear of the border hills. No Westerner had yet brought one out of the wild.

The brothers cross hard country, track the shy beast by its sign, and at last bring one down. Their panda reached the West as proof the tales were true. The book is a brisk tale of camp, trail, and sportsmanship. It also marks the hour the panda stepped from rumor into the world's zoos.
russell-marriage-morals-1929:
Marriage and Morals, published in 1929, was Russell's most controversial book on social questions. It argues that the sexual morality of his day, built on fear and ignorance, damaged marriages and warped children's lives.

Russell defends sex education, easier divorce, and tolerance for unions outside marriage, and he questions whether strict monogamy serves most couples. The book scandalized Britain and America; a decade later it was used to bar him from a New York professorship. Views then called prophetic now read as temperate. The scandal is history, and the argument can finally be heard on its merits.
sarpi-council-of-trent-1629:
Paolo Sarpi, a Venetian friar and adviser, wrote his Istoria del Concilio Tridentino in 1619 as a secret history of the Council of Trent. The council had remade the Catholic Church in answer to the Reformation, and Sarpi, no friend of Rome, told how it really worked. His manuscript was smuggled out of Venice for printing, and Nathaniel Brent's English translation appears here in the 1629 printing.

Sarpi shows pope, bishops, and princes bargaining behind the council's solemn face. His case is that Rome bent a church council to its own power. The book became the great anti-papal history of the council, checked and fought over ever since. Few works of history carried such risk to their maker.
swift-modest-proposal-1729:
Jonathan Swift published A Modest Proposal anonymously in Dublin in 1729. Ireland was starving under English trade rules and landlord neglect, and Swift had spent years writing angry pamphlets about it. This pamphlet pretends to be calm economic advice from a helpful planner.

The proposer, with tables and figures, suggests that poor Irish families sell their babies as food for the rich. Swift keeps the tone reasonable while the horror builds line by line. The real targets are the landlords, officials, and economists whose policies already treated the Irish as less than human. The work is the most famous satire in English and still shocks new readers.
thomson-narrative-life-medical-discoveri:
Thomson told his own story in A Narrative of the Life and Medical Discoveries, printed in 1829. The New Hampshire farmer traces his path from sickly youth to founder of a healing system. He recalls watching his mother's illness, testing plants on himself, and slowly building his method.

Trials, rivals, and charges of harm fill the later chapters, and Thomson answers them all as persecution. He presents his vindication as proof that nature's remedies beat learned medicine. The book reads as both memoir and manifesto, the founding document of the Thomsonian movement in its maker's own words.
thucydides-peloponnesian-war-hobbes-1629:
Thucydides wrote his History of the Peloponnesian War in Greek, and Thomas Hobbes Englished it in 1629. Hobbes's was the first English Thucydides made straight from the Greek text of the history. The translator later wrote Leviathan, and his hard political sense suits this hard history well.

Athens and Sparta fight a long war that grinds Greece down over twenty-seven years. Speeches state each side's case with cold logic, from Pericles to the Melian dialogue's threats. Plague at Athens and the Sicilian disaster mark the arc of imperial overreach and fall. Thucydides claims no fables, only what men did and why power moved them to act. Hobbes prized him as the most political writer who ever lived in Greece.
tob-10229:
Herbert Giles translated the writings of Chuang Tzu, the most playful of the Taoist classics. Chuang Tzu tells stories and spins paradoxes rather than laying down rules. In the most famous, he dreams he is a butterfly, then wonders whether the butterfly is now dreaming him.

Talking skulls, useless trees that survive because nobody can use them, and a butcher whose blade never dulls carry the teaching. Rigid distinctions between big and small, useful and useless, life and death dissolve as the tales turn. Readers who find Laozi severe will find Chuang Tzu funny, strange, and quietly radical about going along with the way of things.
tob-10829:
H. P. Blavatsky explained her own system in The Key to Theosophy in 1889, choosing plain question-and-answer form. An imaginary inquirer asks, and Blavatsky replies: What is Theosophy? What happens after death? Who are the mahatmas? How should a Theosophist live? The movement's official primer was written to settle confusion.

Dialogue lets her correct popular misunderstandings one by one, including charges that Theosophy is Buddhism in disguise or a new religion. The tone is direct, sometimes combative, but the structure stays clear. V1 evidence recommends starting here before tackling The Secret Doctrine, advice a century of readers has confirmed by experience.
tob-4029:
Adam Smith published An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations in 1776, the year America declared independence. The book founded economics as a discipline. Its opening example, the pin factory, shows the division of labor multiplying output, and its argument builds from workshops to whole trading nations.

Markets coordinate self-interest toward public benefit, in Smith's famous image, as if by an invisible hand, while monopolies and tariffs draw his sustained attack. Smith is subtler than his later slogans: he assigns government real duties in defense, justice, and public works. Nations still govern, and argue, inside the frame this book built.
tob-4129:
Mead wrote Fragments of a Faith Forgotten in 1900 to rescue the Gnostics from the reports of their enemies. Valentinus, Basilides, and Marcion receive fair hearings as thinkers, not mere heretics. Short sketches build a picture of the second century's wildest Christian movements.

Mead reads the fragments with sympathy and a scholar's care, asking what the Gnostics meant before asking where they erred. The book made Gnosticism a modern subject of study rather than a footnote of abuse. Verified from the 1919 edition, it remains the work that taught occult and academic readers alike to take the heretics seriously.
travels-ibn-battuta-lee-1829:
Samuel Lee translated The Travels of Ibn Batuta into English in 1829 for the Oriental Translation Committee. It was the first English rendering of the Rihla, drawn from an Arabic abridgment. Ibn Battuta, a Moroccan scholar, left home in 1325 for the pilgrimage to Mecca and did not settle again for nearly thirty years.

His road ran some seventy-five thousand miles, from Morocco to China and from Anatolia to East Africa. Courts, shrines, plagues, and shipwrecks fill his plain, curious record. He served sultans as judge in Delhi and the Maldives along the way. Lee's version gave English readers the greatest traveler of the medieval world. No other medieval journey covers so much of the earth.
un-ga-res-29: Scheduling, not war or peace, fills Resolution 29 of the General Assembly, passed on 9 February 1946. Urgent questions were already before the new UN bodies, which would keep working between sessions. The text rules that the sitting session will pause in February and count as the first part of the first regular session. The second part would open in September, with the new headquarters work in the meantime.
un-ga-res-a-69-29:
A Middle East free of nuclear arms has been the Assembly's stated goal since the 1970s, and Resolution A/69/29 renews the call. The text recalls the chain of votes back to 1974. All states of the region are urged to take the swift, workable steps the plan needs. Till the zone stands, they should pledge in solemn form to make, get, or hold no nuclear arms.

No third party should be let to base such arms on their soil. All atomic plants in the region should sit under the checks of the world atomic body. Pledges to that end should be lodged with the Security Council. The ban on attacks on atomic plants is stressed as well.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: Adopted on 9 February 1946 at the twenty-sixth plenary meeting, General Assembly Resolution 29 It set the calendar of the first session. Urgent work was already with the new organs. A special session could be called if needed. The Assembly voted to adjourn in February as the first part of the first regular session. It voted to meet again on the first Tuesday after 2 September 1946, for the second part.

General Assembly resolution 69/29 (2014) is the Assembly's annual call for a nuclear-weapon-free zone in the Middle East, a proposal it has backed by consensus since 1980. It urges the region's states to take practical steps toward the zone. It urges them to join the Non-Proliferation Treaty. It urges them to place all nuclear activities under International Atomic Energy Agency safeguards. Meanwhile they should refrain from developing or hosting nuclear weapons. The Secretary-General is asked to keep consulting the region's states and to report to the seventieth session.
un-sc-res-1029:
UNAMIR was wound down to its final months on 12 December 1995. The Secretary-General's report of 1 December set out the mission's state. Rwanda's foreign minister had written in August and November about the government's terms. Elements of the old regime were arming in the camps across the border, the Council noted with concern. Refugee return in safety and true reconciliation were the stated goals.

The Council extended UNAMIR's mandate for a final period, to 8 March 1996. The mandate was adjusted to stress help for refugee repatriation and for the government's rebuilding work. Troop strength would fall to 1,200, and military observers and support staff to 200. The civilian police part would be withdrawn. The Secretary-General had to start planning the full pullout once the mandate ended. He was also to study handing the mission's non-lethal gear to Rwanda's government.
un-sc-res-129: Lebanon and Jordan are the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 129, adopted unanimously on 7 August 1958. Both states had complained of outside interference. American troops had landed in Lebanon and British troops in Jordan. Vetoes at two earlier meetings had blocked the Council from acting. Finding itself unable to carry out its chief duty for peace, the Council calls an emergency special session of the General Assembly. The move hands the crisis to the full membership. That session later backed steps meant to speed the foreign troops home.
un-sc-res-1329:
The war crimes tribunals are the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 1329, adopted on 30 November 2000. The tribunals for the former Yugoslavia and for Rwanda had heavy case loads. Their presidents asked for more judges so trials could end sooner. Both courts had also improved the way they worked.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council amends both statutes. It creates a pool of twenty-seven temporary judges for the Yugoslavia tribunal. The shared appeals chamber grows for both courts. Two extra judges will be elected for the Rwanda tribunal, and two of its judges will sit on appeals. Leaders, the text notes, should face trial before these courts rather than minor actors.
un-sc-res-1429:
Lack of progress on Western Sahara worried the Council in the summer of 2002. On 30 July 2002 it called a political solution critically needed. The deadlock caused suffering in the territory. It also risked unrest in the region. Trade and growth across the Maghreb suffered too. The Council wanted prisoners freed and the fate of missing people settled.

The text backs the Secretary-General and his envoy in full. It asks the parties and nearby states to cooperate with them. It urges work with the United Nations refugee agency on trust-building steps. Family visits between divided Sahrawi families were one such step. The referendum mission, MINURSO, kept its role while talks were sought.
un-sc-res-1529:
Resolution 1529 answered Haiti's February 2004 crisis, when armed revolt spread and President Jean-Bertrand Aristide left the country. The Security Council allowed member states to send a multinational force at once. Its job was to restore order and protect relief work.

Inside the text, the Council welcomes the new interim leadership and demands an end to violence against civilians. The foreign force was a bridge, meant to hold the country until a longer UN mission could take over. The resolution captures Haiti at a breaking point, with the world stepping in.
un-sc-res-1629: Resolution 1629 was adopted on October 3, 2005, according to its record, and is kept here in a Wikisource transcription. Short formal texts like this one often handle the Council's housekeeping of world affairs in a few paragraphs. The entry preserves the complete act, from the members' opening findings to the operative decisions that close it.
un-sc-res-1729: Resolution 1729, adopted in 2006, is a Security Council act kept here as a Wikisource transcription of the UN record. Routine renewals and urgent orders share its format, which is part of its interest. The entry shows the format plainly: grounds recited, prior texts recalled, and then the Council's decision set down in numbered order.
un-sc-res-1829:
Sierra Leone's integrated office was remade as a peacebuilding office on 4 August 2008. UNIOSIL had served the country's recovery well, the Council said. Peaceful local elections in July 2008 marked a fresh milestone. The Secretary-General's report of 29 April advised the new shape. The peacebuilding cooperation framework with the Peacebuilding Commission was moving forward.

The Council asked the Secretary-General to establish the United Nations Integrated Peacebuilding Office in Sierra Leone, UNIPSIL, from 1 October 2008. It would run for an initial twelve months, succeeding UNIOSIL. The office had to focus on backing the government in peace consolidation and growth. A fully integrated United Nations team, with a single voice, was underlined. Close work with ECOWAS and other partners was stressed. The government bore the main duty for the country's peace and security, the Council said. All Sierra Leonean leaders were called to guard the calm the country had won.
un-sc-res-1929:
Resolution 1929, adopted in June 2010, was the toughest round of UN sanctions placed on Iran over its nuclear program. Iran had enriched uranium to a higher level and hidden a new site near Qom. The Council answered with broad new restrictions.

The text bans sales of major weapons to Iran, targets its Revolutionary Guard and shipping lines, and allows cargo inspections on the high seas. It also expands the lists of people and firms facing frozen assets. The resolution marked the peak of world pressure on Tehran before the diplomacy that led to the 2015 nuclear deal.
un-sc-res-2029:
United Nations Security Council Resolution 2029 concerns the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda. The Council adopted it on 21 December 2011. The tribunal, set up after the 1994 genocide, was racing to finish its trials before closing. A new residual body was due to take over its leftover work in July 2012.

The text extends the terms of four permanent judges and eight temporary judges to 30 June 2012. They stay until that date or until their trials end, if sooner. The Council urges states to help arrest the last fugitives still at large. It also presses states to accept people who were cleared or who finished their prison terms.
un-sc-res-229: U Thant's first term as Secretary-General was ending in 1966. On 2 December 1966 the Security Council met in private to judge his record. It praised his proven qualities and high sense of duty. His reappointment, the Council said, would best serve the organization's larger interests. It therefore recommended that the General Assembly appoint him for another term. The short text is the Council's formal part in choosing the world's top official. U Thant served until the end of 1971.
un-sc-res-29: Two new states won the Security Council's blessing in Resolution 29 of 1947. A Council team had weighed a long list of bids for UN membership. Some were fresh looks at old bids: Albania, Mongolia, Transjordan, Ireland, and Portugal. Others were new: Hungary, Italy, Romania, Austria, Yemen, and Bulgaria. Pakistan's fresh bid was weighed as well. Of all these, the Council urges the General Assembly to admit just two: Yemen and Pakistan.
un-sc-res-329: Entered in the record as Resolution 329, this Security Council text is catalogued at 1968. Behind each numbered text lies a meeting, a draft, and a vote, even when the final wording runs to a few lines. Read in sequence with its neighbours, it helps trace how Council practice grew across the postwar decades. No summary replaces it; the record itself is the content of the entry.
un-sc-res-429:
On the Golan Heights, United Nations observers kept watch between Israel and Syria. On 31 May 1978 the Security Council renewed their mission, UNDOF, for six more months. The Secretary-General had reported on the force. The Council noted efforts toward a just and durable peace in the Middle East. It also voiced concern at the tension that still hung over the area.

The new term ran until 30 November 1978. The Council called on the parties to carry out resolution 338 at once. That 1973 text demanded a ceasefire and peace talks. The Secretary-General had to report at the term's end. One Council member, China, did not take part in the vote.
un-sc-res-829:
Security Council Resolution 829, adopted on May 26, 1993, recommended Monaco for membership in the United Nations. The small principality on the French Riviera, ruled by the Grimaldi family for centuries, had long handled its foreign ties through France. By the 1990s it sought a direct voice of its own in the world body.

The Assembly admitted Monaco two days later. Monaco's size raised a gentle question the council set aside: how small can a member be? The vote answered that statehood and acceptance of the Charter, not size, set the bar. The brief resolution thus widened the UN's claim to speak for states of every scale.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Resolution 1029, adopted on 12 December 1995, sets the final chapter for the UN Assistance Mission for Rwanda, UNAMIR. The mission had been created in 1993, before the genocide, and reshaped several times since. Reports told of armed buildups and raids into Rwanda by members of the former regime, while the safe return of refugees and true national healing stayed the Council's stated goals.

The Council extends UNAMIR for a final period until 8 March 1996, with a narrower job. The mission is to help refugees return home safely, aid the refugee agency's supply work, and guard the International Tribunal for Rwanda for the time being. Its troops drop to 1,200, with 200 observers and support staff. Planning for a full pullout within six weeks after the mandate ends is ordered.

Deadlock in the Council during a Middle East crisis produced Resolution 129. It was adopted unanimously on 7 August 1958. At two recent meetings, the permanent members had split. That split stopped the Council from doing its main job: guarding international peace and security. The agenda items before it could not move.

The members therefore handed the problem upward. They decided to call an emergency special session. The General Assembly, with every member state voting, would take up the matter. This was the same escape route used over Hungary in 1956. It let the wider membership speak when vetoes froze the Council.

The war-crimes tribunals are enlarged by Resolution 1329, adopted unanimously on 30 November 2000. Both tribunals — for the former Yugoslavia and for Rwanda — faced long dockets, and their presidents had asked for more judges so trials could finish sooner. The Council also took the view that senior leaders, not minor actors, should be the tribunals' priority.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council creates a pool of ad litem judges for the Yugoslavia tribunal. The pool holds 27 judges elected by the General Assembly, assigned to trials as needed for up to three years each. It enlarges the shared Appeals Chambers of both tribunals and orders two additional judges elected for the Rwanda tribunal, two of whose judges will sit on the Appeals Chambers. The statutes of both tribunals are amended by annexes to the resolution. A report on ending the Yugoslavia tribunal's temporal jurisdiction is also requested.

Stalemate itself is the subject of this Sahara text of 2002. On 30 July, the Council adopted Resolution 1429 without dissent. It stressed that the lack of progress was a grave concern. The territory's people kept suffering for it. The whole region faced the risk of unrest. The Maghreb's growth stayed blocked as well.

The Council had weighed the Secretary-General's February report. Four options for the territory sat in that report. The old vote plan stays valid, the text underlines. Deep gaps between the parties over it are noted all the same. Strong backing goes to the Secretary-General and his envoy. Their hunt for a political deal both sides can accept must press on.

Haiti's political, security, and humanitarian situation had collapsed into violence when this text passed on 29 February 2004. The country's president had resigned, and an acting president sworn in under the constitution appealed for urgent outside support. An emergency force is the Council's answer.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council authorized the immediate deployment of a Multinational Interim Force for no more than three months. Its tasks are to help restore order, support the constitutional process, protect human rights, and let aid workers reach people in need. States are called on to supply troops, equipment, and money at once. A longer-term United Nations force, the Council signals, will follow.

A narrow staffing decision for the Yugoslavia war crimes tribunal is made on 30 September 2005. Judge Christine Van Den Wyngaert had been elected a permanent judge, but her term was not due to start until 17 November 2005. The Council assigned her early, as a permanent judge, to the Mrksic case, which was due to open on 3 October 2005. The usual timing rules in the tribunal's Statute were set aside for this purpose.

The Golan Heights observer force is renewed for six months on 15 December 2006, until 30 June 2007. UNDOF continues its watch between Israeli and Syrian forces. The parties are called on to carry out resolution 338 of 1973 at once. The force's enforcement of the zero-tolerance policy on sexual exploitation and abuse is welcomed. A closing report on developments is asked for.

Resolution 1829, adopted on 4 August 2008, reshapes the UN presence in Sierra Leone once more. Calm local elections had been held in July 2008, and the army and police were growing more skilled. The earlier integrated office, UNIOSIL, was ending, and the Peacebuilding Commission was now working with the government on long-term needs.

The Council asks for a new United Nations Integrated Peacebuilding Office in Sierra Leone, UNIPSIL, for twelve months from 1 October 2008. Its work covers easing tensions before they turn into conflict. It also covers watching human rights and the rule of law. It backs the fight against corruption. It supports local government and a review of the 1991 constitution. The office must work closely with the Peacebuilding Commission, ECOWAS, and the Mano River Union. Reports are due every four months.

On 9 June 2010 the Security Council adopted Resolution 1929, a fourth round of sanctions on Iran over its nuclear program. The Council said Iran had still not met the demands of the International Atomic Energy Agency. Iran had not suspended its sensitive nuclear work. The text also reaffirmed the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons.

The new measures banned the sale to Iran of heavy weapons. The list covered tanks, combat aircraft, attack helicopters, and warships. Iran was barred from investing abroad in uranium mining and enrichment work. States were told to inspect suspect cargo and to block activity linked to missiles. They also had to watch dealings with Iranian banks and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. Long lists at the end name the companies and bodies placed under the sanctions.

Resolution 2029, adopted on 21 December 2011, keeps judges of the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda in post as the court heads toward closure. The tribunal was told to finish all work by 31 December 2014 and hand over to the International Residual Mechanism, whose Rwanda branch would start on 1 July 2012. Finding new homes for acquitted people and those who had finished their sentences remained a problem.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends the terms of four permanent trial judges and eight ad litem judges until 30 June 2012, or until their trials end. It presses UN bodies to help the tribunal keep the staff it needs. It urges all states to help catch and hand over the remaining fugitives. It praises states that have taken in acquitted people or those who finished their sentences, and asks others to do the same.

Keeping U Thant in office is the business of Resolution 229, adopted at a private meeting on 2 December 1966. The Burmese diplomat had served as Secretary-General since 1961, steering the United Nations through the Congo crisis and other Cold War strains. Council members praised his proven qualities and high sense of duty.

The Council recommends his appointment for another term, saying his return would serve the organization best. Under the Charter, the General Assembly makes the appointment, but only on the Council's recommendation. U Thant accepted a second term that ran until the end of 1971, making this short text part of the record of his decade leading the UN.

Applications to join the United Nations came back before the Council in 1947. A committee on new members had looked again at a long list of bids, from countries in Europe and beyond. Resolution 29 records the result of that review. The Council weighed the views its members had stated on each application. In the end it recommended to the General Assembly that two applicants be admitted: Yemen and Pakistan. The other bids in the round did not win the Council's backing at that time.

Zambia decided in 1973 to stop sending its trade along the southern route through Rhodesia. The boycott would last until the rebellion there ended and majority rule was established. The step backed the Council's sanctions, but it strained Zambia's economy. A special mission had reported on Zambia's urgent needs. Resolution 329 was adopted unanimously on 10 March 1973.

The Council praised Zambia's decision. It appealed to all states for immediate help. Technical, financial, and material aid were all requested. United Nations bodies were asked to organize assistance at once. Trade and development agencies were among those named. The help would let Zambia keep its traffic moving by other routes. It would also build Zambia's economic independence from the racist regime in Rhodesia.

The Golan watch rolled on with this renewal of 1978. On 31 May, the Council adopted Resolution 429. Fourteen members voted yes and none voted no. China took no part in the vote. The Secretary-General had reported on the observer force, UNDOF. The Council noted the push for a lasting Middle East peace. It voiced concern at the tension in the area.

The text calls on the parties to carry out Resolution 338 at once. It renews the observer mandate for six months, to 30 November 1978. A closing report from the Secretary-General is due then. The vote came two months after the Council built a new force for Lebanon.

Monaco's seat at the United Nations begins with Resolution 829, adopted on 26 May 1993. The Council weighed the bid of Monaco, a principality filed as document S/25796. The tiny city-state on the French Riviera had long kept a limited international profile, relying on France for defense while running its own affairs.

The Council recommends that the General Assembly admit Monaco to membership. The Assembly acted the same day, and Monaco took its seat. In the Assembly's one-state-one-vote system, the second-smallest country in the world votes as an equal of the largest. The resolution was adopted at the meeting right after the one recommending Eritrea, a busy week for admissions.
undset-the-snake-pit-olav-audunssn-i-192:
Olav Audunsson's story begins in The Snake Pit, the first book of Undset's second medieval saga, in Archer's 1929 English version. Olav, a landowner in thirteenth-century Norway, marries the woman he loves. She brings a hard secret into the marriage: a child by another man.

Honor, sin, and silence shape Olav's life from the wedding onward. Undset writes a sterner tale here than in the Kristin books. Love does not free her hero; it binds him to guilt and duty. Readers meet a man who will carry one dark choice for the rest of his days.
usama-ibn-munqidh-memoirs-hitti-1929:
Usama ibn Munqidh, a Syrian prince of the castle of Shayzar, fought the Crusaders, hunted with falcons, and served the courts of Damascus and Cairo. Late in life he wrote the Kitab al-I'tibar, the Book of Learning by Example. Philip Hitti translated it into English in 1929. It is the great personal memoir of the Crusader age from the Muslim side.

Usama tells of battles, sieges, hunts, and doctors, and of his odd friendships with Frankish knights. His tales of Frankish medicine and justice are famous, told with dry wonder. He writes as a man of eighty looking back on a world of war and courtesy. No other voice brings that age so close.
von-stein-mokele-mbembe-bolsche-1929:
A German trek brings back a tale of a live dinosaur in the report set in print by Wilhelm Bolsche in 1929. Bolsche quotes the notes of von Stein, who led a trek through the Congo in 1913 and 1914. Tribes there told of a vast beast in the swamps and streams, with a long neck and a bulk like an elephant, that kills hippos yet eats no flesh at all.

Von Stein took the tales as grave and matched. No beast was seen by his men. The report is the root source for the beast since named mokele-mbembe. All hunts since start here.
waite-holy-kabbalah-1929:
Waite traced the secret tradition of Israel through two thousand years in The Holy Kabbalah of 1929. The massive study follows Jewish Kabbalah and its Christian heirs in the West. Waite wrote as both scholar and mystic, a rare mix in his field.

He treats the Zohar, the schools of Spain and Safed, and the Christian scholars who took the lore up. His care is to sift the record from the myth that clings to it. The book was the standard English survey of its subject for its age. Students of Christian Kabbalah still keep it close at hand.
walker-appeal-1829: Walker's 1829 Appeal urged enslaved Blacks to revolt for freedom. The South banned it. The Tower library holds the full text. It cried resistance. Chains bound. Words freed. Courage sparked. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
whitehead-aims-education-1929:
The Aims of Education, published in 1929, collects Whitehead's essays on education, universities, and the rhythm of learning. Its title essay gives his famous standard: education is the art of the utilization of knowledge.

Whitehead attacks inert ideas, knowledge received and never used, as the chief enemy of schooling. He proposes a rhythm for learning: romance, precision, and generalization, repeated at every stage. Other essays treat the place of classics, mathematics, and technical training. The book influenced generations of teachers and university planners. Its prose has the ease of a master summarizing a lifetime's thought about how minds grow.
whitehead-function-reason-1929:
The Function of Reason, published in 1929, prints Whitehead's Princeton lectures on a neglected question: what reason is for. Against the view of reason as a judge sitting above life, he presents it as an organ of fresh life within life itself.

Reason, Whitehead argues, promotes the art of life in three ways: to live, to live well, and to live better. He traces reason's work from animal appetites to science and the slow climb of civilized life. The lectures are brief, aphoristic, and humane. They distill the spirit of his process thought into a defense of speculation itself.
whitehead-process-reality-1929:
Process and Reality, published in 1929, is Whitehead's complete system, built from the Gifford Lectures he gave at Edinburgh in 1927 and 1928. Its subtitle calls it an essay in cosmology. It proposes that the world's basic units are not things but events, moments of experience.

Everything, from electrons to God, is process: becoming, perishing, and passing value into what follows. The terms he coins are famously hard, yet the vision is generous, a universe of feeling and fresh creation. The book founded process philosophy and later fed process theology. It is among the boldest works of its kind in English.
wolfe-look-homeward-angel-1929:
Thomas Wolfe was twenty-nine, a Harvard-trained playwright teaching in New York, when Look Homeward, Angel appeared in 1929. He had written the huge manuscript in a flood, and editor Maxwell Perkins cut it into shape. Wolfe set it in Altamont, his barely disguised Asheville, North Carolina.

Eugene Gant grows up in his mother's boardinghouse, the youngest of a stormy, gifted family. His father carves tombstone angels, his brother Ben dies young, and Eugene hungers for everything: books, women, cities, fame. Wolfe's prose pours out in torrents of memory and appetite, too much and unforgettable at once. Asheville recognized itself and was furious. The novel is the most exuberant debut in American fiction.
woolf-room-of-ones-own-1929:
Virginia Woolf published A Room of One's Own in 1929, growing from lectures she gave at Cambridge women's colleges in 1928. Woolf asked why so few women had written great literature. Her answer became a founding claim of feminist literary criticism.

A woman must have money and a room of her own if she is to write fiction, Woolf argued. She imagined Shakespeare's sister, as gifted as her brother, crushed by a world that barred her from school and stage. Woolf traced women's writing from letters to novels as their material freedom grew. The essay's wit and anger still open courses on women and literature.
wurzburg-hexen-leut-verzeichnis-1629:
Names fill this 1629 print and little else: a list of the witch people burned at Würzburg. Verzeichnis der Hexen-Leut zu Würzburg names 157 men, women, and children put to the fire. The prince-bishop's hunt was then at its height in the German lands.

Clergy, councilors, wives, and young students stand in the roll beside the poor. Each line is one life ended by the court and the stake. The print was sold as news and warning in its own day. Few papers of the German hunts chill a reader more than this bare list.
